instruction: Explain Persistent vector for a Nim programmer: the problem it solves, when to use it and when not, and its cost.
output:
## Intent
A persistent array: a trie with 32 children per node, indexed five bits at a time. A read follows one root-to-leaf path; an update copies that one path and shares everything else, so the old vector stays valid.

## Use when / avoid when
- Use it for large indexed collections updated functionally: editors, snapshots, undo histories, state in a reducer.
- Use it when cheap `push` at the end and `get`/`updated` by index are all you need.
- Avoid it for front insertion and removal: use `skew_list` or `deque`.
- Avoid it when a plain `seq` is mutated locally and never shared: copying a `seq` is faster for small sizes.

## Complexity
| Operation | Time | Space |
|---|---|---|
| `get` | O(log32 n) | O(1) |
| `push`, `updated` | O(log32 n) nodes visited; each copied node holds up to 32 slots | O(log32 n) new nodes |
| `toSeq` | O(n log32 n) | O(n) |

instruction: Explain Red-black tree for a Nim programmer: the problem it solves, when to use it and when not, and its cost.
output:
## Intent
A balanced binary search tree kept balanced by node colours: the root is black, a red node has no red child, and every path from a node to a leaf has the same number of black nodes. Persistent insertion copies one path and rebalances locally.

## Use when / avoid when
- Use `RbMap` or `RbSet` when you need ordered iteration, a deterministic order or sorted output together with fast lookup.
- Use it when old versions of the map must stay valid.
- Avoid it for lookup-only maps with large keys sets where order does not matter: `hamt` has shallower paths.
- Avoid it if you need deletion in this package: it is not provided. Use `hamt` (which has `remove`) and sort when reading (`toSortedSeq`).

## Complexity
| Operation | Time | Space |
|---|---|---|
| `put`, `get`, `contains`, `incl` | O(log n) worst case | `put`: O(log n) new nodes |
| `toSeq` | O(n) | O(n) |
| `len` | O(1) | O(1) |

Height is at most 2 log2(n + 1).

instruction: Explain Segment tree for a Nim programmer: the problem it solves, when to use it and when not, and its cost.
output:
## Intent
An immutable tree over an array whose every node stores the combination of the elements below it, for a monoid (an associative `combine` with an `identity`). Range queries combine O(log n) stored values; a point update copies one path.

## Use when / avoid when
- Use it for repeated range sums, minima, maxima, gcds or any associative summary over an array that also receives point updates.
- Use it when old versions must stay valid (a persistent segment tree).
- Avoid it when the data never changes: a prefix-sum array answers sums in O(1).
- Avoid it when the operation is not associative: the result would depend on how the tree splits ranges.

## Complexity
| Operation | Time | Space |
|---|---|---|
| `fromSeq` | O(n) | O(n) |
| `query` | O(log n) | O(log n) stack |
| `updated` | O(log n) | O(log n) new nodes |
| `get`, `total` | O(log n), O(1) | O(1) |

instruction: Explain Skew-binary random-access list for a Nim programmer: the problem it solves, when to use it and when not, and its cost.
output:
## Intent
A persistent sequence that is as cheap as a cons list at the front and still supports indexing. It is a short list of complete binary trees whose sizes are 2^k - 1; because the sizes follow the skew-binary number system, adding an element never causes a long carry.

## Use when / avoid when
- Use it for a stack that also needs `get(i)` and functional `updated(i, x)`, for example environments, de Bruijn indices or functional arrays that grow at the front.
- Avoid it when you append at the back: use `pvector`.
- Avoid it when you never index: `cons_list` is simpler.

## Complexity
| Operation | Time | Space |
|---|---|---|
| `cons`, `head`, `tail` | O(1) worst case | O(1) new |
| `get`, `updated` | O(log n) | `updated`: O(log n) new nodes |
| `toSeq`, `fromSeq` | O(n) | O(n) |

instruction: Explain Generational slot map (handles into one owner) for a Nim programmer: the problem it solves, when to use it and when not, and its cost.
output:
## Intent
Several parts of a program often need to refer to the same thing: a unit, a connection, a node. The shortcut that compiles is a shared `ref` (and a lock or a counter around it), which allocates, hides who owns the value and makes every access pay for the sharing. A slot map keeps every value in one place, a flat `seq` of slots, and gives out a small `Handle` per value: the slot index and the generation the slot had. Other code keeps handles, not values, and asks the owner when it needs one. Removing a value bumps the slot's generation, so a handle to it is rejected even after the slot holds something else.

## Use when / avoid when
- Use it for entities, nodes and resources that are created, destroyed and referred to over time (game units, scene nodes, sessions, timers), when other data needs to point at them.
- Use it when a collection is read and changed in the same pass; the handles stay valid across the deferred changes (see `command_buffer`).
- Use `linked_list` when the order of the elements matters and splicing by handle is the point; the slot map has no order beyond slot order.
- Use `hash_table` when the key is meaningful outside the program (a name, an id from the outside). A handle is only meaningful to the map that issued it.
- Avoid it for a collection that is only appended and scanned: a `seq` is simpler.

## Complexity
| Operation | Time | Space |
|---|---|---|
| `get`, `contains`, `len`, `isEmpty` | O(1) | O(1) |
| `insert`, `put`, `remove` with the map moved in | O(1); `insert` into a new slot is amortised O(1) for the growth of the `seq` | O(1) extra; no allocation for `put`, `remove` or an `insert` into a freed slot |
| the same when the caller still uses the map it passed in | O(n): the slots are copied once | O(n) |
| `pairs` | O(slots), dead slots included | O(1) |
| `==`, `invariantsHold` | O(slots) | O(1) |

Measured with `-d:nimAllocStats` (tests/test_ds_slot_map.nim): 50 `put`s on maps of 10, 100 and 1000 values, each moved in, allocate nothing; the same 50 `put`s, each on a map the caller keeps reading afterwards, allocate 50 times (one copy of the slots per call). `m = m.put(h, x).map` also copies: the result tuple is a temporary and its field is copied out, so assign the result to a `let` first. A generation is an `int`; wrapping needs 2^63 removals of one slot.

instruction: Explain Sparse table for a Nim programmer: the problem it solves, when to use it and when not, and its cost.
output:
## Intent
Answer range queries in O(1) for an operation that tolerates overlap, after an O(n log n) build. Level `k` stores the combination of every window of `2^k` elements. A query over `[l, r)` combines two windows of the largest power-of-two size that fits, one at the left end and one at the right end; the windows overlap and together cover the range.

## Use when / avoid when
- Use it for static data queried many times with min, max, gcd, bitwise and, bitwise or: range minimum queries are the standard case.
- Avoid it when the data changes: use `segment_tree` (O(log n) update and query) instead.
- Avoid it when the operation is not idempotent (sum, product, xor, count): use `fenwick_tree` for sums or `segment_tree` for any monoid.
- Avoid it when n is huge and memory is tight: it stores n log n values.

## Complexity
| Operation | Time | Space |
|---|---|---|
| `fromSeq` | O(n log n) | O(n log n) |
| `query`, `get` | O(1) | O(1) |

instruction: Explain Splay tree for a Nim programmer: the problem it solves, when to use it and when not, and its cost.
output:
## Intent
A binary search tree that moves every key it touches to the root with zig, zig-zig and zig-zag rotations, so recently used keys are cheap to reach again. A classic splay tree does this by mutating on every read. A persistent value cannot, so here a lookup returns the answer together with the new tree, and the caller carries that tree forward.

## Use when / avoid when
- Use it for single-threaded access patterns with locality: a few keys asked for again and again, or sequential scans.
- Use it when you do not want to store balance information in the nodes.
- Avoid it when many readers hold the same version: the amortized bound does not apply to a version that is reused, and its deepest key costs O(n) every time. Reach for `rb_tree` or `treap`.
- Avoid it when worst-case per-operation time matters: a single operation can take O(n).

## Complexity
| Operation | Time | Space |
|---|---|---|
| `lookup`, `insert`, `delete` | O(log n) amortized when the returned tree is carried forward; O(n) worst case for one operation | O(path) new nodes |
| `contains`, `depthOf` | O(height), O(n) worst case | O(1) |
| `len`, `isEmpty`, `rootKey` | O(1) | O(1) |
| `toSeq` | O(n) | O(n) |

instruction: Explain Stack, queue and the monotonic stack for a Nim programmer: the problem it solves, when to use it and when not, and its cost.
output:
## Intent
A stack gives back the newest item first, a queue gives back the oldest item first. Both are small enough to be plain values here: `push`, `pop`, `enqueue` and `dequeue` return a new container. The monotonic stack is a technique built on a stack: scan once while the stack keeps its values in order, and each element leaves the stack exactly when its answer (for example the next greater element) is known.

## Use when / avoid when
- Use `Stack` for undo history, expression evaluation, depth-first search with an explicit stack and bracket matching, when old versions are rarely kept.
- Use `Queue` for breadth-first search and work lists in arrival order.
- Use `nextGreaterIndex` for "nearest later element that is greater" questions: stock spans, next warmer day, histogram areas.
- Use `cons_list` as a persistent stack and `bankers_queue` as a persistent queue when old versions must stay cheap: here every update copies the storage, O(n).
- Inside one routine, a local `var seq` with `add` and `pop` (or a `std/deques` `Deque`) is the fast shape, and it is allowed because no caller can see it. The monotonic stack below does that.

## Complexity
| Operation | Time | Space |
|---|---|---|
| `top`, `front`, `len`, `isEmpty` | O(1) | O(1) |
| `push`, `pop`, `enqueue`, `dequeue` | O(n): the storage is copied to keep the old version valid | O(n) |
| `nextGreaterIndex`, `nextGreater` | O(n) | O(n) |

instruction: Explain Suffix trie (and why not a suffix tree) for a Nim programmer: the problem it solves, when to use it and when not, and its cost.
output:
## Intent
A suffix structure stores every suffix of a text so that substring questions are answered by walking from the root: does a pattern occur, how often, which substring repeats. This page implements a suffix trie: one node per character, with a count of the suffixes through each node. It is simple and immutable, but has O(n^2) nodes, so it is for small texts and for learning.

A suffix tree is the compressed form: unary paths are merged into single edges labelled by text ranges, giving O(n) nodes, and Ukkonen's algorithm builds it in O(n) with suffix links and an end index shared and mutated while building. That construction does not fit this repository's persistent, value-only style without losing the O(n) bound, so it is not written here. For real texts use `suffix_array` (with its LCP array), which answers the same questions in O(n) space.

## Use when / avoid when
- Use it to see what a suffix tree answers, and as an oracle to test faster implementations on short strings.
- Use it when the text is a few hundred characters at most (`maxTextLen` is 400).
- Avoid it for real texts: the trie has up to n(n+1)/2 nodes. Use `suffix_array` in `nimcs/algo` (suffix array plus LCP array), which answers the same questions in O(n) space.
- A real suffix tree compresses unary paths and is built in O(n) by Ukkonen's algorithm. That construction relies on suffix links and end indices shared and mutated while building; it was not written here because it does not fit the persistent, value-only style without losing the O(n) bound.

## Complexity
| Operation | Time | Space |
|---|---|---|
| `buildSuffixTrie` | O(n^2 * sigma) for alphabet size sigma, because each of n suffixes copies a path of up to n nodes | O(n^2) nodes |
| `count`, `contains` | O(m * sigma) for a pattern of length m | O(1) |
| `distinctSubstrings`, `longestRepeated` | O(nodes) = O(n^2) | O(n) stack |
| `shortestAbsent` | O(nodes * sigma) | O(nodes) |

Compare with a suffix tree (O(n) space, O(m) search, Ukkonen O(n) build) and a suffix array (O(n) space, O(m log n) search).

instruction: Explain Treap for a Nim programmer: the problem it solves, when to use it and when not, and its cost.
output:
## Intent
An ordered set that is a binary search tree on the keys and a max-heap on a priority stored in each node. The priority is a fixed mixing function of a seed and the key, so the tree is balanced in expectation and, for one seed, its shape depends only on the key set, never on the insertion order. Updates are `split` and `merge`, which copy one path and share the rest.

## Use when / avoid when
- Use it when an ordered set must also be cut at a key (`split`) or joined with another set of a disjoint key range (`merge`) cheaply.
- Use it when a deterministic shape matters: the same seed and keys give the same tree on every run and in every insertion order, which makes tests and snapshots stable.
- Avoid it when a worst-case height bound is required: the bound is expected O(log n), not guaranteed. Reach for `rb_tree` instead.
- Avoid it for unordered lookup: `hamt` is the better fit.
- A skip list solves the same ordered-set problem with mutable towers of forward pointers; the treap is the persistent, deterministic choice here, so there is no skip list in this repository.

## Complexity
| Operation | Time | Space |
|---|---|---|
| `insert`, `delete`, `split`, `merge`, `contains` | O(log n) expected, O(n) worst case | O(log n) new nodes |
| `len`, `isEmpty` | O(1) | O(1) |
| `minKey`, `maxKey` | O(height) | O(1) |
| `toSeq`, `preorder` | O(n) | O(n) |

The expectation is over the seed: a priority function that behaves like random numbers gives expected height O(log n). An adversary who knows the seed and the function can choose keys that build a chain, so pick the seed from outside the data when the keys are untrusted.

instruction: Explain Persistent trie for a Nim programmer: the problem it solves, when to use it and when not, and its cost.
output:
## Intent
A set of strings stored as a tree of characters: the path from the root spells a word, and a flag marks where a word ends. Words with a common prefix share the nodes of that prefix, so prefix queries are a walk plus a traversal.

## Use when / avoid when
- Use it for autocompletion, prefix search, dictionary lookups and longest-prefix matching.
- Use it when the sorted list of words with a prefix is the answer you want.
- Avoid it for whole-key lookup only: `hamt` or `rb_tree` use less memory per key.
- Avoid it for huge alphabets with sparse children where a sorted `seq` of children would be scanned linearly; switch the child table to a map.

## Complexity
| Operation | Time | Space |
|---|---|---|
| `contains`, `hasPrefix` | O(L x alphabet) for a word of length L (linear scan of sorted children) | O(1) |
| `insert` | O(L x alphabet) | O(L) new nodes |
| `keysWithPrefix` | O(L + size of the output subtree) | O(output) |

instruction: Explain Persistent union-find for a Nim programmer: the problem it solves, when to use it and when not, and its cost.
output:
## Intent
Disjoint sets with `find` and `union`, built on persistent maps so that `union` returns a new structure and earlier versions stay valid. It answers "are a and b in the same group?" while allowing you to go back.

## Use when / avoid when
- Use it for backtracking search, speculative merges, undo, or any algorithm that revisits earlier states (offline connectivity with rollback, constraint solving).
- Use it for Kruskal-style algorithms when you need to keep intermediate forests.
- Avoid it when only the latest state matters and speed counts: use the imperative array version with path compression (near-constant amortized time). This one pays an O(log n) map lookup per step and, without compression, an O(log n) path.

## Complexity
| Operation | Time | Space |
|---|---|---|
| `find`, `same` | O(log n) links, each an O(log n) map lookup | O(1) |
| `union`, `add` | O(log n) plus the two finds | O(log n) new map nodes |
| `findCompress` | O(path length x log n) | new nodes for the compressed links |

instruction: Explain Write-ahead log for a Nim programmer: the problem it solves, when to use it and when not, and its cost.
output:
## Intent
Before a change is applied to the state, it is written to a log; after a crash the state is rebuilt by replaying the log. Here the log is a value: an append-only sequence of records, each with a sequence number and a CRC-32, that `replay` folds into state, `encode` turns into bytes and `recover` reads back, dropping a torn tail instead of trusting it.

## Use when / avoid when
- Use it when a state machine (a key-value store, a counter, an order book) must survive a crash and the log is the source of truth: the state is a pure function of the records.
- Use it to test recovery logic without a disk: cut or damage the bytes of `encode` at every position and check what `recover` keeps.
- Avoid it as the file layer itself: writing, `fsync`, truncating the file to `keptBytes`, segment rotation and checkpoints are effects and belong in the shell around this value. This page covers the value only.
- Avoid it when you need tamper evidence: CRC-32 finds accidental damage only; use a keyed MAC or a hash chain (`merkle_tree`) against an adversary.
- Avoid it when appends are the hot path of a very large log: `append` copies the record sequence (see Complexity); reach for a file-backed log or a persistent sequence such as `pvector`.

## Complexity
| Operation | Time | Space |
|---|---|---|
| `append` | O(n) in the records held (the value copies its sequence) plus O(payload) | O(n) new sequence |
| `appendAll` of k payloads | O(n + total payload) | O(n + k) |
| `replay` | O(n) calls of `apply` | what `apply` keeps |
| `encode`, `recover` | O(total bytes); `recover` also copies each record body once to check it | O(total bytes) |
| `at`, `len`, `nextSeq` | O(1) | O(1) |

instruction: Explain Zipper for a Nim programmer: the problem it solves, when to use it and when not, and its cost.
output:
## Intent
A zipper is a cursor into an immutable structure. It keeps the focused element and, in reverse, everything needed to put the structure back together. Moving the focus and replacing the focused element take constant time and share everything else.

## Use when / avoid when
- Use it for editors (text cursor), backtracking parsers, tree rewriting and "change this one place" updates.
- Use it when you navigate in small steps and edit near the focus.
- Avoid it when you transform every node: plain recursion is simpler.
- Avoid it for random access: use `pvector`.

## Complexity
| Operation | Time | Space |
|---|---|---|
| `moveLeft`, `moveRight`, `downLeft`, `downRight`, `up` | O(1) | O(1) new |
| `modify`, `replace`, `setFocus` | O(1) | O(1) new |
| `rebuild`, `toSeq` | O(depth) / O(n) | O(depth) / O(n) |

instruction: Explain Algebraic data types for a Nim programmer: the problem it solves, when to use it and when not, and its cost.
output:
## Intent
A closed set of shapes is one type with a variant per shape. A function over it is a `case` with one branch for each shape and no catch-all, so adding a shape makes the compiler point at every function that must handle it. Data that is only valid for one shape lives only in that shape's branch, which makes impossible states impossible to write.

## Use when / avoid when
- Use for expression trees, commands, events, protocol messages, tokens: anything with a fixed list of cases.
- Use an enum when the cases carry no data.
- Avoid class hierarchies with `method`: new operations then touch every class, and the compiler cannot check exhaustiveness.
- Avoid an object variant for an open set that plugins extend; use a table of functions or a `Result`-returning registry instead.

## Complexity
`eval`, `size`, `show` and `simplify` are O(n) in the number of nodes; recursion depth equals tree depth, so a degenerate tree of a million nodes can exhaust the stack. `simplify` allocates a new tree. `==` is O(n).

instruction: Explain Composition and pipelines for a Nim programmer: the problem it solves, when to use it and when not, and its cost.
output:
## Intent
Small functions become a program by being composed: the output of one is the input of the next. Composition is associative and has a neutral element (`identity`), so a pipeline can be grouped any way, split into pieces and reassembled without changing its meaning. `compose(f, g)` is "g, then f"; `andThen(f, g)` is the same function in reading order.

## Use when / avoid when
- Use when the same chain of steps is applied in many places or built from a list at run time.
- Use plain method-call chains (`input.parse.validate.render`) when the steps are fixed at the call site; Nim's call syntax is already a pipeline.
- Avoid composing functions that can fail with unrelated error types: chain them with `flatMap` on `Result` (see `result.md`).
- Avoid deep closure stacks in hot code: each composed step is a closure call.

## Complexity
Building a composition is O(1) (`composeAll`: O(k) to copy k steps). Calling it costs the sum of its steps plus one closure call per step. Fusing two maps halves the number of passes and the intermediate sequences.

instruction: Explain Equational reasoning for a Nim programmer: the problem it solves, when to use it and when not, and its cost.
output:
## Intent
In pure code, `let y = f(x); y + y` and `f(x) + f(x)` mean the same, and a short argument can show that two whole routines are equal. That lets you refactor by substituting equals for equals: fuse stages, drop a repeated step, replace a loop with a formula. The argument is the proof; a property test on generated inputs is the evidence that the argument has no hole.

## Use when / avoid when
- Use to speed up or simplify a pure pipeline without changing what it computes, and to explain why a rewrite is safe.
- Use a property test of `old(x) == new(x)` on generated inputs next to every such rewrite.
- Avoid it where a step has an effect (printing, a counter, randomness, time): substituting a call by its value, or the reverse, changes the program.
- Avoid it on floating-point sums and products: `(a + b) + c` and `a + (b + c)` can differ, so reassociation is not an equal step there. Rewrite exact integer arithmetic freely.

## Complexity
The fused pipeline is one pass with O(1) extra space; the staged one is O(n) time per stage and O(n) extra space per intermediate list. The closed form is O(1) against the loop's O(n). The chunked count is O(n) in total, and the chunks are independent, which is what permits splitting the work.

instruction: Explain Fold for a Nim programmer: the problem it solves, when to use it and when not, and its cost.
output:
## Intent
A fold reduces a sequence to one value by feeding each element and the accumulator so far to a step function. Sum, count, maximum, reverse, map and filter are all folds that differ only in the step and the starting value. Writing the step as a pure function makes the loop trivial to reason about; `scan` keeps every intermediate value and `unfold` goes the other way, from a seed to a sequence.

## Use when / avoid when
- Use when a result is built by visiting every element once, in order.
- Use `scan` when the running values matter (prefix sums, balances over time).
- Use `unfold` to generate a bounded sequence from a state (countdown, Collatz steps).
- Avoid a fold when the loop needs early exit on a condition: write a `for` with `return`, or `lazy_stream.md` for lazy pipelines.
- Avoid when a standard routine says it better (`sum`, `max`, `sorted`).

## Complexity
`foldLeft`, `foldRight` and `scan`: O(n) steps, O(1) extra space for the fold (`scan`: O(n) for the result). A step that grows the accumulator (appending to a `seq` by `&`) makes the whole fold O(n^2); keep the accumulator constant-size or use a local `add` loop.

instruction: Explain Functor, applicative and monad for a Nim programmer: the problem it solves, when to use it and when not, and its cost.
output:
## Intent
A functor is a container with a `map` that changes what is inside and leaves the shape alone; an applicative can also combine independent containers (`ap`, `map2`); a monad can run a step whose next step depends on the previous result (`flatMap`). The names describe shapes that `Option`, `Result`, `seq` and `Stream` already share. Naming the shape tells you which laws each type must obey and which operation to reach for.

## Use when / avoid when
- Use `map` when a pure function changes the content and the container's case (present / absent, ok / error) must not change.
- Use `map2` or `ap` to combine values that do not depend on each other; use `flatMap` when a later step needs an earlier value (`Result` railway, list of choices).
- Avoid `flatMap` where `map2` is enough: the independent form shows readers that no step depends on another.
- Avoid inventing a shared `Functor` type: see "What Nim's types cannot say" below. Write each type its own `map`, and a duck-typed generic when one routine must serve several.

## Complexity
`Option` and `Result` operations are O(1). `ap` on lists is O(|fs| * |xs|) time and space; `flatMap` on `seq` is linear in the total length of the produced lists. `Stream` `map` is O(1) to build and costs when pulled.

instruction: Explain Idempotence for a Nim programmer: the problem it solves, when to use it and when not, and its cost.
output:
## Intent
An operation is idempotent when doing it twice has the same effect as doing it once: `f(f(x)) == f(x)`. That is what makes retries safe. A client that does not know whether its request arrived can send it again; a store that merges a set, upserts by key, or applies a command identified by an idempotency key ends in the same state either way. The idea is a law, so it is tested as a property.

## Use when / avoid when
- Use for normal forms (trim, canonical case, sorted unique), set insertion, upsert by key, and any command that may be delivered more than once.
- Use an idempotency key for operations that are not naturally idempotent (a payment, a counter increment): record the key, ignore a repeat.
- Avoid claiming idempotence for "add 1" or "append": they change the result every time.
- Avoid one global "seen" set shared by unrelated operations; keep the keys with the state they guard.

## Complexity
`normalizeSpaces` is O(n). `setInsert` and `apply` find the position in O(log n) and rebuild the sequence in O(n). `upsertByKey` is O(n). For large state use a persistent map or a set structure from the `ds` area.

instruction: Explain Immutable update for a Nim programmer: the problem it solves, when to use it and when not, and its cost.
output:
## Intent
Instead of changing a value in place, an update takes the old value and returns a new one; the old one stays valid. Every earlier version can still be read, compared or restored, and no other holder of the old value is surprised. Nim makes this cheap and safe: objects and sequences are values, assignment copies, and a `sink` parameter lets the compiler move instead of copy when the caller is done with the old value.

## Use when / avoid when
- Use for domain values (carts, accounts, settings, parsed documents) that several parts of a program read.
- Use when undo, history or "what did it look like before" is wanted.
- Avoid copying very large structures per update: use a persistent structure that shares nodes (see the `ds` area, for example a banker's queue or a persistent map).
- Avoid for a hot inner loop where one local `var` is enough and nobody else sees it.

## Complexity
Each update here copies the item sequence: O(n) time and space for n items, which is fine for small values. Moves (`sink` with a last use) avoid the copy but the update still touches O(n) for `removed`. For large collections use a persistent structure with O(log n) updates.

instruction: Explain Lazy streams for a Nim programmer: the problem it solves, when to use it and when not, and its cost.
output:
## Intent
A lazy stream computes an element only when it is asked for. `map`, `filter`, `take` and `takeWhile` build a new stream without doing any work and without allocating an intermediate sequence; `toSeq(limit)` finally pulls the elements through the whole pipeline once. Because a stream is an immutable value, it can be walked again with the same result, and infinite streams are safe as long as something cuts them.

## Use when / avoid when
- Use for "the first k things that satisfy a property" over an unbounded or very large source.
- Use to keep a multi-stage pipeline from allocating a sequence per stage.
- Avoid when the data is small: an eager `seq` pipeline is simpler and faster.
- Avoid a `filter` on an infinite stream that never matches: pulling it never returns. Cut with `takeWhile` first when you can.
- For a one-shot walk inside one routine, Nim's own `iterator`s are lighter than a stream value.

## Complexity
Building a stage is O(1). Pulling one element through k stages costs O(k) plus the cost of skipped elements in `filter`. `fromSeq` copies the input once and its stages then share that block (O(1) per step). Each pull allocates a small closure; the memory in use is proportional to the pipeline depth, not to the number of elements walked. Walking the same stream twice repeats the work (no caching).

instruction: Explain Monoid for a Nim programmer: the problem it solves, when to use it and when not, and its cost.
output:
## Intent
A monoid is a way to combine two values (`combine`) together with a value that changes nothing (`empty`). Two laws make it one: identity (`combine(empty, x) == x == combine(x, empty)`) and associativity (`combine(combine(a, b), c) == combine(a, combine(b, c))`). Associativity lets a fold group its work any way, such as splitting a list across threads and combining the halves, and identity gives an empty input a natural answer.

## Use when / avoid when
- Use for aggregates: totals, maxima, concatenation, merging records or tables, collecting statistics.
- Use `foldMap` to map and combine in one pass.
- Avoid when there is no neutral element (the average, for example, is not a monoid; keep a sum and a count, which is).
- Avoid assuming commutativity: string concatenation is associative but order matters.

## Complexity
`mconcat` and `foldMap` are O(n) combines and O(1) extra space. Merging two tables is O(size of the second) combines. A `combine` that copies (`seq` concatenation) makes a left fold O(n^2) in total length.

instruction: Explain Option operations for a Nim programmer: the problem it solves, when to use it and when not, and its cost.
output:
## Intent
`Option[T]` states in the type that a value may be absent. Compared with a sentinel (`-1`, `""`, `nil`) it cannot be mistaken for real data, and the compiler makes the caller look at it. The standard library covers the basics; `nimcs/fp/option_ops` adds what is missing when options meet each other or meet `Result`.

## Use when / avoid when
- Use when "not found" or "not given" is an ordinary answer.
- Use `okOr` when the caller needs a reason; the absence then joins a `Result` railway.
- Avoid sentinels: a `-1` index flows into arithmetic without a complaint.
- Avoid `Option` when the reason matters: use `Result` (see `result.md`).

## Complexity
All operations are O(1), except `sequence`, `catSome` and `firstSome`, which are O(n) in the list length (`firstSome` stops at the first hit). `sequence` and `catSome` allocate one result sequence.

instruction: Explain Phantom types for a Nim programmer: the problem it solves, when to use it and when not, and its cost.
output:
## Intent
A phantom type parameter appears in a type's name but not in its data: `Id[User]` and `Id[Order]` are both an `int` at run time and are different types to the compiler. The parameter is a label that the type checker compares, so mixing two kinds of id, adding metres to seconds, or passing unchecked text where checked text is required becomes a compile error and costs nothing at run time.

## Use when / avoid when
- Use for identifiers of different entities that are all integers or strings (`Id[User]`, `Id[Order]`).
- Use for quantities with units (`Quantity[Meter]`), where the unit change must be an explicit function.
- Use for a state that a routine requires (`Email[Validated]`): the type records that a check ran.
- Avoid it when the value must be unforgeable. A `distinct` type can be converted explicitly by any caller (`Email[Validated]("x")` compiles); use an object with a private field and a smart constructor (`smart_constructor.md`).
- Avoid it when a run-time value is needed to tell the cases apart (a tag read from a file); use an object variant (`adt.md`).

## Complexity
No run-time cost: the types have the representation of `int` or `string`, and each wrapper or unwrapper is a conversion that disappears in the generated C. `validateEmail` is O(length of the text).

instruction: Explain Result railway for a Nim programmer: the problem it solves, when to use it and when not, and its cost.
output:
## Intent
A routine that can fail for a reason returns `Result[T, E]`: either `ok` with a value or `err` with the reason. Steps are chained with `flatMap`, so the first failure stops the chain and its reason is what the caller sees, with no exception and no sentinel value. The signature tells the caller that failure is possible and what kind.

## Use when / avoid when
- Use when failure is expected and the caller must decide what to do (parsing, validation, lookup that needs a reason).
- Use when several fallible steps run in sequence and the first failure should win.
- Avoid for plain absence with no reason: use `Option[T]` (see `option_ops.md`).
- Avoid for broken preconditions the caller could have checked: that is a `Defect`, not an error value.
- In an application that already depends on the `results` package, keep using that; this module only resembles it (`ok` and `err` take a type argument, and `.value` on an error raises), so do not mix the two.

## Complexity
Every operation is O(1) apart from the cost of the callback. A `Result` is stored inline; no allocation happens for the railway itself.

instruction: Explain Smart constructors for a Nim programmer: the problem it solves, when to use it and when not, and its cost.
output:
## Intent
A domain value (a username, a quantity, an email) is checked once, at the boundary, by a constructor that returns `Result`. After that, the program carries a type that cannot be wrong, so no other function checks again. This is "parse, don't validate": the output of parsing is a different type from its input, and the type is the proof. The proof only holds if no other code can build the type: a `distinct` type does not give that (see Pitfalls), a sealed object does.

## Use when / avoid when
- Use for every value that has rules: ranges, lengths, alphabets, units, identifiers.
- Make the type a sealed object (private field, `{.requiresInit.}`) when it must guarantee a rule; use a `distinct` type for units and identifiers that only need to stay apart from other types.
- Avoid validating in many places "to be safe": that spreads the rule and lets copies drift apart.
- Avoid a sealed type for values with no rule and no mixing risk; a plain type is enough.
- Avoid trusting `distinct` alone to carry an invariant: `Quantity(5000)` compiles anywhere, and `var q: Quantity` is 0.

## Complexity
Parsing a username is O(length); a quantity is O(1). A sealed object with one field has the size of that field; a `distinct` type has no run-time cost at all.

instruction: Explain Tail recursion and loops for a Nim programmer: the problem it solves, when to use it and when not, and its cost.
output:
## Intent
A recursive routine whose last action is the recursive call is in tail form: nothing is left to do afterwards, so in principle its frame could be reused. Nim does not guarantee that. Whether a tail call becomes a jump depends on the C compiler and its settings, so a recursion that goes as deep as its input is not safe for large inputs even in tail form. The reliable pattern is: find the invariant with a recursion, carry the partial result in an accumulator argument, then write the final routine as a loop with local `var`s.

## Use when / avoid when
- Use plain recursion when the depth is small and bounded by the structure (a balanced tree's height, a handful of levels) and the recursive form is the clearest statement of the idea.
- Use the accumulator form to derive the loop: the accumulator arguments become the loop's local variables.
- Use the loop for anything whose depth grows with `n` or with the length of a list.
- Avoid exponential recursion (`fibNaive`) beyond tiny inputs; the accumulator form is linear.

## Complexity
`sumTo*`: O(n) time; the naive and accumulator recursions use O(n) stack unless the backend reuses frames (not guaranteed), the loop O(1). `fibNaive` is exponential in time; `fibAcc` and `fibLoop` are O(n) time. `gcd*` is O(log min(a, b)) time.

instruction: Explain Type classes: concepts and generics for a Nim programmer: the problem it solves, when to use it and when not, and its cost.
output:
## Intent
A type class is "any type that supports these operations". In Nim a plain generic `[T]` is parametric polymorphism (one body for every `T`, which may only move values around), and a generic with a `concept` constraint (`[T: Orderable]`) is a constrained one (the body may use the operations the concept names). An instance is just a type that defines those operations. The compiler checks that the operations exist; whether they obey the laws of the class is yours to test, once per instance.

## Use when / avoid when
- Use a `concept` when one routine must serve several unrelated types (`maxOf` for `int`, `string`, your `Version`).
- Use a plain `[T]` when the routine never looks inside the value (`backwards`, `swap`, `map`): it then works for every type and the compiler rejects any use of an operation `T` is not known to have.
- Avoid a `concept` for a closed set of shapes that you own; an object variant (`adt.md`) is checked for exhaustiveness, a concept is not.
- Avoid expecting a concept to state a law: it can say `(x < y) is bool`, not "`<` is transitive". Put the law in a property test.

## Complexity
Constrained generics are resolved at compile time, one specialised copy per instance type: no dispatch cost at run time, more code. `maxOf`, `minOf`, `isSorted` are O(n); `insertSorted` is O(n) and allocates a new sequence; `isTotalOrderOn` is O(1) per triple.

instruction: Explain Typestate for a Nim programmer: the problem it solves, when to use it and when not, and its cost.
output:
## Intent
Some values are legal for different operations at different times: a draft may be written, a published blob may only be read. Keep the state in the type (`Blob[Draft]`, `Blob[Published]`), give each operation the state it is right for, and let a transition (`publish`) take one state and return the other. Then an operation that is wrong in a state does not compile, instead of being a check that somebody has to remember to run.

The defect this prevents: a file server let a client write a temporary file and then rename it into a content-addressed area, after which it had to be read-only. The policy kept treating the open handle by its old temporary path, so the client could still overwrite content that had been verified. The state ("still a draft" or "published") lived in a path string next to the handle, and nothing connected the two. With typestate, "a draft you may write" and "a published, read-only blob" are different types, `publish` consumes the draft and returns the published value, and `write` on a published value does not compile.

## Use when / avoid when
- Use when an operation is legal only in some states and the state changes through your own code (open and closed, draft and published, unverified and verified, connected and disconnected).
- Use when a wrong-state call is expensive: it corrupts verified data, leaks a resource, or sends a message that cannot be taken back.
- Use at the boundary where the state becomes known at run time (a record read from disk): one checked constructor per state turns the unchecked record into the typed value, so everything after it is checked by the compiler.
- Avoid it when the state is only ever known at run time and changes in a loop driven by input (a protocol reading arbitrary messages): use an object variant and `Result` (`state_machine.md`), the compiler cannot follow a state chosen by data.
- Avoid it for a value with one legal state and a rule on its content: that is a smart constructor (`smart_constructor.md`), not a typestate.
- Avoid a type per state when two states differ only in one flag nobody branches on; a field is enough.

## Complexity
Zero run-time cost for the states: `Draft` and `Published` are never constructed, and `Blob[Draft]` and `Blob[Published]` are each exactly one `string`, as large as a `string` (FP-TYPESTATE-08); the checks happen at compile time. The operations cost what the data costs: `write` and `publish` copy the bytes (O(n)), `contentId` reads them once (O(n)). The bridge costs one comparison for a draft and one digest for a published record. A `static` enum parameter has the same zero cost; a variant with `Result` pays a tag and a branch per call.

instruction: Explain Abstract Factory for a Nim programmer: the problem it solves, when to use it and when not, and its cost.
output:
## Intent
A client needs several products that must belong together (all widgets of one theme) and must not
name their concrete shape. The OO pattern is an interface with one `createX()` per product. In
Nim, the family is a plain object whose fields are proc values; choosing the family is choosing
one value of that object.

## Use when / avoid when
- Use when two or more products must stay mutually consistent and the family is picked once
  (theme, platform, vendor).
- Use a single proc value (`factory_method.md`) when there is only one product.
- Avoid when products do not constrain each other: just pass them separately.
- Avoid growing the kit casually: adding a product means touching every family. If the set of
  products is open, use a `Table` of named procs instead.

## Complexity
Constructing a kit allocates its closures once; each product call is an indirect call. Keep the kit
in a `let` and reuse it.

instruction: Explain Actor for a Nim programmer: the problem it solves, when to use it and when not, and its cost.
output:
## Intent
Concurrent parties that share nothing and talk only by messages. The usual object version gives each actor a mutable inbox and a mutable handler, run by threads, so ordering, "become" (changing behaviour) and failure live in hidden state. In functional Nim an actor is one pure transition `step(self, state, msg): Reaction`: the next state and a list of effects as data (send a message to an address, spawn an actor, stop). A mailbox is a persistent FIFO value. A host loop that is not part of the actor delivers one message at a time and performs the effects, so the behaviour is tested without threads, timers or mocks, and a message log replays to the same states.

## Use when / avoid when
- Use when many independent parties each own some state and communicate asynchronously: sessions, devices, workers, game entities, protocol endpoints.
- Use instead of `observer.md` when parties must keep a private state and a private order of messages rather than all folding one shared event; use instead of `state.md` alone when the machine also talks to other machines (its transitions emit sends); use instead of `command.md` when the receiver is a long-lived party with an address, not a value applied to one state.
- Use `request_reply.md` for asking and `supervisor.md` for failure; neither is part of this page.
- Avoid when one state with one reducer is enough (`observer.md`, `state.md`): addresses and mailboxes add nothing there.
- Avoid when the effect must happen in the middle of a decision and feed its result back at once; a message round trip is slower than a call.

## Complexity
`tell` and `take` are amortised O(1) when each mailbox version is used once. `deliver` is O(1) plus the cost of `step` and of copying the state and the actor table (the reference host copies `cells` per delivery, O(actors)); a production host keeps its tables in mutable storage and uses the same `step`. `runRounds` is O(budget) deliveries.

instruction: Explain Adapter for a Nim programmer: the problem it solves, when to use it and when not, and its cost.
output:
## Intent
Existing code produces or expects one shape; the new code uses another. The OO pattern wraps an
object in a class that implements the interface the client expects. In Nim the "interface" is a
type, so the adapter is a **func between two types**. Adapting a source of values is mapping that
func over what the source returns.

## Use when / avoid when
- Use at the boundary where a foreign shape enters (legacy strings, a third-party record, a wire
  format): convert once, then use only the domain type inside.
- Make the conversion total: return a `Result` with a specific error, never raise.
- Avoid adapting in place deep inside the code, so that the foreign shape spreads.
- Avoid an adapter class holding the adaptee as a field with forwarding methods: a func does it.

## Complexity
O(length of the input) per conversion; `adaptAll` is O(total length). No allocation besides the result.

instruction: Explain Anti-corruption layer for a Nim programmer: the problem it solves, when to use it and when not, and its cost.
output:
## Intent
Translate a foreign model at the border so it never leaks inward. Another system's model has its own words, codes and number formats, and it changes when its owners decide. The layer is the only place that knows both models. It turns a foreign record into your own type through the same smart constructor as every order of your own, and turns it back when you must send one. Your code takes your type and cannot be handed a foreign record.

## Use when / avoid when
- Use when a model you do not control meets one you do: a supplier's message format, a legacy database, a partner's API.
- Use when the foreign model changes or comes in several versions: each version is one more pair of functions and nothing inward moves.
- Avoid between two parts of your own model: translation there hides a design that should be shared.
- Avoid when the foreign model is the one you want; then adopt it openly and say so, rather than wrapping it.

## Complexity
Each translation is O(length of the record). `translateAll` is O(batch size) and keeps the refusals in memory.

instruction: Explain Atomic publish (temporary name, fsync, rename, fsync the directory) for a Nim programmer: the problem it solves, when to use it and when not, and its cost.
output:
## Intent
Replace a file so that a reader sees the old content or the new content, never a part of it, and so that this still holds if the machine stops at any instant. Write the new content under a temporary name in the same directory, flush it to the disk, rename it onto the visible name, then flush the directory. The rename is the only moment the visible name changes; before it the reader has the old file, after it the new one.

## Use when / avoid when
- Use for a file that others read while you replace it: a configuration, an index, a manifest, a cache entry, a downloaded artifact that a build reads.
- Use when a crash in the middle must not leave the visible name empty or cut; a program that restarts and finds a half-written config has lost more than the write.
- Use with `idempotent_command.md`: publishing the same content again changes nothing, so a retried command is safe.
- Use a name that is the hash of the content (see Nim shape) when the same content may be published many times or by many writers; the name then says what the file must contain.
- Avoid it for a file that is appended to in place, such as a log or a journal. Appending cannot be done by renaming; use an append-only file with a checksum per record (`event_sourcing.md`).
- Avoid it across directories on different file systems: `rename` is atomic only inside one file system, so the temporary file must be made in the target's directory, never in `/tmp`.
- Avoid it when the data may be lost by design (a cache that is rebuilt on a miss): the two fsyncs cost milliseconds each, and `smNone` or a plain write is enough.

## Complexity
Time: O(n) in the content length for the write, plus two fsyncs, which dominate (milliseconds on a disk). The model's `apply` copies the directory value: O(files). Space: the content once more on disk until the rename.

instruction: Explain Branch by abstraction for a Nim programmer: the problem it solves, when to use it and when not, and its cost.
output:
## Intent
Replace an implementation inside the trunk, behind an interface, in small steps, instead of on a long-lived branch. First the callers are moved behind an abstraction that the old implementation fills. Then the new implementation is written behind the same abstraction. A stage value says which one answers: old, shadow (the old answers while both run and a mismatch is reported) or new. The callers do not change when the stage does.

## Use when / avoid when
- Use when a replacement takes many commits, other work must keep landing on the trunk, and the replacement cannot be reached from outside by a route table.
- Use when you want evidence that the new implementation agrees with the old one on real inputs before it answers.
- Avoid when the replacement fits in one commit.
- Avoid when the two implementations cannot both run: the shadow stage needs it, so without it the stage collapses to a switch.
- Remove the losing side when the stage reaches new for good; an abstraction with one implementation and a dead switch is clutter.

## Complexity
The shadow stage runs both implementations, so it costs the sum of the two. The other stages cost one.

instruction: Explain Bridge for a Nim programmer: the problem it solves, when to use it and when not, and its cost.
output:
## Intent
Two dimensions vary independently (shapes and rendering backends). With inheritance that is a class
per pair. The OO pattern splits them: an abstraction holds a reference to an implementation
interface. The saving (N + M definitions instead of N x M) exists only if the implementation side
is a small **fixed** set of primitives that every abstraction lowers to. Here the primitive is a
single `line`: a `Backend` is an object with one proc field, a `Shape` lowers itself to line
segments (`lower`), and `draw` feeds the segments to the backend. A new shape adds one `lower` case
and touches no backend; a new backend adds one `line` proc and touches no shape.

## Use when / avoid when
- Use when two independent axes would otherwise multiply (shape x backend, message x transport,
  report x output format) **and** you can name a small primitive set that sits between them.
- Use a generic proc over the backend type when the backend is fixed at compile time and you want
  static dispatch; the record of procs is for choosing at run time.
- Avoid giving the backend one primitive per shape kind (`rect`, `circle`, ...): then every new
  shape edits every backend, the axes are coupled, and it is not a bridge.
- Avoid when one axis has a single value: a plain proc is enough.

## Complexity
`draw` is O(segments of the shape) plus the backend's cost per segment; `drawAll` is O(total
segments). Each backend call is an indirect call. Circles are an octagon: precision is traded for
the fixed primitive.

instruction: Explain Builder for a Nim programmer: the problem it solves, when to use it and when not, and its cost.
output:
## Intent
An object has many settings, some optional, with rules that span several fields (TLS needs a
certificate). The OO pattern collects settings in a mutable builder. In Nim the builder is an
immutable value: each `withX` returns a changed copy, and `build` is the single place that checks
the whole combination and returns a `Result`. The finished `ServerConfig` can only exist valid.

## Use when / avoid when
- Use when a record has more than a few settings, defaults, or cross-field rules.
- Use a plain object constructor with named arguments when there are few fields and no cross-field
  rule; Nim's `Foo(a: 1, b: 2)` is already a builder.
- Avoid a `bool` parameter per option (BN-02); each `withX` names the option.
- Avoid a mutable builder with `var` setters: the old state is lost and a half-built builder can
  leak.

## Complexity
Each setter copies the builder: O(size of builder), which is a handful of fields. `build` is O(1)
in the number of checks. If a builder grows large collections, hold them in a persistent structure
instead of a `seq`.

instruction: Explain Bulkhead for a Nim programmer: the problem it solves, when to use it and when not, and its cost.
output:
## Intent
One shared pool of workers lets a single slow tenant or dependency hold every worker, and then everyone waits. A bulkhead gives each compartment its own number of permits, so overload stays inside the compartment that caused it. The whole state is one value (limit and permits in use per compartment); admission is a pure function that returns the new value and the answer.

## Use when / avoid when
- Use around calls that share a scarce resource and can be grouped: per tenant, per downstream service, per priority class.
- Use when a refusal is acceptable and can be handled by the caller (fail fast, queue, shed).
- Avoid it for limiting a rate over time; that is `token_bucket.md`. A bulkhead limits calls in flight.
- Avoid deciding by queue length or deadline here; `load_shedding.md` does that, and the two combine: the bulkhead protects capacity per compartment, shedding protects latency in the queue.

## Complexity
`tryAcquire` and `release` copy the two tables, so they are O(c) in the number of compartments c (the price of returning a new value and keeping the old one valid); with a persistent map they would be O(log c). `usage` is O(c log c). Space is O(c).

instruction: Explain Caretaker for a Nim programmer: the problem it solves, when to use it and when not, and its cost.
output:
## Intent
Revocable forwarding. A caretaker gives a client a forwarder, a capability that passes operations on to a target, and keeps a revoker, the capability that cuts the forwarder off. Before revocation the forwarder behaves like the target; after it, every use fails with an error value. Classic caretakers use a mutable cell that all forwarders read. Here the revocation state is data threaded through the calls: `forward` takes the caretaker as an argument and `revoke` returns a new one whose slot has dropped the target.

## Use when / avoid when
- Use when a grant must be taken back: a session token, a plugin's access, a lease, a delegated capability (`object_capability.md`).
- Use when the caretaker can live in the one place that owns the resource, such as an actor's state (`actor.md`) or a store threaded through the program, and clients call through that owner.
- Use instead of an expiry check inside the target (`proxy.md` with a flag): the target does not know about revocation and cannot forget to check it.
- Avoid when independent parties must see a revocation immediately without passing through any owner. Then a shared mutable cell (a `ref` read by every forwarder) is the right tool: it gives up the value semantics and the replayable laws, so confine it to that edge and say so.
- Avoid for a grant that only expires with time: pass the tick and compare (`retry_backoff.md` shows time as data).

## Complexity
`wrap`, `forward`, `revoke` and `isRevoked` are O(log32 n) in the number of forwarders; `liveCount` is O(n log n).

instruction: Explain Chain of Responsibility for a Nim programmer: the problem it solves, when to use it and when not, and its cost.
output:
## Intent
A request should be handled by the first of several candidates that is willing, without the sender knowing which. The OO pattern links handler objects, each holding its successor. In functional Nim a handler is `proc(request): Option[Response]` and a chain is a plain `seq` of them: "pass it on" is moving to the next element and the answer is the first `some`. The linked structure disappears.

## Use when / avoid when
- Use for approvals by authority, middleware, parsers that try alternatives, fallbacks (cache, then disk, then network), validation rules where the first failing rule answers.
- Use `orElse` to build handlers in pieces: it is associative with `never` as identity, so chains nest freely.
- Avoid when every handler must run (that is a pipeline or `observer`).
- Avoid when the handler choice is a simple lookup by key: use a table.

## Complexity
`firstSome` is O(h) handler calls in the worst case for h handlers and stops at the first answer, so the cost depends on how early the answering handler sits (order cheap or common handlers first). `orElse` allocates one closure per combination; deeply nested `orElse` adds one call frame per level.

instruction: Explain Circuit breaker for a Nim programmer: the problem it solves, when to use it and when not, and its cost.
output:
## Intent
Calling a dependency that keeps failing makes every caller wait for a timeout and keeps the dependency loaded while it tries to recover. A breaker watches the outcomes and refuses calls for a while once failures persist, then lets one probe call through to find out whether the dependency is back. Here the breaker is an object variant (closed, open, half-open) whose transitions are pure functions of the breaker, the config and the time passed in.

## Use when / avoid when
- Use around calls to a remote service, a database or any dependency that can be down for longer than one retry.
- Use together with `retry_backoff.md`: backoff spaces out the retries of one caller, the breaker stops every caller once the failures are persistent.
- Avoid it for failures caused by the request itself (a bad argument): they say nothing about the dependency's health, so do not report them as failures.
- Avoid a breaker per call site when many sites share one dependency; share one value (or one per dependency) so they see the same failures.

## Complexity
Every operation is O(1) time and space; the breaker is one small value.

instruction: Explain Command for a Nim programmer: the problem it solves, when to use it and when not, and its cost.
output:
## Intent
A request must be stored, logged, replayed or reversed. The OO pattern turns the request into an object with `execute` and `undo`. In functional Nim the command is data (an object variant), execution is a pure function `apply(state, command): Result[state, Error]`, and undo is another command: the inverse, computed from the state before the edit. The invoker, receiver and "command object" collapse into a value, a function and a list.

## Use when / avoid when
- Use when operations must be replayable (event log, test script), serialisable, undoable or sent over a wire.
- Use inverse commands when states are large and edits are small; use `memento` snapshots when states are small or structurally shared and the inverse is hard to compute.
- Avoid when you only need "call this later": store a closure (see `strategy`) instead of inventing a command type.
- Avoid when there is no undo and no log: a plain function call is the command.

## Complexity
`apply` is O(n) in the text length (strings are rebuilt); `inverse` is O(len of the removed text). Each `exec`/`undo`/`redo` copies the stacks (`&` allocates), so a long history costs O(h) per step; use a persistent list from `ds` when h is large. Space is O(sum of removed or inserted text).

instruction: Explain Command buffer (read, then write) for a Nim programmer: the problem it solves, when to use it and when not, and its cost.
output:
## Intent
A step often has to remove the things that die and add the things that split, and the natural loop does both to the collection it is reading. In Nim that fails at run time: the `for` loop over a `seq` asserts that the length did not change. The ways around it that compile are a copy of the collection per frame, or a `ref` per element that several places mutate. A command buffer splits the step in two: a read pass decides and records the changes as data, a write pass applies them to the owner afterwards.

## Use when / avoid when
- Use it when a pass over a collection has to add or remove elements, or change elements that other elements refer to: game or simulation steps, graph rewrites, UI trees, a scheduler's tick.
- Use it when the changes should be inspectable, loggable or replayable before they happen; the plan is a `seq` of plain values.
- Use `command` when each change needs an inverse for undo; the buffer is the same idea without history. Use `functional_core` when the effects leave the program (I/O): there the commands are performed by a shell, here they are applied to a value.
- Avoid it when the pass changes only the element it is looking at and nothing else depends on it: update in place or build a new `seq` with `map`.

## Complexity
| Operation | Time | Space |
|---|---|---|
| `plan` | O(n) for n units | O(c) for c commands |
| `applyCmd` with the world moved in | O(1): a slot map update | O(1) extra; none for damage and despawn, amortised for spawn |
| `applyAll` of c commands | O(c) | O(1) extra beyond spawns |
| `step` | O(n + c) | O(c) for the plan |

The world is a `sink` parameter: a caller that moves it in at its last use pays for no copy of the units. A caller that still uses the world afterwards gets one copy of the slots per `applyAll` or `step` call (O(n)), and an unchanged old world; the batch does not copy per command. Measured with `-d:nimAllocStats` (tests/test_patterns_command_buffer.nim): 5 damage commands and 5 despawn commands applied to worlds of 10, 100 and 1000 units, each moved in, allocate nothing. `step` itself allocates the plan.

instruction: Explain Composite for a Nim programmer: the problem it solves, when to use it and when not, and its cost.
output:
## Intent
Treat one object and a group of objects uniformly in a part-whole structure (a file or a directory of
files). The OO pattern gives leaf and group a shared interface. In Nim the tree is **one object
variant** whose group case holds a `seq` of the same type (no `ref` needed), and every operation on
the whole tree is an instance of a single `fold`.

## Use when / avoid when
- Use for trees where a node is either a leaf or a list of nodes: file systems, UI trees,
  expressions, menus.
- Write a new operation as a choice of the two arguments of `fold`, not as a new recursive proc, so
  the recursion exists once.
- Avoid when the structure is a graph with sharing or cycles: a tree variant would duplicate or loop.
- Avoid a base class with `add`/`remove` on leaves; the variant makes illegal calls unrepresentable.

## Complexity
`fold` visits each node once: O(n) time. Intermediate results of children are kept in a `seq`, so
extra space is O(width) per level plus recursion depth O(height). Very deep trees can overflow the
stack; flatten with an explicit work list if depth is unbounded.

instruction: Explain CQRS (command query responsibility segregation) for a Nim programmer: the problem it solves, when to use it and when not, and its cost.
output:
## Intent
Use different models for changing and for reading. The write side checks a command against the current state and answers with events or a reason for refusing. The read side never decides anything: each read model is a projection, a fold over the events, shaped for one question. Here both sides consume the same event log (a choice of this example, not a requirement of CQRS).

## Use when / avoid when
- Use when reads and writes have different shapes (a validated stock table for deciding, a dashboard of totals for display) or need to evolve independently.
- Use when you want to add a new read model later by replaying the log.
- Avoid for simple CRUD where one table serves both purposes.
- CQRS does not require event sourcing: read models can be fed from any change notification, and the write side can keep plain state. This module uses an event log because it makes the projections easy to state as folds; `event_sourcing.md` is the optional next step where the log, not the state, is the source of truth.

## Complexity
`decide` and `evolve` are O(s) in the number of distinct skus s (the stock is a sorted list). A dashboard projection is O(e) for e events; the incremental form `continueDashboard` is O(new events). Rebuilding stock is O(e * s).

instruction: Explain Decompose conditional for a Nim programmer: the problem it solves, when to use it and when not, and its cost.
output:
## Intent
A condition that mixes several ideas in one expression (an age, a weekday, an hour, a flag) is understood only by running it in your head, and a change to one clause can silently change the precedence of another. Decomposing it gives each idea a named predicate, gives the outcome a value type that says which rule applied, and keeps the decision a short list in priority order.

## Use when / avoid when
- Use when a condition has three or more clauses, mixes `and` with `or`, or you cannot say the rule aloud in one sentence.
- Use when someone will ask "why did this case get that result": the tier is the answer, not a trace.
- Avoid when the condition is one comparison; a name for it adds nothing.
- Avoid when the branches are kinds of one tag: that is `replace_conditional_with_polymorphism.md`.

## Complexity
O(1) per decision; each predicate is a comparison, and the priority list evaluates them left to right with short circuit.

instruction: Explain Decorator for a Nim programmer: the problem it solves, when to use it and when not, and its cost.
output:
## Intent
Add behaviour around an object without changing it or its interface. The OO pattern wraps an
object in another object with the same interface. In Nim a handler is a proc value
(`Request -> Response`) and a decorator is a function from handler to handler, `proc(h: Handler):
Handler`. Stacking decorators is function composition.

## Use when / avoid when
- Use for cross-cutting behaviour around a core: authorisation, headers, tracing, retries, timing.
- Use `compose` and `stack` to build a pipeline from a list, outermost first.
- Avoid subclassing the core to add one behaviour: that multiplies classes per combination.
- Avoid decorators that need hidden state (a counter, a cache): make the state an explicit value
  (see `proxy.md`) or move it to the shell.

## Complexity
Each decorator adds one closure allocation when the pipeline is built and one indirect call per
request. Build the pipeline once and reuse it.

instruction: Explain Dependency record (dependency injection by passing a record of procs) for a Nim programmer: the problem it solves, when to use it and when not, and its cost.
output:
## Intent
Business logic that needs the clock and a mail sender takes them as one argument, a record whose fields are procs. Production builds the record from the real procs; a test builds another from a fixed clock and a sender that appends to a list. No interface type, no mocking framework, no global to reset between tests.

## Use when / avoid when
- Use for the handful of effects a unit needs: time, randomness, a sender, a store.
- Use when a test double should be a few lines of ordinary code.
- Avoid when the order and content of effects must be inspected, rewritten or replayed; make the program data (`free_interpreter.md`).
- Avoid passing a record with dozens of fields; split it per use case so each routine sees only what it needs.

## Complexity
One pass over the invoices: O(n) calls of `send`. The record adds one indirect call per effect and no allocation beyond the closures.

instruction: Explain Event sourcing for a Nim programmer: the problem it solves, when to use it and when not, and its cost.
output:
## Intent
Store what happened, not what is true now. The state of an entity is the fold of its events: start from an empty state and apply each event in order. The log only grows; a past state is a prefix of the fold; a snapshot is a saved intermediate value that lets you skip the prefix.

## Use when / avoid when
- Use when history matters (audit trail, undo, "what was the balance last Tuesday") or when several views must be derived from the same facts.
- Use when you want to rebuild state after a bug fix by replaying.
- Avoid when only the current value matters and nobody will ask how it came about; a plain record is simpler.
- To refuse invalid changes before they become facts, put a command side in front (`cqrs.md`); events themselves are never refused.

## Complexity
`replay` is O(n) time and O(1) extra space for n events. `replayFrom` with a snapshot costs O(tail). `appended` is O(n) here because it copies the `seq`; a persistent queue (`bankers_queue.md`) makes it amortized O(1) when logs are long.

instruction: Explain Extract function for a Nim programmer: the problem it solves, when to use it and when not, and its cost.
output:
## Intent
A long routine that computes four named things in a row, with a comment between each, hides four functions. Extracting each one gives it a name, a signature that lists what it needs and a result that can be tested alone, and leaves the original as a short sequence that reads like the comments did. Behaviour does not change; the test compares the old routine with the new one.

## Use when / avoid when
- Use when a comment says "now compute X", when a block has one input and one output, or when you want to test one step without the others.
- Use when two routines repeat the same block with different surroundings.
- Avoid when the block reads and writes many locals: bundle them first (`introduce_parameter_object.md`), or the extracted function takes a long argument list and is no clearer.
- Avoid extracting one-line expressions that already read well.

## Complexity
Unchanged by the refactoring: O(lines) for the subtotal and O(1) for each other step.

instruction: Explain Extract type for a Nim programmer: the problem it solves, when to use it and when not, and its cost.
output:
## Intent
Two or more fields that always travel together (an amount and a currency code) appear side by side in every signature, and every caller must remember the rules that tie them: only the same currency adds, only known codes exist, an amount is not negative. Extracting a value type moves those rules into one smart constructor and one set of operations, so a caller cannot build or combine a wrong value without being told.

## Use when / avoid when
- Use when the same group of fields is passed together in three or more places, or a rule mentions them together.
- Use when a bug came from swapping or mixing two values of the same base type.
- Avoid when the fields are independent and merely adjacent; a type would invent a relation that does not exist.
- Avoid a `distinct` alias when the value has two fields; use an `object` with private fields and a smart constructor.

## Complexity
O(1) per operation; the code lookup is a scan of the three enum values. The value is two machine words.

instruction: Explain Facade for a Nim programmer: the problem it solves, when to use it and when not, and its cost.
output:
## Intent
Callers need one or two answers from a subsystem and should not know its steps, their order, or how
many there are. The OO pattern puts one simple class in front of several. In Nim the **module
boundary is the facade**: the steps are not exported, and the exported surface is a small API.

## Use when / avoid when
- Use when a task is a fixed sequence of steps (normalise, tokenise, count, rank) that callers would
  otherwise repeat or get in the wrong order.
- Export the one or two routines callers need; leave the steps unexported so they can change.
- Avoid when callers genuinely need the steps individually: export those, with no wrapper.
- Avoid a facade object with fields holding the subsystems: a module of funcs does it with no state.

## Complexity
Time O(n + u log u) for n characters and u unique words (counting, then sorting). Space O(n).

instruction: Explain Factory Method for a Nim programmer: the problem it solves, when to use it and when not, and its cost.
output:
## Intent
A shared algorithm must work with a product whose concrete shape it should not know. The OO pattern
solves this with an overridable `createProduct()` in a base class. In functional Nim the creating
step is simply a parameter: a proc value (`ExporterFactory`) that the algorithm calls. No base class,
no subclass per product.

## Use when / avoid when
- Use when one routine (`publish`) is reused with several ways of making its collaborator and the
  caller picks the way.
- Use a generic parameter instead of a proc value when the choice is known at compile time and you
  want it inlined.
- Avoid when there is a single product: call the constructor. A factory with one implementation is
  indirection without a reason.
- Avoid a `case` on a kind inside the algorithm: that hard-codes the product list there.

## Complexity
One extra proc call per product; no allocation beyond the product itself. The factory proc is a
closure value, so a call through it is an indirect call.

instruction: Explain Flyweight for a Nim programmer: the problem it solves, when to use it and when not, and its cost.
output:
## Intent
Many equal values are stored many times (the same font name on every run of text). The OO pattern
shares one object among all users and keeps a factory table of shared objects. In functional Nim the
shared thing is a small symbol (`Sym`, an index) and the table is an **explicit immutable pool value**:
`intern(pool, s)` returns the new pool and the symbol. There is no global table, so interning is
deterministic and testable.

## Use when / avoid when
- Use when a large number of values repeat from a small set and you compare or store them often
  (identifiers, tags, font and style names, keys).
- Pass the pool through the code that interns; return it from the routine that extends it.
- Avoid when values are mostly unique or small: the pool costs more than it saves.
- Avoid a module-level `var` pool: it is a singleton in disguise (`singleton.md`).

## Complexity
Looking up an existing string is O(1) expected (hash table). `intern` takes the pool by value and
copies it when it adds a new string, which is O(size of pool): interning n new strings one by one
is O(n^2). `internAll` copies the pool once and then interns in one pass, so it is O(size of pool +
n) expected; use it whenever you have the strings together. If you must intern one at a time into a
big pool, back the pool with a persistent map. `resolve` is O(1).

instruction: Explain Free interpreter (program as data) for a Nim programmer: the problem it solves, when to use it and when not, and its cost.
output:
## Intent
Describe a computation as a value instead of performing it. A `Program` is a list of instruction values (`put`, `get`, `delete`, `whenMissing`); building one does nothing. A separate interpreter gives it meaning: a pure one folds it over an in-memory store, a printer renders it, a real one would talk to a database. Choosing the interpreter is dependency injection, and because the program is data it can also be rewritten before it runs.

## Use when / avoid when
- Use when you want to test, print, count or optimise a sequence of effects without performing them.
- Use when several backends must run the same program and agree (a fake and a real one).
- Avoid when the program never needs inspecting; a record of procs (`dependency_record.md`) is lighter.
- Avoid when the set of operations changes often and you do not need to look inside programs; `tagless_final.md` avoids the instruction type.

## Complexity
`runPure` is O(n * s) for n executed instructions and s keys (the store is a sorted list; a persistent map gives O(n log s)). `pretty` and `size` are O(n). `simplify` is O(n) with an output stack.

instruction: Explain Functional core, imperative shell for a Nim programmer: the problem it solves, when to use it and when not, and its cost.
output:
## Intent
Tangled code decides and acts in the same breath: it reads a sensor, compares, switches a relay and prints. Split it. The core is a pure function that takes the current state and the new input and returns the next state together with a list of effect descriptions (plain data). The shell is a thin loop that fetches inputs, calls the core and performs the effects. All rules live in the core; the shell has none.

## Use when / avoid when
- Use when logic and I/O are mixed and you want to test the rules without a clock, a device or a network.
- Use when the same decision must be replayed or explained later (the effect list is the explanation).
- Avoid for a one-line effect with no decision in it; call the effect directly.
- When the decisions themselves are a closed table of transitions, reach for `state_machine.md`; when the effects must be inspected or rewritten as a program, reach for `free_interpreter.md`.

## Complexity
`decide` is O(1) time and space (at most two effects). The shell is O(n) over n readings.

instruction: Explain Idempotent command for a Nim programmer: the problem it solves, when to use it and when not, and its cost.
output:
## Intent
Make a command safe to deliver more than once. The client attaches a key to each command. The ledger remembers, for every key, the command and the response it produced. A repeat of the same command returns the stored response and changes nothing; a different command under a used key is a conflict. The handler is a pure function from (ledger, command) to (ledger, response).

## Use when / avoid when
- Use for anything a client may retry after a timeout: payments, orders, sign-ups, webhooks received at least once.
- Use when the retry must see the same answer as the original attempt, including a refusal.
- Avoid when the operation is naturally idempotent (setting a field to a value) and has no response worth replaying.
- In production the entry list is a keyed table with an expiry; the list here keeps the example short and ordered.

## Complexity
`handle` is O(k) for k stored keys here (linear lookup) and copies the entry list on a new key; with a hash map and a persistent structure both become O(1) or O(log k). Space grows with the number of distinct keys until entries expire.

instruction: Explain Interpreter for a Nim programmer: the problem it solves, when to use it and when not, and its cost.
output:
## Intent
Evaluate sentences of a small language. The OO pattern gives every grammar rule a class with an `interpret(context)` method. In functional Nim the grammar is one object variant (an algebraic data type) and each interpretation is a function with an exhaustive `case`: a fold over the tree.
