Write the Nim module `eulerian_path.nim` (Eulerian path and circuit (Hierholzer)).

Eulerian trails by Hierholzer's algorithm: walk every edge of a graph exactly once.

A trail that uses every edge once exists exactly when the edges form one connected piece and the
degrees allow it. Undirected: zero or two vertices of odd degree (a self-loop adds 2). Directed:
every vertex has out-degree equal to in-degree, except possibly one start vertex with one more
out than in and one end vertex with one more in than out. Hierholzer's algorithm follows unused
edges until it is stuck, which can only happen back at the start of a closed loop, and splices
the loops it finds on the way back: an explicit stack of vertices, a pointer into each
adjacency list, and the vertices written out in the order they are abandoned, reversed. Use it
for route inspection, stroke-order puzzles and de Bruijn sequences.

A trail is the list of vertices visited, so it has one more entry than the graph has edges; a
graph with no edge has the empty trail. The answer is deterministic: the start is the
unbalanced or odd-degree vertex when there is one, else the smallest vertex that has an edge,
and edges are taken in the graph's neighbour order.

Public API:
```nim
func eulerianPath(g: Graph): Option[seq[int]]
func eulerianCircuit(g: Graph): Option[seq[int]]
```

Write the Nim module `external_sort.nim` (External merge sort).

External merge sort, simulated in memory: sort data that does not fit in fast memory by
forming sorted runs and merging them k at a time.

The external store is modelled as a sequence of runs, each a sorted `seq[int]`; nothing touches
a file. Phase 1 (run formation) reads `memory` items at a time, sorts them in memory and writes
them back as one run, giving ceil(n / memory) runs. Phase 2 merges up to `fanIn` runs into one
with a k-way merge driven by a small heap, pass after pass, until one run is left. Use the
shape when the data lives on disk or across the network and the cost that matters is how often
every item is moved, not comparisons; for data that fits in memory use `merge_sort` or
`heap_sort`.

I/O cost model (what `IoCost` counts): a pass reads each item once and writes each item once,
so run formation costs n reads and n writes, and each merge pass costs another n reads and n
writes. With r = ceil(n / memory) runs and fan-in k the number of merge passes is
ceil(log_k r) (zero when r <= 1), so the total is n * (1 + passes) reads and the same number of
writes. Items are counted, not blocks; divide by the block size B for block transfers when
every run is stored in whole blocks.

Public API:
```nim
type ExtSortError = enum
  eeBadMemory,              ## memory must hold at least one item
  eeBadFanIn                 ## the fan-in must be at least 2 (a 1-way merge never ends)
type Run = seq[int]
type IoCost = object
  mergePasses*: int
  reads*: int                ## items read from the store, run formation included
  writes*: int               ## items written to the store, run formation included
type Sorted = object
  items*: seq[int]
  cost*: IoCost
func `==`(a, b: IoCost): bool
func formRuns(data: openArray[int]; memory: int): Result[seq[Run], ExtSortError]
func mergeRuns(runs: openArray[Run]): Run
func expectedMergePasses(runCount, fanIn: int): int
func externalSort(data: openArray[int]; memory, fanIn: int): Result[Sorted, ExtSortError]
```

## External merge sort, simulated in memory: sort data that does not fit in fast memory by
## forming sorted runs and merging them k at a time.
##
## The external store is modelled as a sequence of runs, each a sorted `seq[int]`; nothing touches
## a file. Phase 1 (run formation) reads `memory` items at a time, sorts them in memory and writes
## them back as one run, giving ceil(n / memory) runs. Phase 2 merges up to `fanIn` runs into one
## with a k-way merge driven by a small heap, pass after pass, until one run is left. Use the
## shape when the data lives on disk or across the network and the cost that matters is how often
## every item is moved, not comparisons; for data that fits in memory use `merge_sort` or
## `heap_sort`.
##
## I/O cost model (what `IoCost` counts): a pass reads each item once and writes each item once,
## so run formation costs n reads and n writes, and each merge pass costs another n reads and n
## writes. With r = ceil(n / memory) runs and fan-in k the number of merge passes is
## ceil(log_k r) (zero when r <= 1), so the total is n * (1 + passes) reads and the same number of
## writes. Items are counted, not blocks; divide by the block size B for block transfers when
## every run is stored in whole blocks.

import std/[algorithm, heapqueue]
import nimcs/fp/result

type
  ExtSortError* = enum
    eeBadMemory   ## memory must hold at least one item
    eeBadFanIn    ## the fan-in must be at least 2 (a 1-way merge never ends)

  Run* = seq[int]    ## one sorted run in the simulated external store

  IoCost* = object
    mergePasses*: int
    reads*: int      ## items read from the store, run formation included
    writes*: int     ## items written to the store, run formation included

  Sorted* = object
    items*: seq[int]
    cost*: IoCost

  Head = object
    value: int
    run: int         ## which run the value came from
    at: int          ## its index inside that run

func `<`(a, b: Head): bool {.raises: [].} =
  (a.value, a.run, a.at) < (b.value, b.run, b.at)   # the run and index only make the order total

func `==`*(a, b: IoCost): bool {.raises: [].} =
  a.mergePasses == b.mergePasses and a.reads == b.reads and a.writes == b.writes

func formRuns*(data: openArray[int]; memory: int): Result[seq[Run], ExtSortError] {.raises: [].} =
  ## Cuts `data` into consecutive chunks of at most `memory` items and sorts each one; there are
  ## ceil(len / memory) runs and no run is empty (EXTSORT-RUNS-01, EXTSORT-RUNS-02).
  if memory < 1:
    return err(seq[Run], eeBadMemory)
  var runs: seq[Run]
  var start = 0
  while start < data.len:
    let stop = min(start + memory, data.len)
    runs.add data[start ..< stop].sorted
    start = stop
  ok(runs, ExtSortError)

func mergeRuns*(runs: openArray[Run]): Run {.raises: [].} =
  ## The k-way merge of sorted runs into one sorted run: a heap holds the current head of each
  ## run and the smallest is taken, so each item costs O(log k) (EXTSORT-MERGE-01).
  var heap = initHeapQueue[Head]()
  var total = 0
  for r, run in runs:
    total += run.len
    if run.len > 0:
      heap.push Head(value: run[0], run: r, at: 0)
  result = newSeqOfCap[int](total)
  while heap.len > 0:
    let top = heap.pop
    result.add top.value
    let next = top.at + 1
    if next < runs[top.run].len:
      heap.push Head(value: runs[top.run][next], run: top.run, at: next)

func expectedMergePasses*(runCount, fanIn: int): int {.raises: [].} =
  ## ceil(log_fanIn runCount) by repeated division, the closed form of the model (EXTSORT-COST-01).
  ## Zero when there is at most one run; `fanIn` must be at least 2, otherwise the answer is 0.
  if fanIn < 2:
    return 0
  var runsLeft = runCount
  while runsLeft > 1:
    runsLeft = (runsLeft + fanIn - 1) div fanIn
    inc result

func externalSort*(data: openArray[int]; memory, fanIn: int): Result[Sorted, ExtSortError] {.raises: [].} =
  ## Sorts `data` with run formation and repeated `fanIn`-way merge passes, and reports the
  ## simulated I/O (EXTSORT-SORT-01, EXTSORT-COST-01). The result equals the in-memory sort.
  if memory < 1:
    return err(Sorted, eeBadMemory)
  if fanIn < 2:
    return err(Sorted, eeBadFanIn)
  let formed = formRuns(data, memory)
  if formed.isErr:
    return err(Sorted, formed.error)
  var runs = formed.value
  var cost = IoCost(reads: data.len, writes: data.len)
  while runs.len > 1:
    var merged: seq[Run]
    var group = 0
    while group < runs.len:
      let stop = min(group + fanIn, runs.len)
      merged.add mergeRuns(runs[group ..< stop])
      group = stop
    runs = merged
    inc cost.mergePasses
    cost.reads += data.len
    cost.writes += data.len
  let items = if runs.len == 1: runs[0] else: newSeq[int]()
  ok(Sorted(items: items, cost: cost), ExtSortError)

Write the Nim module `greedy.nim` (Greedy algorithms and the exchange argument).

Greedy algorithms and the exchange argument, shown on interval scheduling: from a set of
half-open intervals [start, finish), pick as many pairwise non-overlapping ones as possible.

The greedy rule is "always take the interval that finishes first among those compatible with what
is already chosen". It is correct because of an exchange argument (see the details page):
any optimal schedule can be changed, one interval at a time, into the greedy one without losing size.
Use a greedy rule only when such an argument exists; otherwise reach for dynamic programming
(`knapsack`) or backtracking. The second example is the fractional knapsack, where items may be
split and "best value per unit of weight first" is optimal (and wrong for whole items). Intervals touching at an end point do not overlap.

## Greedy algorithms and the exchange argument, shown on interval scheduling: from a set of
## half-open intervals [start, finish), pick as many pairwise non-overlapping ones as possible.
##
## The greedy rule is "always take the interval that finishes first among those compatible with what
## is already chosen". It is correct because of an exchange argument (see the details page):
## any optimal schedule can be changed, one interval at a time, into the greedy one without losing size.
## Use a greedy rule only when such an argument exists; otherwise reach for dynamic programming
## (`knapsack`) or backtracking. The second example is the fractional knapsack, where items may be
## split and "best value per unit of weight first" is optimal (and wrong for whole items). Intervals touching at an end point do not overlap.

import std/[algorithm, options]

type
  Interval* = object
    ## The half-open range [start, finish). The fields are private so that the only way to build
    ## one is `interval`, which rejects empty and reversed ranges (TECH-GREEDY-04).
    startAt, finishAt: int

func interval*(start, finish: int): Option[Interval] {.raises: [].} =
  ## An interval must be non-empty: start < finish (TECH-GREEDY-04).
  if start < finish: some(Interval(startAt: start, finishAt: finish))
  else: none(Interval)

func start*(i: Interval): int {.raises: [].} = i.startAt
func finish*(i: Interval): int {.raises: [].} = i.finishAt

func overlaps*(a, b: Interval): bool {.raises: [].} =
  ## Do the half-open ranges share a point? Touching ranges do not (TECH-GREEDY-01).
  a.startAt < b.finishAt and b.startAt < a.finishAt

func scheduleIndices*(xs: openArray[Interval]): seq[int] {.raises: [].} =
  ## Indices into `xs` of a maximum set of pairwise non-overlapping intervals, ordered by time.
  ## Ties on the finish time are broken by earlier start, then by lower index, so the answer is
  ## deterministic and does not depend on any hash order (TECH-GREEDY-01 .. TECH-GREEDY-03).
  var keyed: seq[(int, int, int)] = @[]   # (finish, start, index): the order the rule scans in
  for i in 0 ..< xs.len:
    keyed.add (xs[i].finishAt, xs[i].startAt, i)
  keyed.sort()
  result = @[]
  var lastFinish = low(int)
  for (finish, start, index) in keyed:
    if start >= lastFinish:
      result.add index
      lastFinish = finish

func schedule*(xs: openArray[Interval]): seq[Interval] {.raises: [].} =
  ## The chosen intervals themselves.
  result = @[]
  for i in scheduleIndices(xs):
    result.add xs[i]

type
  Lot* = object
    ## An item that may be taken in part.
    weight*, value*: int

  Share* = object
    ## `taken` units of the weight of lot `index`, with 0 < taken < weight.
    index*, taken*: int

  FractionalPacking* = object
    ## `whole` lists the lots taken completely (ascending index); `partial` is the one lot cut
    ## short, if any. The total value is the fraction `valueNum / valueDen`, `valueDen` > 0.
    whole*: seq[int]
    partial*: Option[Share]
    valueNum*, valueDen*: int

func fractionalKnapsack*(lots: openArray[Lot]; capacity: int): Option[FractionalPacking] {.raises: [].} =
  ## Best value when lots may be split: take lots by decreasing value per unit of weight until the
  ## capacity is used up, cutting the last one (TECH-GREEDY-05 .. TECH-GREEDY-08). Lots of weight 0
  ## are always taken. None for a negative capacity, weight or value. Products of a weight and a
  ## value are assumed to fit `int`.
  if capacity < 0:
    return none(FractionalPacking)
  var items: seq[Lot] = @[]
  for lot in lots:
    if lot.weight < 0 or lot.value < 0:
      return none(FractionalPacking)
    items.add lot
  var whole: seq[int] = @[]
  var wholeValue = 0
  var heavy: seq[int] = @[]
  for i in 0 ..< items.len:
    if items[i].weight == 0:
      whole.add i
      wholeValue += items[i].value
    else:
      heavy.add i
  heavy.sort(proc(a, b: int): int {.raises: [].} =
    # a before b when value[a]/weight[a] > value[b]/weight[b], compared without division.
    let lhs = items[a].value * items[b].weight
    let rhs = items[b].value * items[a].weight
    if lhs > rhs: -1
    elif lhs < rhs: 1
    else: cmp(a, b))
  var remaining = capacity
  var partial = none(Share)
  var num = 0
  var den = 1
  for i in heavy:
    if items[i].weight <= remaining:
      whole.add i
      wholeValue += items[i].value
      remaining -= items[i].weight
    else:
      if remaining > 0:
        partial = some(Share(index: i, taken: remaining))
      break
  whole.sort()
  if partial.isSome:
    let cut = items[partial.get.index]
    den = cut.weight
    num = wholeValue * den + cut.value * partial.get.taken
  else:
    num = wholeValue
  some(FractionalPacking(whole: whole, partial: partial, valueNum: num, valueDen: den))

Write the Nim module `huffman.nim` (Huffman coding).

Huffman coding: a prefix-free binary code that gives frequent symbols short code words.

Use it to see how a greedy choice (always merge the two lightest subtrees) builds an optimal
symbol-by-symbol code. The code words are returned as strings of '0' and '1' so that a reader
can print and compare them; a real encoder would pack bits. Ties are broken by weight, then
by the smallest symbol inside a subtree, and the first subtree taken becomes the 0 side, so the
same frequencies give the same code whatever order they arrive in. Nothing is changed in place.

Write the Nim module `insertion_sort.nim` (Insertion sort).

Insertion sort: grow a sorted prefix by sliding each next element left to its place.

Use it for short inputs (a few dozen elements) or inputs that are already nearly sorted, where
its O(n) best case beats the O(n log n) sorts; it is also the base case that real library sorts
switch to for small slices. It is stable. The input is never changed: the result is a new `seq`.

Public API:
```nim
func insertionSort[T](xs: openArray[T]; less: Less[T]): seq[T]
func insertionSort[T](xs: openArray[T]): seq[T]
```
output:
## Insertion sort: grow a sorted prefix by sliding each next element left to its place.
##
## Use it for short inputs (a few dozen elements) or inputs that are already nearly sorted, where
## its O(n) best case beats the O(n log n) sorts; it is also the base case that real library sorts
## switch to for small slices. It is stable. The input is never changed: the result is a new `seq`.

type Less[T] = proc(a, b: T): bool {.noSideEffect, raises: [].}

func insertionSort*[T](xs: openArray[T]; less: Less[T]): seq[T] {.raises: [].} =
  ## Ascending by `less` (a strict weak order: `less(a, b)` means "a must come before b").
  ## Elements that are equal under `less` keep their input order (SORT-INSERT-05).
  var sorted = @xs
  for i in 1 ..< sorted.len:
    let item = sorted[i]
    var j = i
    while j > 0 and less(item, sorted[j - 1]):
      sorted[j] = sorted[j - 1]
      dec j
    sorted[j] = item
  sorted

func insertionSort*[T](xs: openArray[T]): seq[T] {.raises: [].} =
  ## Ascending by `<`.
  insertionSort(xs, proc(a, b: T): bool {.noSideEffect, raises: [].} = a < b)

Write the Nim module `kmp.nim` (Knuth–Morris–Pratt search).

Knuth–Morris–Pratt substring search: never move backwards in the text.

The failure table says, for each prefix of the pattern, how long its longest proper border is
(a prefix that is also a suffix). After a mismatch the search resumes from that border instead of
from scratch, so the work is linear in `text.len + pattern.len`. Use it for one pattern over
streaming or adversarial text; `z_algorithm` gives the same answers by another route, and
`rabin_karp` is the choice for many patterns of one length.

Positions are 0-based start offsets of every occurrence, overlapping ones included. An empty
pattern occurs at every offset 0 .. text.len (STR-KMP-04).

Write the Nim module `lca.nim` (Lowest common ancestor (binary lifting)).

Lowest common ancestor by binary lifting.

A rooted tree is given as a parent array (the root's parent is -1). Preprocessing stores, for
every vertex v and every k, the 2^k-th ancestor `up[k][v]`, in O(n log n) space; any ancestor
k steps up is then reached by the set bits of k, and the LCA of u and v is found by lifting the
deeper vertex to the other's depth and then lifting both together while their ancestors differ.
Each query costs O(log n). Use it when a tree is fixed and many queries follow (distances,
path queries); for a single query walking up the parent array is simpler, and an Euler tour
with a sparse table gives O(1) queries at the same preprocessing cost.

The structure is an immutable value; a query never changes it. A vertex outside the tree is
answered with none rather than an error, since asking about it is an ordinary question.

Write the Nim module `lis.nim` (Longest increasing subsequence).

Longest strictly increasing subsequence in O(n log n), with reconstruction.

Keep, for every length L, the smallest tail value of an increasing subsequence of length L
found so far; the tails are sorted, so each new element is placed by binary search. Parent
links then rebuild one subsequence. Use it for patience-sorting style problems, "fewest moves
to sort" questions and as the fast alternative to a quadratic table. For the non-strict
version, compare with `<=` by searching for the first tail greater than the element.

Public API:
```nim
func lisIndices[T](xs: openArray[T]): seq[int]
func lis[T](xs: openArray[T]): seq[T]
func lisLength[T](xs: openArray[T]): int
```
output:
## Longest strictly increasing subsequence in O(n log n), with reconstruction.
##
## Keep, for every length L, the smallest tail value of an increasing subsequence of length L
## found so far; the tails are sorted, so each new element is placed by binary search. Parent
## links then rebuild one subsequence. Use it for patience-sorting style problems, "fewest moves
## to sort" questions and as the fast alternative to a quadratic table. For the non-strict
## version, compare with `<=` by searching for the first tail greater than the element.

func lisIndices*[T](xs: openArray[T]): seq[int] {.raises: [].} =
  ## Indices (ascending) of one longest strictly increasing subsequence. Of the longest ones it
  ## returns the one that ends in the smallest final value (the last tail kept); the choice is
  ## fixed by the input, so repeated calls agree (DP-LIS-04).
  var tailIdx: seq[int] = @[]       # tailIdx[L-1] = index of the best tail of length L
  var parent = newSeq[int](xs.len)  # previous index in the subsequence, or -1
  for i in 0 ..< xs.len:
    var lo = 0
    var hi = tailIdx.len
    while lo < hi:
      let mid = (lo + hi) div 2
      if xs[tailIdx[mid]] < xs[i]: lo = mid + 1
      else: hi = mid
    parent[i] = if lo > 0: tailIdx[lo - 1] else: -1
    if lo == tailIdx.len: tailIdx.add i
    else: tailIdx[lo] = i
  var rev: seq[int] = @[]
  var at = if tailIdx.len > 0: tailIdx[tailIdx.len - 1] else: -1
  while at >= 0:
    rev.add at
    at = parent[at]
  result = newSeq[int](rev.len)
  for k in 0 ..< rev.len:
    result[k] = rev[rev.len - 1 - k]

func lis*[T](xs: openArray[T]): seq[T] {.raises: [].} =
  ## The values of one longest strictly increasing subsequence (DP-LIS-01 .. DP-LIS-03).
  let idx = lisIndices(xs)
  result = newSeq[T](idx.len)
  for k in 0 ..< idx.len:
    result[k] = xs[idx[k]]

func lisLength*[T](xs: openArray[T]): int {.raises: [].} =
  lisIndices(xs).len

Write the Nim module `max_flow.nim` (Maximum flow and bipartite matching).

Maximum flow (Edmonds-Karp) and, as an application, maximum bipartite matching.

Use it to ask how much can be sent from a source to a sink through capacity-limited arcs (pipes,
links, assignments). The weight of each arc of a `Graph` is its capacity. Edmonds-Karp
repeatedly sends flow along a shortest (fewest-arcs) path in the residual graph, which bounds
the number of augmentations by V * E / 2 whatever the capacities are. The answer carries the
flow, and a minimum cut found from the last residual graph, so the max-flow = min-cut law can
be checked on every result. An undirected graph gives each direction of an edge its full
capacity. Sums of capacities must fit in an `int` (an overflow is a Defect, not a value).

```nim
  flows*: seq[Edge]          ## per ordered pair (source, target) the flow it carries (weight > 0), ascending
  sourceSide*: seq[int]      ## vertices still reachable from the source in the last residual graph, ascending
```

Write the Nim module `meet_in_middle.nim` (Meet in the middle).

Meet in the middle: subset sums in about 2^(n/2) work instead of 2^n.

Split the items into two halves, list every subset sum of each half (at most 2^(n/2) sums), sort
both lists, and combine them: a subset of the whole is one subset of each half, so a target is
reached exactly when some left sum plus some right sum equals it, which a binary search on the
sorted right list finds. Use it when n is too big for 2^n (n around 30 to 40) but too small for
a pseudo-polynomial table because the values are large; when the values are small, `knapsack`
style dynamic programming is cheaper.

Subsets are counted by index: two equal items are distinct choices, and the empty subset has
sum 0. Items may be negative. To keep every sum inside `int`, at most `MaxItems` items of
absolute value at most `MaxItemValue` are accepted and the target must have absolute value at
most `MaxTarget`.

Write the Nim module `merge_sort.nim` (Merge sort).

Merge sort: sort runs of width 1, 2, 4, ... by merging neighbouring sorted runs.

Use it when you need a stable O(n log n) sort with a guaranteed worst case and can afford O(n)
extra space. This version is bottom-up (no recursion, so no stack depth to worry about) and
ping-pongs between two buffers. The input is never changed.

Public API:
```nim
func mergeSort[T](xs: openArray[T]; less: Less[T]): seq[T]
func mergeSort[T](xs: openArray[T]): seq[T]
```
output:
## Merge sort: sort runs of width 1, 2, 4, ... by merging neighbouring sorted runs.
##
## Use it when you need a stable O(n log n) sort with a guaranteed worst case and can afford O(n)
## extra space. This version is bottom-up (no recursion, so no stack depth to worry about) and
## ping-pongs between two buffers. The input is never changed.

type Less[T] = proc(a, b: T): bool {.noSideEffect, raises: [].}

func mergeRuns[T](src: seq[T]; dst: var seq[T]; lo, mid, hi: int; less: Less[T]) {.raises: [].} =
  ## Merges the sorted runs src[lo ..< mid] and src[mid ..< hi] into dst[lo ..< hi].
  ## Takes from the right run only when it is strictly smaller, which is what keeps the sort stable.
  var i = lo
  var j = mid
  var k = lo
  while i < mid and j < hi:
    if less(src[j], src[i]):
      dst[k] = src[j]
      inc j
    else:
      dst[k] = src[i]
      inc i
    inc k
  while i < mid:
    dst[k] = src[i]
    inc i
    inc k
  while j < hi:
    dst[k] = src[j]
    inc j
    inc k

func mergeSort*[T](xs: openArray[T]; less: Less[T]): seq[T] {.raises: [].} =
  ## Ascending by `less`, stable: equal elements keep their input order (SORT-MERGE-05).
  var src = @xs
  var dst = @xs
  var width = 1
  while width < src.len:
    var lo = 0
    while lo < src.len:
      let mid = min(lo + width, src.len)
      let hi = min(lo + 2 * width, src.len)
      mergeRuns(src, dst, lo, mid, hi, less)
      lo += 2 * width
    swap(src, dst)
    width *= 2
  src

func mergeSort*[T](xs: openArray[T]): seq[T] {.raises: [].} =
  ## Ascending by `<`.
  mergeSort(xs, proc(a, b: T): bool {.noSideEffect, raises: [].} = a < b)

Write the Nim module `quick_sort.nim` (Quick sort (functional)).

Quick sort, functional form: split around a pivot into smaller, equal and larger parts, sort the
outer two recursively and concatenate.

Use it to show divide and conquer without in-place index juggling. The three-way split puts
every element equal to the pivot in the middle part, so inputs with many duplicates do not
degrade. The pivot is the median of the first, middle and last element, which makes sorted and
reverse-sorted inputs fast; an adversarial input can still reach O(n^2) time and O(n) recursion
depth. Prefer `merge_sort` or `heap_sort` when a worst-case bound matters. Each part keeps its
input order, so this version happens to be stable. The input is never changed.

Public API:
```nim
func quickSort[T](xs: openArray[T]; less: Less[T]): seq[T]
func quickSort[T](xs: openArray[T]): seq[T]
```
output:
## Quick sort, functional form: split around a pivot into smaller, equal and larger parts, sort the
## outer two recursively and concatenate.
##
## Use it to show divide and conquer without in-place index juggling. The three-way split puts
## every element equal to the pivot in the middle part, so inputs with many duplicates do not
## degrade. The pivot is the median of the first, middle and last element, which makes sorted and
## reverse-sorted inputs fast; an adversarial input can still reach O(n^2) time and O(n) recursion
## depth. Prefer `merge_sort` or `heap_sort` when a worst-case bound matters. Each part keeps its
## input order, so this version happens to be stable. The input is never changed.

type Less[T] = proc(a, b: T): bool {.noSideEffect, raises: [].}

func pivotOf[T](xs: openArray[T]; less: Less[T]): T {.raises: [].} =
  ## Median of the first, middle and last element (xs is not empty).
  let a = xs[0]
  let b = xs[xs.len div 2]
  let c = xs[xs.len - 1]
  if less(a, b):
    if less(b, c): b
    elif less(a, c): c
    else: a
  else:
    if less(a, c): a
    elif less(b, c): c
    else: b

func quickSort*[T](xs: openArray[T]; less: Less[T]): seq[T] {.raises: [].} =
  ## Ascending by `less`. Equal elements keep their input order (SORT-QUICK-05).
  if xs.len <= 1:
    return @xs
  let pivot = pivotOf(xs, less)
  var smaller, equal, larger: seq[T]
  for x in xs:
    if less(x, pivot): smaller.add x
    elif less(pivot, x): larger.add x
    else: equal.add x
  quickSort(smaller, less) & equal & quickSort(larger, less)

func quickSort*[T](xs: openArray[T]): seq[T] {.raises: [].} =
  ## Ascending by `<`.
  quickSort(xs, proc(a, b: T): bool {.noSideEffect, raises: [].} = a < b)

Write the Nim module `rabin_karp.nim` (Rabin–Karp search).

Rabin–Karp search: slide a window over the text, keeping a polynomial hash of the window
that is updated in O(1) when the window moves, and compare characters only where the hash of
the window equals the hash of the pattern.

The modulus is explicit and validated (`HashModulus` is a distinct type built by `hashModulus`; the name differs from `number_theory.Modulus` so both modules can be imported together). A hash
match is only a candidate: every candidate is verified against the text, so the result never
contains a false positive whatever the modulus (STR-RK-03); a small modulus only makes the
search slower, never wrong. Use it for many same-length patterns (hash them once) or when a
rolling fingerprint is wanted; for one pattern with guaranteed linear time use `kmp`.

## Strongly connected components (Kosaraju): groups of vertices that can all reach each other.
##
## Use it to collapse a directed graph into its acyclic skeleton, find mutually recursive modules
## or deadlock groups. The algorithm is two depth-first passes: one on the graph to get the finish
## order, one on the transposed graph in reverse finish order. O(V + E). On an undirected graph it
## gives the connected components. Output is canonical: each component ascending, components in
## ascending order of their smallest vertex.

import std/algorithm
import nimcs/algo/graph
import nimcs/algo/dfs

func stronglyConnectedComponents*(g: Graph): seq[seq[int]] {.raises: [].} =
  ## Partition of all vertices into components (GRAPH-SCC-01): two vertices share a component
  ## exactly when each reaches the other (GRAPH-SCC-02).
  let n = g.vertexCount
  let reversed = g.transpose
  let finish = dfsForest(g).postorder
  var visited = newSeq[bool](n)
  for i in countdown(finish.len - 1, 0):
    let root = finish[i]
    if visited[root]: continue
    visited[root] = true
    var component: seq[int]
    var stack = @[root]
    while stack.len > 0:
      let u = stack.pop
      component.add u
      for a in reversed.neighbors(u):
        if not visited[a.target]:
          visited[a.target] = true
          stack.add a.target
    component.sort
    result.add component
  result.sort(proc(a, b: seq[int]): int = cmp(a[0], b[0]))

Write the Nim module `sieve.nim` (Sieve of Eratosthenes).

Sieve of Eratosthenes: all primes up to a limit by crossing off the multiples of each prime.

Use it when many primality answers are needed below a known bound: O(n log log n) time and
O(n) space for every prime up to n, against O(sqrt n) per query for trial division
(`isPrimeTrial`). For a single huge number use a probabilistic test instead of either.
A limit below 2 has no primes, so the answer is simply empty.

Write the Nim module `suffix_array.nim` (Suffix array and LCP array).

Suffix array by prefix doubling, and the LCP array by Kasai's method.

The suffix array lists the start offsets of all suffixes of a string in sorted order. Prefix
doubling ranks suffixes by their first 1, 2, 4, ... characters, sorting pairs of ranks until all
ranks differ: O(n log^2 n) with a comparison sort. The LCP array stores, next to each suffix, the
length of the prefix it shares with the previous suffix in sorted order; Kasai computes it in O(n)
by never letting the shared length drop by more than one between neighbouring text positions.

Use it for substring search by binary search, counting distinct substrings and longest
repeated substring. For a single search `kmp` or `z_algorithm` is simpler; a suffix tree
answers the same questions with a larger structure.

Public API:
```nim
func suffixArray(s: string): seq[int]
func isSuffixArrayOf(sa: openArray[int]; s: string): bool
func lcpArray(s: string; sa: openArray[int]): Option[seq[int]]
func countDistinctSubstrings(s: string): int
```

Write the Nim module `three_way_merge.nim` (Three-way merge (base, ours, theirs)).

Three-way merge: combine two edits (`ours`, `theirs`) of one common ancestor (`base`), keeping
what only one side changed and reporting what both changed differently as a value.

Two levels. `mergeKeyed` merges maps (a directory tree, path by path): each key is decided on
its own from three `Option`s, and a key both sides changed differently is a `KeyConflict`.
`merge3` merges sequences (diff3 on lines): `ours` and `theirs` are each aligned with `base`
through `lcs`, the lines all three still share are `Stable`, and what lies between them is
taken from the one side that changed it (`Clean`) or reported as a `Conflict`. Neither level
raises or picks a side silently.

Public API:
```nim
type KeyConflict[V] = object
  key*: string
  base*, ours*, theirs*: Option[V]
type KeyedMerge[V] = object
  case isClean*: bool
  of true:
    merged*: Table[string, V]
  of false:
    resolved*: Table[string, V]
    conflicts*: seq[KeyConflict[V]]
type Side = enum
  sOurs, sTheirs, sBoth
type ChunkKind = enum
  ckStable, ckClean, ckConflict
type Chunk[T] = object
  case kind*: ChunkKind
  of ckStable:
    stable*: seq[T]
  of ckClean:
    side*: Side
    taken*: seq[T]
  of ckConflict:
    base*, ours*, theirs*: seq[T]
func `==`[V](a, b: KeyedMerge[V]): bool

func conflict[T](base, ours, theirs: seq[T]): Chunk[T]
```

output:
## Three-way merge: combine two edits (`ours`, `theirs`) of one common ancestor (`base`), keeping
## what only one side changed and reporting what both changed differently as a value.
##
## Two levels. `mergeKeyed` merges maps (a directory tree, path by path): each key is decided on
## its own from three `Option`s, and a key both sides changed differently is a `KeyConflict`.
## `merge3` merges sequences (diff3 on lines): `ours` and `theirs` are each aligned with `base`
## through `lcs`, the lines all three still share are `Stable`, and what lies between them is
## taken from the one side that changed it (`Clean`) or reported as a `Conflict`. Neither level
## raises or picks a side silently.

import std/[options, tables, algorithm, strutils]
import nimcs/algo/lcs

type
  KeyConflict*[V] = object
    ## A key both sides changed differently: its three versions, `none` for absent.
    key*: string
    base*, ours*, theirs*: Option[V]

  KeyedMerge*[V] = object
    ## The outcome of `mergeKeyed`: the merged map, or the keys that need a decision together
    ## with what was already settled.
    case isClean*: bool
    of true:
      merged*: Table[string, V]
    of false:
      resolved*: Table[string, V]
      conflicts*: seq[KeyConflict[V]]

  Side* = enum
    sOurs, sTheirs, sBoth

  ChunkKind* = enum
    ckStable, ckClean, ckConflict

  Chunk*[T] = object
    ## A piece of a sequence merge: lines all three share, lines one side (or both, the same
    ## way) changed, or a hunk both sides changed differently. A `Clean` chunk may be empty (a
    ## deletion).
    case kind*: ChunkKind
    of ckStable:
      stable*: seq[T]
    of ckClean:
      side*: Side
      taken*: seq[T]
    of ckConflict:
      base*, ours*, theirs*: seq[T]

# ─── keyed merge ────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────

func `==`*[V](a, b: KeyedMerge[V]): bool {.raises: [].} =
  ## Nim cannot derive `==` for an object variant.
  if a.isClean != b.isClean: return false
  if a.isClean: a.merged == b.merged
  else: a.resolved == b.resolved and a.conflicts == b.conflicts

func look[V](t: Table[string, V]; key: string): Option[V] {.raises: [].} =
  t.withValue(key, found):
    return some(found)
  none(V)

func swapSides*[V](c: KeyConflict[V]): KeyConflict[V] {.raises: [].} =
  ## The same conflict seen from the other side.
  KeyConflict[V](key: c.key, base: c.base, ours: c.theirs, theirs: c.ours)

func swapSides*[V](m: KeyedMerge[V]): KeyedMerge[V] {.raises: [].} =
  ## What `mergeKeyed(base, theirs, ours)` gives when `m` came from `mergeKeyed(base, ours, theirs)`.
  if m.isClean:
    result = m
  else:
    var swapped: seq[KeyConflict[V]] = @[]
    for c in m.conflicts: swapped.add swapSides(c)
    result = KeyedMerge[V](isClean: false, resolved: m.resolved, conflicts: swapped)

func mergeKeyed*[V](base, ours, theirs: Table[string, V]): KeyedMerge[V] {.raises: [].} =
  ## Per key: unchanged or changed the same way on both sides, take it; changed on one side only,
  ## take that side; changed differently on both (delete against modify included), conflict
  ## (STR-MERGE3-01..06). Absent is a value like any other, so a deletion is a change.
  var keys: seq[string] = @[]
  for k in base.keys: keys.add k
  for k in ours.keys: keys.add k
  for k in theirs.keys: keys.add k
  keys.sort()
  var settled = initTable[string, V]()
  var conflicts: seq[KeyConflict[V]] = @[]
  var previous = ""
  for i, k in keys:
    if i > 0 and k == previous: continue
    previous = k
    let b = base.look(k)
    let o = ours.look(k)
    let t = theirs.look(k)
    let chosen =
      if o == t or t == b: some(o)
      elif o == b: some(t)
      else: none(Option[V])
    if chosen.isSome:
      if chosen.get.isSome: settled[k] = chosen.get.get
    else:
      conflicts.add KeyConflict[V](key: k, base: b, ours: o, theirs: t)
  if conflicts.len == 0:
    KeyedMerge[V](isClean: true, merged: settled)
  else:
    KeyedMerge[V](isClean: false, resolved: settled, conflicts: conflicts)

func conflictKeys*[V](m: KeyedMerge[V]): seq[string] {.raises: [].} =
  ## The conflicting keys in ascending order; empty for a clean merge.
  result = @[]
  if not m.isClean:
    for c in m.conflicts: result.add c.key

# ─── sequence merge ─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────

func stable*[T](lines: seq[T]): Chunk[T] {.raises: [].} =
  Chunk[T](kind: ckStable, stable: lines)

func clean*[T](side: Side; taken: seq[T]): Chunk[T] {.raises: [].} =
  Chunk[T](kind: ckClean, side: side, taken: taken)

func conflict*[T](base, ours, theirs: seq[T]): Chunk[T] {.raises: [].} =
  Chunk[T](kind: ckConflict, base: base, ours: ours, theirs: theirs)

func swapSides*[T](chunks: seq[Chunk[T]]): seq[Chunk[T]] {.raises: [].} =
  ## What `merge3(base, theirs, ours)` gives when `chunks` came from `merge3(base, ours, theirs)`
  ## (STR-MERGE3-09).
  result = @[]
  for c in chunks:
    case c.kind
    of ckStable: result.add c
    of ckClean:
      let s = case c.side
        of sOurs: sTheirs
        of sTheirs: sOurs
        of sBoth: sBoth
      result.add clean(s, c.taken)
    of ckConflict: result.add conflict(c.base, c.theirs, c.ours)

func `==`*[T](a, b: Chunk[T]): bool {.raises: [].} =
  ## Nim cannot derive `==` for an object variant.
  if a.kind != b.kind: return false
  case a.kind
  of ckStable: a.stable == b.stable
  of ckClean: a.side == b.side and a.taken == b.taken
  of ckConflict: a.base == b.base and a.ours == b.ours and a.theirs == b.theirs

func matchOf[T](base, other: openArray[T]): seq[int] {.raises: [].} =
  ## For each base index, the index it is matched to in `other`, or -1. The matching is one
  ## embedding of `lcs(base, other)` into each side (leftmost), so it is increasing on both.
  let common = lcs(base, other)
  result = newSeq[int](base.len)
  for i in 0 ..< base.len: result[i] = -1
  var at = 0
  var inOther = 0
  for i in 0 ..< base.len:
    if at < common.len and base[i] == common[at]:
      while other[inOther] != common[at]: inc inOther
      result[i] = inOther
      inc inOther
      inc at

func slice[T](a: openArray[T]; lo, hiExcl: int): seq[T] {.raises: [].} =
  result = @[]
  for i in lo ..< hiExcl: result.add a[i]

func addStable[T](chunks: var seq[Chunk[T]]; lines: seq[T]) {.raises: [].} =
  if lines.len == 0: return
  if chunks.len > 0 and chunks[^1].kind == ckStable:
    for l in lines: chunks[^1].stable.add l
  else:
    chunks.add stable(lines)

func addRegion[T](chunks: var seq[Chunk[T]]; b, o, t: seq[T]) {.raises: [].} =
  ## One stretch between two lines that all three share.
  if b.len == 0 and o.len == 0 and t.len == 0: return
  if o == t:
    if o == b: chunks.addStable b
    else: chunks.add clean(sBoth, o)
  elif o == b: chunks.add clean(sTheirs, t)
  elif t == b: chunks.add clean(sOurs, o)
  else: chunks.add conflict(b, o, t)

func merge3*[T](base, ours, theirs: openArray[T]): seq[Chunk[T]] {.raises: [].} =
  ## diff3: the chunks, in order, that read as the merged sequence once every `Conflict` is
  ## decided (STR-MERGE3-07..11). Lines that `lcs` matches in `ours` and in `theirs` against the
  ## same base line are stable; each stretch between them is classified by comparing the three
  ## versions of it.
  let mo = matchOf(base, ours)
  let mt = matchOf(base, theirs)
  result = @[]
  var nextBase = 0
  var nextOurs = 0
  var nextTheirs = 0
  for i in 0 .. base.len:
    let atEnd = i == base.len
    if not atEnd and (mo[i] < 0 or mt[i] < 0): continue
    let inOurs = if atEnd: ours.len else: mo[i]
    let inTheirs = if atEnd: theirs.len else: mt[i]
    result.addRegion(base.slice(nextBase, i), ours.slice(nextOurs, inOurs), theirs.slice(nextTheirs, inTheirs))
    if not atEnd: result.addStable @[base[i]]
    nextBase = i + 1
    nextOurs = inOurs + 1
    nextTheirs = inTheirs + 1

func conflictCount*[T](chunks: seq[Chunk[T]]): int {.raises: [].} =
  for c in chunks:
    if c.kind == ckConflict: inc result

func mergeLines*[T](chunks: seq[Chunk[T]]): Option[seq[T]] {.raises: [].} =
  ## The merged sequence, or `none` while a conflict is open.
  var lines: seq[T] = @[]
  for c in chunks:
    case c.kind
    of ckStable: lines.add c.stable
    of ckClean: lines.add c.taken
    of ckConflict: return none(seq[T])
  some(lines)

func toLines*(text: string): seq[string] {.raises: [].} =
  ## Split on `\n`; a final newline ends the last line instead of starting an empty one.
  result = @[]
  if text.len == 0: return
  let parts = text.split('\n')
  let n = if text[^1] == '\n': parts.len - 1 else: parts.len
  for i in 0 ..< n: result.add parts[i]

func render*(chunks: seq[Chunk[string]]; oursLabel = "ours"; baseLabel = "base";
    theirsLabel = "theirs"): string {.raises: [].} =
  ## The text of a merge, one `\n`-ended line per element; each conflict is fenced as
  ## `<<<<<<< ours`, `||||||| base`, `=======`, `>>>>>>> theirs` (STR-MERGE3-12).
  result = ""
  for c in chunks:
    case c.kind
    of ckStable:
      for l in c.stable: result.add l & "\n"
    of ckClean:
      for l in c.taken: result.add l & "\n"
    of ckConflict:
      result.add "<<<<<<< " & oursLabel & "\n"
      for l in c.ours: result.add l & "\n"
      result.add "||||||| " & baseLabel & "\n"
      for l in c.base: result.add l & "\n"
      result.add "=======\n"
      for l in c.theirs: result.add l & "\n"
      result.add ">>>>>>> " & theirsLabel & "\n"

Write the Nim module `topo_sort.nim` (Topological sort).

Topological sort (Kahn's algorithm): repeatedly take a vertex with no remaining incoming arc.

Use it to order tasks, build steps or modules so that every dependency comes before what needs
it. It runs in O((V + E) log V) because the ready vertices sit in a small priority queue; that
makes the answer the lexicographically smallest valid order, which is deterministic. A cycle has
no valid order: the error carries one cycle, so the caller can report it.

Public API:
```nim
type TopoCycle = object
  vertices*: seq[int]
func topoSort(g: Graph): Result[seq[int], TopoCycle]
```

Write the Nim module `two_pointers.nim` (Two pointers and sliding window).

Two pointers and sliding window: scan a sequence once with two moving indices.

Use them when a property can only improve (or only worsen) as an index moves, so each index
needs to move one way only and the total work is O(n) instead of O(n^2). Here: finding a pair
of a sorted sequence that adds to a target (pointers from both ends), the longest window of
non-negative numbers whose sum stays within a bound (window grows right, shrinks left), and the
sums of all windows of one fixed size. Sums are `int`; the caller keeps them from overflowing.

Public API:
```nim
type PairError = enum
  peNotSorted,              ## the input is not in ascending order, so the method would give wrong answers
  peNoPair                   ## no two elements add up to the target
type Window = object
  start*, len*: int
type WindowError = enum
  weNegativeElement,        ## the window method needs non-negative numbers: a negative one breaks "shrinking never raises the sum"
  weNegativeBound,          ## no window, not even the empty one, has a sum below zero
  weBadSize                  ## a fixed window size below one
func `==`(a, b: Window): bool
func pairWithSum(sortedXs: openArray[int]; target: int): Result[(int, int), PairError]
func longestWindowAtMost(xs: openArray[int]; bound: int): Result[Window, WindowError]
func windowSums(xs: openArray[int]; size: int): Result[seq[int], WindowError]
```

Write the Nim module `z_algorithm.nim` (Z-algorithm).

The Z-array: for every position i, the length of the longest common prefix of the string and
its suffix starting at i, computed in linear time by reusing the rightmost match window.

Use it for pattern search (`zFindAll`), borders and periods of a string. It answers the same
questions as `kmp` with a simpler invariant (the window `[l, r)` is a match of the prefix),
which is why it is a good first linear-time string algorithm to learn.

Convention: `z[0]` is the length of the whole string (the suffix at 0 is the string itself).

Public API:
```nim
func zArray(s: string): seq[int]
func zFindAll(text, pattern: string): seq[int]
```
output:
## The Z-array: for every position i, the length of the longest common prefix of the string and
## its suffix starting at i, computed in linear time by reusing the rightmost match window.
##
## Use it for pattern search (`zFindAll`), borders and periods of a string. It answers the same
## questions as `kmp` with a simpler invariant (the window `[l, r)` is a match of the prefix),
## which is why it is a good first linear-time string algorithm to learn.
##
## Convention: `z[0]` is the length of the whole string (the suffix at 0 is the string itself).

func zArray*(s: string): seq[int] {.raises: [].} =
  ## `result[i]` = length of the longest common prefix of `s` and `s[i .. ^1]` (STR-ZALGO-01, STR-ZALGO-02).
  result = newSeq[int](s.len)
  if s.len == 0:
    return
  result[0] = s.len
  var l = 0
  var r = 0   # s[l ..< r] equals s[0 ..< r - l]
  for i in 1 ..< s.len:
    var k = 0
    if i < r:
      k = min(r - i, result[i - l])
    while i + k < s.len and s[k] == s[i + k]:
      inc k
    result[i] = k
    if i + k > r:
      l = i
      r = i + k

func zFindAll*(text, pattern: string): seq[int] {.raises: [].} =
  ## Start offsets of all occurrences of `pattern` in `text`, ascending. An empty pattern occurs
  ## at every offset 0 .. text.len (STR-ZALGO-03, STR-ZALGO-04).
  ##
  ## Z is computed on `pattern & text` with no separator: a value `z[i] >= pattern.len` at
  ## i >= pattern.len means `s[i ..< i + m]` equals the pattern, and that range lies inside `text`.
  result = @[]
  let m = pattern.len
  if m == 0:
    for i in 0 .. text.len:
      result.add i
    return
  let z = zArray(pattern & text)
  for i in m ..< z.len:
    if z[i] >= m:
      result.add i - m

Write the Nim module `avl_tree.nim` (AVL tree (persistent)).

Persistent AVL tree: a self-balancing ordered set.

A binary search tree in which, at every node, the heights of the two subtrees differ by at most
one. Each node stores its height; after an insert or delete, `balance` restores the rule on the
way back up the path with one single or double rotation. The rule keeps the height below
1.4405 log2(n + 2), so `insert`, `delete` and `contains` are O(log n) worst case. Nodes are
immutable `ref`s, so an update copies only the path it walks and the old tree stays valid.
Use it when lookups dominate (AVL trees are a little more rigidly balanced than red-black
trees); use `rb_tree` for a map with the same guarantees. The item type needs `<`; two items
are equal when neither is smaller.

Public API:
```nim
type AvlTree[T] = object
func emptyAvl[T](): AvlTree[T]
func len[T](t: AvlTree[T]): int
func isEmpty[T](t: AvlTree[T]): bool
func contains[T](t: AvlTree[T]; x: T): bool
func insert[T](t: AvlTree[T]; x: T): AvlTree[T]
func delete[T](t: AvlTree[T]; x: T): AvlTree[T]
func height[T](t: AvlTree[T]): int
func smallest[T](t: AvlTree[T]): Option[T]
func toSeq[T](t: AvlTree[T]): seq[T]
func fromSeq[T](items: openArray[T]): AvlTree[T]
func invariantsHold[T](t: AvlTree[T]): bool
```

Write the Nim module `b_tree.nim` (B-tree).

B-tree: a persistent ordered set whose nodes hold many keys.

Every node stores between `t - 1` and `2t - 1` sorted keys (`t` is the minimum degree; the root
may hold fewer), an internal node has one more child than keys, and all leaves are at the same
depth. A search therefore reads O(log_t n) nodes, and each node is a contiguous run of keys:
that is what pays off when a node is a disk page or a few cache lines. Insertion splits a
node that grows past `2t - 1` keys and pushes the median up; only the nodes on one
root-to-leaf path are copied, so the old tree stays valid. The set is insert-only here
(deletion needs borrow and merge cases that add length without adding a new idea); use
`rb_tree` for a binary balanced set, `std/sets` when order does not matter.

Public API:
```nim

func minDegree[T](t: BTree[T]): int
func len[T](t: BTree[T]): int
func isEmpty[T](t: BTree[T]): bool
func contains[T](t: BTree[T]; x: T): bool
```

Write the Nim module `bankers_queue.nim` (Banker's queue).

Persistent FIFO queue made of two lists (a "banker's queue" without laziness).

`front` holds the elements about to leave in order, `rear` holds the newest elements in reverse.
Pushing conses onto `rear`; popping drops from `front`; when `rear` grows longer than `front`
the two are joined by reversing `rear` once. Every operation is O(1) amortized when each
version of the queue is used once (the ephemeral use of a queue). A persistent version that is
popped many times from the same state can pay the reversal again each time; when that matters
use a real-time queue or `deque`. Use a queue for breadth-first search, work lists and
producer/consumer pipelines in functional code.

Public API:
```nim

func len[T](q: BankersQueue[T]): int
func isEmpty[T](q: BankersQueue[T]): bool
func push[T](q: BankersQueue[T]; x: T): BankersQueue[T]
func peek[T](q: BankersQueue[T]): Option[T]
func pop[T](q: BankersQueue[T]): BankersQueue[T]

func fromSeq[T](items: openArray[T]): BankersQueue[T]
```

## the two are joined by reversing `rear` once. Every operation is O(1) amortized when each
## version of the queue is used once (the ephemeral use of a queue). A persistent version that is
## popped many times from the same state can pay the reversal again each time; when that matters
## use a real-time queue or `deque`. Use a queue for breadth-first search, work lists and
## producer/consumer pipelines in functional code.

import std/options
import nimcs/ds/cons_list

type
  BankersQueue*[T] = object
    front: ConsList[T]
    rear: ConsList[T]
    lenFront: int
    lenRear: int

func emptyQueue*[T](): BankersQueue[T] {.raises: [].} =
  BankersQueue[T]()

func len*[T](q: BankersQueue[T]): int {.raises: [].} =
  q.lenFront + q.lenRear

func isEmpty*[T](q: BankersQueue[T]): bool {.raises: [].} =
  q.len == 0

func rebalanced[T](q: BankersQueue[T]): BankersQueue[T] =
  ## Invariant: lenRear <= lenFront, hence `front` is empty only for the empty queue.
  if q.lenRear <= q.lenFront: q
  else:
    BankersQueue[T](front: q.front.append(q.rear.reverse), rear: emptyList[T](),
      lenFront: q.len, lenRear: 0)

func push*[T](q: BankersQueue[T]; x: T): BankersQueue[T] {.raises: [].} =
  ## Enqueue at the back.
  BankersQueue[T](front: q.front, rear: q.rear.cons(x), lenFront: q.lenFront,
    lenRear: q.lenRear + 1).rebalanced

func peek*[T](q: BankersQueue[T]): Option[T] {.raises: [].} =
  ## The element that `pop` removes next.
  q.front.head

func pop*[T](q: BankersQueue[T]): BankersQueue[T] {.raises: [].} =
  ## The queue without its oldest element; the empty queue stays empty.
  if q.isEmpty: q
  else:
    BankersQueue[T](front: q.front.tail, rear: q.rear, lenFront: q.lenFront - 1,
      lenRear: q.lenRear).rebalanced

func toSeq*[T](q: BankersQueue[T]): seq[T] {.raises: [].} =
  ## Elements from oldest to newest.
  q.front.toSeq & q.rear.reverse.toSeq

func fromSeq*[T](items: openArray[T]): BankersQueue[T] {.raises: [].} =
  var q = emptyQueue[T]()
  for x in items:
    q = q.push(x)
  q

Write the Nim module `binary_heap.nim` (Binary heap (array-based min-heap)).

Array-based binary min-heap, as a value.

The items sit in one `seq` where the children of index `i` are `2i + 1` and `2i + 2` and no
child is smaller than its parent, so the minimum is always at index 0. `push` appends and sifts
up, `pop` moves the last item to the root and sifts down, `heapify` builds a heap from any
sequence in O(n) by sifting down from the last parent to the root. The type is a value
(ADR-NCK-0002): `push` and `pop` return a new heap and copy the array, O(n); the O(log n) sift is
the cheap part. Build with `heapify` and drain with `toSortedSeq` (both do their sifting on a
local copy), or use `std/heapqueue` inside one routine when in-place updates are fine. When old
versions must stay cheap, use the persistent `leftist_heap`, `pairing_heap` or `binomial_heap`.
The item type needs `<`.

## Array-based binary min-heap, as a value.
##
## The items sit in one `seq` where the children of index `i` are `2i + 1` and `2i + 2` and no
## child is smaller than its parent, so the minimum is always at index 0. `push` appends and sifts
## up, `pop` moves the last item to the root and sifts down, `heapify` builds a heap from any
## sequence in O(n) by sifting down from the last parent to the root. The type is a value
## (ADR-NCK-0002): `push` and `pop` return a new heap and copy the array, O(n); the O(log n) sift is
## the cheap part. Build with `heapify` and drain with `toSortedSeq` (both do their sifting on a
## local copy), or use `std/heapqueue` inside one routine when in-place updates are fine. When old
## versions must stay cheap, use the persistent `leftist_heap`, `pairing_heap` or `binomial_heap`.
## The item type needs `<`.

import std/options

type
  BinaryHeap*[T] = object
    items: seq[T]

func emptyHeap*[T](): BinaryHeap[T] {.raises: [].} =
  BinaryHeap[T]()

func len*[T](h: BinaryHeap[T]): int {.raises: [].} =
  h.items.len

func isEmpty*[T](h: BinaryHeap[T]): bool {.raises: [].} =
  h.items.len == 0

func siftUp[T](a: var seq[T]; start: int) =
  var i = start
  while i > 0:
    let parent = (i - 1) div 2
    if a[i] < a[parent]:
      swap(a[i], a[parent])
      i = parent
    else:
      break

func siftDown[T](a: var seq[T]; start, limit: int) =
  ## Sifts the item at `start` down within the first `limit` items.
  var i = start
  while true:
    let l = 2 * i + 1
    let r = l + 1
    var smallest = i
    if l < limit and a[l] < a[smallest]: smallest = l
    if r < limit and a[r] < a[smallest]: smallest = r
    if smallest == i: break
    swap(a[i], a[smallest])
    i = smallest

func push*[T](h: BinaryHeap[T]; x: T): BinaryHeap[T] {.raises: [].} =
  var a = h.items
  a.add x
  a.siftUp(a.len - 1)
  BinaryHeap[T](items: a)

func peek*[T](h: BinaryHeap[T]): Option[T] {.raises: [].} =
  if h.items.len == 0: none(T) else: some(h.items[0])

func pop*[T](h: BinaryHeap[T]): BinaryHeap[T] {.raises: [].} =
  ## The heap without its minimum; the empty heap stays empty.
  if h.items.len <= 1: BinaryHeap[T]()
  else:
    var a = h.items
    a[0] = a[a.len - 1]
    a.setLen(a.len - 1)
    a.siftDown(0, a.len)
    BinaryHeap[T](items: a)

func heapify*[T](items: openArray[T]): BinaryHeap[T] {.raises: [].} =
  ## Floyd's construction, O(n): sift down every parent, last one first.
  var a = @items
  for i in countdown(a.len div 2 - 1, 0):
    a.siftDown(i, a.len)
  BinaryHeap[T](items: a)

func toSortedSeq*[T](h: BinaryHeap[T]): seq[T] {.raises: [].} =
  ## Heap sort on a copy, O(n log n); the heap itself is untouched. Each round moves the current
  ## minimum to the end of the shrinking heap, so the array ends up in descending order and is
  ## read backwards.
  var a = h.items
  var last = a.len - 1
  while last > 0:
    swap(a[0], a[last])
    a.siftDown(0, last)
    dec last
  result = newSeq[T](a.len)
  for i in 0 ..< a.len:
    result[i] = a[a.len - 1 - i]

func invariantsHold*[T](h: BinaryHeap[T]): bool {.raises: [].} =
  ## No item is smaller than its parent.
  for i in 1 ..< h.items.len:
    if h.items[i] < h.items[(i - 1) div 2]: return false
  true

Write the Nim module `binomial_heap.nim` (Binomial heap).

Binomial heap: a persistent min-heap whose merge works like binary addition.

A heap is a list of binomial trees in increasing rank, at most one tree per rank, exactly like
the set bits of n. A tree of rank r has 2^r nodes; linking two trees of rank r gives one of
rank r+1 (a carry). `insert`, `merge` and `deleteMin` are O(log n) worst case; `insert` is O(1)
amortized only for ephemeral use (a run of inserts where each version is used once), because
a persistent program can repeat the longest carry chain from one old version. Use it when you
want the arithmetic analogy to guide the reasoning and a worst-case O(log n) bound for all
three operations.

Write the Nim module `bit_vector.nim` (Bit vector).

Bit vector: a fixed-size set of the integers 0 ..< n, one bit each, packed into 64-bit words.

The size is part of the value and never changes. Membership, `count` (population count),
`rank` (how many members are below an index) and `select` (the index of the k-th member) are
word operations, so a set of n small integers takes n/8 bytes and set algebra (union,
intersection, difference, complement) runs 64 elements at a time. A `BitVector` is a value:
`withBit` and `withoutBit` return a new vector and copy n/64 words. Use it when the universe is
a known range of small integers (flags, visited marks, sieve results, dense id sets). Use
`std/sets` for sparse or non-integer members, and `bloom_filter` when memory must stay below
one bit per possible member and a false positive is acceptable (a bit vector never lies).

Write the Nim module `bloom_filter.nim` (Bloom filter).

Bloom filter with value semantics: a compact set that may say "yes" for an absent key but never
says "no" for a present one.

`add` returns a new filter (the bit array is copied, O(bits / 64)); the old filter is unchanged.
The `k` bit positions of a key come from two base hashes as `h1 + i * h2` (double hashing), so
only two hash computations are needed however large `k` is. Both hashes come from `std/hashes`
on `(salt, key)` pairs and are deterministic; the stride is chosen coprime to the bit count so a
key sets `min(hashCount, bits)` distinct bits for every bit count. Use it to skip expensive
lookups for keys that are certainly absent; do not use it when a false positive is unacceptable
or when you must delete.

Write the Nim module `bst.nim` (Binary search tree (unbalanced, persistent)).

Unbalanced binary search tree, persistent: a set of ordered items.

Every node holds one item, with smaller items in the left subtree and larger ones in the right.
Nodes are immutable `ref`s; `insert` and `delete` copy only the path they walk and share the rest
with the old tree, which stays valid. There is no rebalancing, so the cost of an operation is
the depth of the tree: O(log n) for items that arrive in random order, O(n) when they arrive
sorted (the tree degenerates into a list). Use it to learn the ordered-tree operations and the
three depth-first traversals; use `rb_tree` or `avl_tree` when the input order is not under
your control. The item type needs `<`; two items are equal when neither is smaller.

Write the Nim module `consistent_hashing.nim` (Consistent hashing).

Consistent hashing: a hash ring with virtual nodes, as a value.

Keys and nodes are hashed onto a circle of 2^64 positions. A node owns several positions (its
virtual nodes, `vnodes` of them, named `<node>#0`, `<node>#1`, ...), and a key belongs to the node
at the first position at or after the key's own, wrapping around at the top. Adding a node takes
over only the arcs just before its new positions and removing a node gives only its arcs to the
next positions, so a change in membership moves a small share of the keys instead of nearly all of
them, as `hash mod n` would. Many virtual nodes per node smooth the share each node gets.

The hash, `ringHash`, is fixed in this module (FNV-1a 64 followed by a bit mixer), so owners are the
same on every run, platform and compiler version, and a ring's layout depends only on which nodes
are present, not on the order they were added. It is not a cryptographic hash.

## Consistent hashing: a hash ring with virtual nodes, as a value.
##
## Keys and nodes are hashed onto a circle of 2^64 positions. A node owns several positions (its
## virtual nodes, `vnodes` of them, named `<node>#0`, `<node>#1`, ...), and a key belongs to the node
## at the first position at or after the key's own, wrapping around at the top. Adding a node takes
## over only the arcs just before its new positions and removing a node gives only its arcs to the
## next positions, so a change in membership moves a small share of the keys instead of nearly all of
## them, as `hash mod n` would. Many virtual nodes per node smooth the share each node gets.
##
## The hash, `ringHash`, is fixed in this module (FNV-1a 64 followed by a bit mixer), so owners are the
## same on every run, platform and compiler version, and a ring's layout depends only on which nodes
## are present, not on the order they were added. It is not a cryptographic hash.

import std/[algorithm, options]
import nimcs/fp/result
export result

type
  RingError* = enum
    reNoVnodes,             ## `vnodes` below 1
    reEmptyName             ## a node with an empty name
  Point = object
    pos: uint64
    node: string
  Ring* = object
    vnodes: int
    members: seq[string]    ## sorted, no duplicates
    points: seq[Point]      ## sorted by (pos, node)

func ringHash*(s: string): uint64 {.raises: [].} =
  ## FNV-1a 64 over the bytes, then the 64-bit finalizer of MurmurHash3 so that nearby strings
  ## land far apart on the ring. Fixed forever: stored placements depend on it.
  var h = 0xcbf29ce484222325'u64
  for c in s:
    h = (h xor uint64(ord(c))) * 0x100000001b3'u64
  h = h xor (h shr 33)
  h = h * 0xff51afd7ed558ccd'u64
  h = h xor (h shr 33)
  h = h * 0xc4ceb9fe1a85ec53'u64
  h xor (h shr 33)

func newRing*(vnodes: int): Result[Ring, RingError] {.raises: [].} =
  ## An empty ring whose nodes will each take `vnodes` positions (at least 1; 64 to 256 is typical).
  if vnodes < 1: err(Ring, reNoVnodes)
  else: ok(Ring(vnodes: vnodes), RingError)

func vnodeCount*(r: Ring): int {.raises: [].} =
  r.vnodes

func len*(r: Ring): int {.raises: [].} =
  ## Number of nodes.
  r.members.len

func nodes*(r: Ring): seq[string] {.raises: [].} =
  ## The nodes in name order.
  r.members

func contains*(r: Ring; node: string): bool {.raises: [].} =
  binarySearch(r.members, node) >= 0

func `==`*(a, b: Ring): bool {.raises: [].} =
  ## Same vnode count and same positions (which implies the same nodes).
  if a.vnodes != b.vnodes or a.points.len != b.points.len: return false
  for i in 0 ..< a.points.len:
    if a.points[i].pos != b.points[i].pos or a.points[i].node != b.points[i].node: return false
  true

func cmpPoint(a, b: Point): int =
  if a.pos != b.pos: (if a.pos < b.pos: -1 else: 1)
  else: cmp(a.node, b.node)

func vnodePosition*(node: string; i: int): uint64 {.raises: [].} =
  ## Where virtual node `i` of `node` sits on the ring. The name `node#i` is unambiguous: the digits
  ## after the last `#` are the index.
  ringHash(node & "#" & $i)

func addNode*(r: Ring; node: string): Result[Ring, RingError] {.raises: [].} =
  ## The ring with `node` added; the same ring when it is already there.
  if node.len == 0: return err(Ring, reEmptyName)
  if node in r: return ok(r, RingError)
  var points = r.points
  for i in 0 ..< r.vnodes:
    points.add Point(pos: vnodePosition(node, i), node: node)
  points.sort(cmpPoint)
  var members = r.members
  members.add node
  members.sort()
  ok(Ring(vnodes: r.vnodes, members: members, points: points), RingError)

func removeNode*(r: Ring; node: string): Ring {.raises: [].} =
  ## The ring without `node`; the same ring when it is not there.
  if node notin r: return r
  var points: seq[Point]
  for p in r.points:
    if p.node != node: points.add p
  var members: seq[string]
  for m in r.members:
    if m != node: members.add m
  Ring(vnodes: r.vnodes, members: members, points: points)

func firstAtOrAfter(r: Ring; h: uint64): int =
  ## Index of the first point with position >= h; wraps to 0 past the end. The ring must not be empty.
  var lo = 0
  var hi = r.points.len
  while lo < hi:
    let mid = lo + (hi - lo) div 2
    if r.points[mid].pos < h: lo = mid + 1
    else: hi = mid
  if lo == r.points.len: 0 else: lo

func owner*(r: Ring; key: string): Option[string] {.raises: [].} =
  ## The node that owns `key`; none when the ring has no node. O(log(nodes * vnodes)).
  if r.points.len == 0: none(string)
  else: some(r.points[firstAtOrAfter(r, ringHash(key))].node)

func owners*(r: Ring; key: string; count: int): seq[string] {.raises: [].} =
  ## Up to `count` distinct nodes for `key` (a replica list): the owner first, then the nodes met
  ## walking clockwise. Fewer when the ring has fewer nodes.
  if r.points.len == 0 or count < 1: return @[]
  let start = firstAtOrAfter(r, ringHash(key))
  var step = 0
  while step < r.points.len and result.len < count:
    let node = r.points[(start + step) mod r.points.len].node
    if node notin result: result.add node
    inc step

Write the Nim module `crdt.nim` (State-based CRDTs).

State-based CRDTs (conflict-free replicated data types) as plain values: `GCounter`, `PNCounter`,
`LwwRegister` and `OrSet`.

Each replica holds its own copy of the state and changes it locally with no coordination. Copies
are brought together with `merge`, which is the join of a semilattice: commutative
(`a.merge(b) == b.merge(a)`), associative and idempotent (`a.merge(a) == a`). Because of those
three laws the order in which copies are merged, how often, and in how many groups, does not matter:
replicas that have seen the same updates hold equal states, whatever route the updates took. Every
local update is itself a merge with a small state (a one-count delta, a one-dot set), which is why
an update can never lose information that a merge would keep.

States are kept in a canonical form (sorted sequences, no zero entries, no duplicates), so `==` on
two states is equality of what they know, not an accident of the order of operations. Nothing here
iterates a hash table.

Rules for the user. A `ReplicaId` must belong to one live copy of the state at a time: two copies
that both update as replica `a` can lose increments (counters) or invent the same tag for two
different additions (`OrSet`). `LwwRegister` order values by (stamp, replica, value), so the
stamps must come from a clock the replicas roughly share, and a replica with a slow clock loses
its writes; the value type needs a `<` that is a strict total order consistent with `==`. `OrSet`
keeps a tombstone for every removed addition and never forgets one, so it grows with the number of
removals. Counter values are `int`: overflow is a `Defect` (`OverflowDefect`), not a wrap.

## State-based CRDTs (conflict-free replicated data types) as plain values: `GCounter`, `PNCounter`,
## `LwwRegister` and `OrSet`.
##
## Each replica holds its own copy of the state and changes it locally with no coordination. Copies
## are brought together with `merge`, which is the join of a semilattice: commutative
## (`a.merge(b) == b.merge(a)`), associative and idempotent (`a.merge(a) == a`). Because of those
## three laws the order in which copies are merged, how often, and in how many groups, does not matter:
## replicas that have seen the same updates hold equal states, whatever route the updates took. Every
## local update is itself a merge with a small state (a one-count delta, a one-dot set), which is why
## an update can never lose information that a merge would keep.
##
## States are kept in a canonical form (sorted sequences, no zero entries, no duplicates), so `==` on
## two states is equality of what they know, not an accident of the order of operations. Nothing here
## iterates a hash table.
##
## Rules for the user. A `ReplicaId` must belong to one live copy of the state at a time: two copies
## that both update as replica `a` can lose increments (counters) or invent the same tag for two
## different additions (`OrSet`). `LwwRegister` order values by (stamp, replica, value), so the
## stamps must come from a clock the replicas roughly share, and a replica with a slow clock loses
## its writes; the value type needs a `<` that is a strict total order consistent with `==`. `OrSet`
## keeps a tombstone for every removed addition and never forgets one, so it grows with the number of
## removals. Counter values are `int`: overflow is a `Defect` (`OverflowDefect`), not a wrap.

import std/options
import nimcs/fp/result
export result

type
  CrdtError* = enum
    ceEmptyReplica          ## a replica id with an empty name
  ReplicaId* = distinct string

func `==`*(a, b: ReplicaId): bool {.borrow.}
func `<`*(a, b: ReplicaId): bool {.borrow.}
func `$`*(r: ReplicaId): string {.borrow.}

func replicaId*(name: string): Result[ReplicaId, CrdtError] {.raises: [].} =
  ## A replica id; the name must not be empty.
  if name.len == 0: err(ReplicaId, ceEmptyReplica)
  else: ok(ReplicaId(name), CrdtError)

# --- G-Counter ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------

type
  Slot = object
    replica: ReplicaId
    count: int            ## always > 0
  GCounter* = object
    ## A counter that only grows: one slot per replica that has counted.
    slots: seq[Slot]

func `==`(a, b: Slot): bool {.raises: [].} =
  a.replica == b.replica and a.count == b.count

func emptyGCounter*(): GCounter {.raises: [].} =
  GCounter(slots: @[])

func `==`*(a, b: GCounter): bool {.raises: [].} =
  a.slots == b.slots

func merge*(a, b: GCounter): GCounter {.raises: [].} =
  ## Slot by slot, the larger count (a replica that is missing counts 0).
  var i = 0
  var j = 0
  var slots: seq[Slot]
  while i < a.slots.len and j < b.slots.len:
    if a.slots[i].replica < b.slots[j].replica:
      slots.add a.slots[i]
      inc i
    elif b.slots[j].replica < a.slots[i].replica:
      slots.add b.slots[j]
      inc j
    else:
      slots.add Slot(replica: a.slots[i].replica, count: max(a.slots[i].count, b.slots[j].count))
      inc i
      inc j
  while i < a.slots.len:
    slots.add a.slots[i]
    inc i
  while j < b.slots.len:
    slots.add b.slots[j]
    inc j
  GCounter(slots: slots)

func countOf*(c: GCounter; r: ReplicaId): int {.raises: [].} =
  ## What replica `r` has counted so far.
  for s in c.slots:
    if s.replica == r: return s.count
  0

func value*(c: GCounter): int {.raises: [].} =
  ## The total over all replicas.
  for s in c.slots:
    result += s.count

func increment*(c: GCounter; r: ReplicaId; by: Natural = 1): GCounter {.raises: [].} =
  ## Replica `r` counts `by` more: a merge with a counter that holds `r`'s new total.
  if by == 0: return c
  c.merge(GCounter(slots: @[Slot(replica: r, count: c.countOf(r) + by)]))

# --- PN-Counter -----------------------------------------------------------------------------------

type
  PNCounter* = object
    ## A counter that goes up and down: a G-Counter of increments and one of decrements.
    ups, downs: GCounter

func emptyPNCounter*(): PNCounter {.raises: [].} =
  PNCounter(ups: emptyGCounter(), downs: emptyGCounter())

func `==`*(a, b: PNCounter): bool {.raises: [].} =
  a.ups == b.ups and a.downs == b.downs

func merge*(a, b: PNCounter): PNCounter {.raises: [].} =
  PNCounter(ups: a.ups.merge(b.ups), downs: a.downs.merge(b.downs))

func value*(c: PNCounter): int {.raises: [].} =
  ## Increments minus decrements, over all replicas.
  c.ups.value - c.downs.value

func increment*(c: PNCounter; r: ReplicaId; by: Natural = 1): PNCounter {.raises: [].} =
  PNCounter(ups: c.ups.increment(r, by), downs: c.downs)

func decrement*(c: PNCounter; r: ReplicaId; by: Natural = 1): PNCounter {.raises: [].} =
  PNCounter(ups: c.ups, downs: c.downs.increment(r, by))

# --- LWW-Register ---------------------------------------------------------------------------------

type
  LwwEntry[T] = object
    stamp: int
    replica: ReplicaId
    val: T
  LwwRegister*[T] = object
    ## A single value; of two writes the later wins. Later means a larger stamp, then a larger replica
    ## id, then a larger value, so every pair of different writes has a winner and merge is symmetric.
    cur: Option[LwwEntry[T]]

func entryLess[T](a, b: LwwEntry[T]): bool =
  if a.stamp != b.stamp: a.stamp < b.stamp
  elif a.replica != b.replica: a.replica < b.replica
  else: a.val < b.val

func `==`[T](a, b: LwwEntry[T]): bool =
  a.stamp == b.stamp and a.replica == b.replica and not (a.val < b.val) and not (b.val < a.val)

func emptyRegister*[T](): LwwRegister[T] {.raises: [].} =
  ## A register nobody has written; it loses to every write.
  LwwRegister[T](cur: none(LwwEntry[T]))

func `==`*[T](a, b: LwwRegister[T]): bool {.raises: [].} =
  if a.cur.isNone or b.cur.isNone: a.cur.isNone and b.cur.isNone
  else: a.cur.get == b.cur.get

func merge*[T](a, b: LwwRegister[T]): LwwRegister[T] {.raises: [].} =
  ## The later of the two writes.
  if a.cur.isNone: b
  elif b.cur.isNone: a
  elif entryLess(a.cur.get, b.cur.get): b
  else: a

func registerOf*[T](stamp: int; replica: ReplicaId; v: T): LwwRegister[T] {.raises: [].} =
  ## A register holding one write.
  LwwRegister[T](cur: some(LwwEntry[T](stamp: stamp, replica: replica, val: v)))

func write*[T](reg: LwwRegister[T]; stamp: int; replica: ReplicaId; v: T): LwwRegister[T] {.raises: [].} =
  ## A local write: a merge with a one-write register. A write with an older stamp than the
  ## register already holds does not replace it.
  reg.merge(registerOf(stamp, replica, v))

func value*[T](reg: LwwRegister[T]): Option[T] {.raises: [].} =
  if reg.cur.isNone: none(T) else: some(reg.cur.get.val)

func stamp*[T](reg: LwwRegister[T]): Option[int] {.raises: [].} =
  if reg.cur.isNone: none(int) else: some(reg.cur.get.stamp)

func writer*[T](reg: LwwRegister[T]): Option[ReplicaId] {.raises: [].} =
  if reg.cur.isNone: none(ReplicaId) else: some(reg.cur.get.replica)

# --- OR-Set ---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------

type
  Tag = object
    replica: ReplicaId
    n: int
  Dot[T] = object
    elem: T
    tag: Tag
  OrSet*[T] = object
    ## A set whose additions carry unique tags. `remove` cancels only the tags it has seen, so an
    ## addition made concurrently with a removal survives the merge ("add wins").
    adds: seq[Dot[T]]       ## strictly increasing by (elem, tag)
    removed: seq[Tag]       ## tombstones, strictly increasing

func `<`(a, b: Tag): bool =
  if a.replica != b.replica: a.replica < b.replica
  else: a.n < b.n

func `<`[T](a, b: Dot[T]): bool =
  if a.elem < b.elem: true
  elif b.elem < a.elem: false
  else: a.tag < b.tag

# sorted-sequence helpers, after the orders they use are declared

func unionSorted[T](a, b: seq[T]): seq[T] =
  ## The union of two strictly increasing sequences, strictly increasing; elements that are neither
  ## less nor greater than each other count once.
  var i = 0
  var j = 0
  while i < a.len and j < b.len:
    if a[i] < b[j]:
      result.add a[i]
      inc i
    elif b[j] < a[i]:
      result.add b[j]
      inc j
    else:
      result.add a[i]
      inc i
      inc j
  while i < a.len:
    result.add a[i]
    inc i
  while j < b.len:
    result.add b[j]
    inc j

func isMember[T](xs: seq[T]; x: T): bool =
  ## Binary search in a strictly increasing sequence.
  var lo = 0
  var hi = xs.len
  while lo < hi:
    let mid = lo + (hi - lo) div 2
    if xs[mid] < x: lo = mid + 1
    elif x < xs[mid]: hi = mid
    else: return true
  false

func emptyOrSet*[T](): OrSet[T] {.raises: [].} =
  OrSet[T](adds: @[], removed: @[])

func `==`*[T](a, b: OrSet[T]): bool {.raises: [].} =
  ## Same additions and same tombstones.
  if a.adds.len != b.adds.len or a.removed.len != b.removed.len: return false
  for i in 0 ..< a.adds.len:
    if a.adds[i] < b.adds[i] or b.adds[i] < a.adds[i]: return false
  for i in 0 ..< a.removed.len:
    if a.removed[i] < b.removed[i] or b.removed[i] < a.removed[i]: return false
  true

func merge*[T](a, b: OrSet[T]): OrSet[T] {.raises: [].} =
  ## The union of the additions and the union of the tombstones.
  OrSet[T](adds: unionSorted(a.adds, b.adds), removed: unionSorted(a.removed, b.removed))

func live[T](s: OrSet[T]; d: Dot[T]): bool =
  not s.removed.isMember(d.tag)

func contains*[T](s: OrSet[T]; x: T): bool {.raises: [].} =
  for d in s.adds:
    if not (d.elem < x) and not (x < d.elem) and s.live(d): return true
  false

func elements*[T](s: OrSet[T]): seq[T] {.raises: [].} =
  ## The members, in increasing order, each once.
  for d in s.adds:
    if s.live(d) and (result.len == 0 or result[result.len - 1] < d.elem):
      result.add d.elem

func len*[T](s: OrSet[T]): int {.raises: [].} =
  s.elements.len

func tombstoneCount*[T](s: OrSet[T]): int {.raises: [].} =
  ## How many removed additions are remembered; it only grows.
  s.removed.len

func nextTag[T](s: OrSet[T]; r: ReplicaId): Tag =
  var top = 0
  for d in s.adds:
    if d.tag.replica == r: top = max(top, d.tag.n)
  for t in s.removed:
    if t.replica == r: top = max(top, t.n)
  Tag(replica: r, n: top + 1)

func add*[T](s: OrSet[T]; r: ReplicaId; x: T): OrSet[T] {.raises: [].} =
  ## Replica `r` adds `x` under a tag it has not used before (one more than the largest it has made).
  let dot = Dot[T](elem: x, tag: s.nextTag(r))
  s.merge(OrSet[T](adds: @[dot], removed: @[]))

func remove*[T](s: OrSet[T]; x: T): OrSet[T] {.raises: [].} =
  ## Cancels every addition of `x` this copy has seen. Removing what is not a member changes nothing.
  var seen: seq[Tag]
  for d in s.adds:
    if not (d.elem < x) and not (x < d.elem): seen.add d.tag
  if seen.len == 0: return s
  s.merge(OrSet[T](adds: @[], removed: seen))

Write the Nim module `deque.nim` (Deque).

Persistent double-ended queue from two lists with rebalancing.

The front list holds the left end in order, the rear list the right end reversed. Pushing and
popping at either end is O(1) except when one list becomes more than twice as long as the other
(plus one): then the elements are split evenly again at O(n). Every operation is O(1) amortized
when each version of the deque is used once (the ephemeral use). A persistent program that
keeps pushing onto the same old version, just short of a rebalance, pays O(n) every time;
there is no worst-case O(1) bound here (a real-time deque needs lazy rotations). Use it when
elements enter or leave at both ends (sliding windows, undo/redo buffers); use
`bankers_queue` when only one end pops.

Public API:

Write the Nim module `fenwick_tree.nim` (Fenwick tree).

Fenwick tree (binary indexed tree): prefix sums with point updates over integers.

Slot `i` (1-based) of a flat array stores the sum of the `lowbit(i)` elements that end at `i`,
where `lowbit(i)` is the largest power of two dividing `i`. A prefix sum adds O(log n) slots
(strip the lowest set bit each step); a point update adds to O(log n) slots (add the lowest set
bit each step). Because a range sum is the difference of two prefix sums, the element type
must have an inverse: this is the integers under `+`. Use it for running totals, rank counting
and inversion counting; use `segment_tree` when the operation is only associative (min, gcd,
string concatenation). A `FenwickTree` is a value: every update returns a new tree, so the
copy of the flat array costs O(n); `addAll` applies many updates with one copy.

Precondition for all sums: every prefix sum fits in `int`.

Public API:
