
Write the Nim module `hamt.nim` (Hash array mapped trie (HAMT)).

Hash array mapped trie (HAMT): a persistent unordered map with O(log32 n) operations.

The hash of a key is read five bits at a time; each trie node stores a 32-bit bitmap saying
which of its 32 slots are used and keeps only the used slots in a compact `seq`. A slot holds
a single pair, a child node, or (when all 60+ hash bits agree) a bucket of colliding pairs.
`put` and `remove` copy one root-to-leaf path and share the rest. The hash comes from
`std/hashes` (`hash(key)`), which is deterministic for ints and strings; iteration order
follows hash bits, so it is never exposed: the only way to list entries is `toSortedSeq`.
Use it for large maps that are updated functionally and need no key order; use `rb_tree` when
you need ordered traversal.

Write the Nim module `hash_table.nim` (Hash table (open addressing, linear probing)).

Hash table with open addressing and linear probing, as a value type.

All entries live in one flat `seq` of slots. A key starts at the slot its hash selects and, when
that slot is taken, moves one slot forward (wrapping around) until it finds its key or an empty
slot. `del` shifts the following entries of the probe run backwards instead of leaving
tombstones, so a lookup never walks over dead slots. The capacity is a power of two and the load
stays at or below three quarters, so a probe run always ends at an empty slot.

The type is a value (ADR-NCK-0002): `put` and `del` return a new table and the old one stays
valid. That costs a copy of the slot array per update, O(n), so the cheap way to build a table
is `fromPairs` (one local table, O(1) amortized per entry) and the cheap way to update a table
in a loop is to keep a `var` local to one routine. Inside one routine, `std/tables` is the better
tool; reach for this module to see how a hash table works or when an immutable snapshot with
a deterministic `sortedPairs` view is wanted, and for `hamt` when old versions must stay cheap.
The key type needs `hash` and `==`; `sortedPairs` also needs `<`.

Write the Nim module `kd_tree.nim` (kd-tree (2-d)).

Static 2-d tree: nearest neighbour and rectangle queries over a fixed set of points.

The tree is built once from a sequence of points. At each level the points are sorted along one
axis (x at the root, then y, then x again), the median becomes the node, and the two halves
become its subtrees, so the tree is balanced with height about log2 n. Nothing is updated
afterwards: the tree is an immutable value, safe to share. `nearest` descends towards the query
point and visits the far side only when the splitting line is at least as close as the best
point found so far; `inRect` visits only subtrees that can overlap the rectangle. Results are
deterministic: a tie in distance goes to the lexicographically smaller point, and `inRect`
returns points in lexicographic order. Use it for repeated spatial queries over points that do
not change; for a set that changes, rebuild, or use a structure with updates (`treap` on one
coordinate when one axis is enough).

Write the Nim module `leftist_heap.nim` (Leftist heap).

Leftist heap: a mergeable persistent min-heap.

A binary tree with the heap order (a parent is not larger than its children) and the leftist
property: the right spine is never longer than the left one. All work follows the right spine,
so `merge`, `insert` and `deleteMin` are O(log n) worst case. Use it when two priority queues
must be combined often; use `pairing_heap` for lower constants in practice.

Write the Nim module `linked_list.nim` (Doubly linked list (arena)).

Doubly linked list in an arena, as a value.

A pointer-based doubly linked list needs two `ref`s per node that point at each other, which is
a cycle: it cannot be immutable, cannot share structure between versions, and is awkward under
ORC. This module keeps the nodes in one `seq` (the arena) and lets them refer to each other by
index. `prev` and `next` are indices, the list is a plain value (ADR-NCK-0002), and `insertAfter`
and `remove` work from a handle in O(1) plus one copy of the arena (O(n)) because an update
returns a new list. Removed slots go on a free list and are reused; each slot carries a
generation that is bumped on removal, so a handle to a removed element is rejected instead of
silently pointing at whatever reused the slot. Use it when elements must be inserted or removed
in the middle through handles (an LRU order, an editor buffer); for a persistent singly linked
list use `cons_list`, for a queue or double-ended use `bankers_queue` or `deque`.

## Doubly linked list in an arena, as a value.
##
## A pointer-based doubly linked list needs two `ref`s per node that point at each other, which is
## a cycle: it cannot be immutable, cannot share structure between versions, and is awkward under
## ORC. This module keeps the nodes in one `seq` (the arena) and lets them refer to each other by
## index. `prev` and `next` are indices, the list is a plain value (ADR-NCK-0002), and `insertAfter`
## and `remove` work from a handle in O(1) plus one copy of the arena (O(n)) because an update
## returns a new list. Removed slots go on a free list and are reused; each slot carries a
## generation that is bumped on removal, so a handle to a removed element is rejected instead of
## silently pointing at whatever reused the slot. Use it when elements must be inserted or removed
## in the middle through handles (an LRU order, an editor buffer); for a persistent singly linked
## list use `cons_list`, for a queue or double-ended use `bankers_queue` or `deque`.

import std/options

const
  noLink = -1

type
  NodeId* = object
    ## A handle to one element: the arena slot and the generation the slot had when it was handed out.
    index*: int
    generation*: int
  Cell[T] = object
    live: bool
    generation: int
    elem: T
    prev, next: int       ## for a dead cell, `next` links the free list
  ArenaList*[T] = object
    cells: seq[Cell[T]]
    head, tail: int
    freeHead: int
    count: int

func emptyList*[T](): ArenaList[T] {.raises: [].} =
  ArenaList[T](head: noLink, tail: noLink, freeHead: noLink)

func len*[T](l: ArenaList[T]): int {.raises: [].} =
  l.count

func isEmpty*[T](l: ArenaList[T]): bool {.raises: [].} =
  l.count == 0

func isValid[T](l: ArenaList[T]; id: NodeId): bool =
  id.index >= 0 and id.index < l.cells.len and l.cells[id.index].live and
    l.cells[id.index].generation == id.generation

func alloc[T](l: var ArenaList[T]; x: T): int =
  ## Takes a slot from the free list or grows the arena; the cell is live and unlinked.
  if l.freeHead != noLink:
    result = l.freeHead
    l.freeHead = l.cells[result].next
    l.cells[result] = Cell[T](live: true, generation: l.cells[result].generation, elem: x,
      prev: noLink, next: noLink)
  else:
    result = l.cells.len
    l.cells.add Cell[T](live: true, generation: 0, elem: x, prev: noLink, next: noLink)
  inc l.count

func linkAfter[T](l: var ArenaList[T]; at: int; x: T): int =
  ## Adds `x` right after slot `at`; `at == noLink` means "before everything" (a new head).
  let n = l.alloc(x)
  let following = if at == noLink: l.head else: l.cells[at].next
  l.cells[n].prev = at
  l.cells[n].next = following
  if at == noLink: l.head = n else: l.cells[at].next = n
  if following == noLink: l.tail = n else: l.cells[following].prev = n
  n

func handle[T](l: ArenaList[T]; index: int): NodeId =
  NodeId(index: index, generation: l.cells[index].generation)

func pushBack*[T](l: ArenaList[T]; x: T): tuple[list: ArenaList[T], id: NodeId] {.raises: [].} =
  var r = l
  let n = r.linkAfter(r.tail, x)
  (r, r.handle(n))

func pushFront*[T](l: ArenaList[T]; x: T): tuple[list: ArenaList[T], id: NodeId] {.raises: [].} =
  var r = l
  let n = r.linkAfter(noLink, x)
  (r, r.handle(n))

func insertAfter*[T](l: ArenaList[T]; id: NodeId;
    x: T): Option[tuple[list: ArenaList[T], id: NodeId]] {.raises: [].} =
  ## Inserts `x` right after the element `id` names; `none` when the handle is stale or out of range.
  if not l.isValid(id): return none(tuple[list: ArenaList[T], id: NodeId])
  var r = l
  let n = r.linkAfter(id.index, x)
  some((list: r, id: r.handle(n)))

func remove*[T](l: ArenaList[T]; id: NodeId): Option[ArenaList[T]] {.raises: [].} =
  ## The list without the element `id` names; `none` when the handle is stale or out of range.
  if not l.isValid(id): return none(ArenaList[T])
  var r = l
  let p = r.cells[id.index].prev
  let n = r.cells[id.index].next
  if p == noLink: r.head = n else: r.cells[p].next = n
  if n == noLink: r.tail = p else: r.cells[n].prev = p
  r.cells[id.index] = Cell[T](live: false, generation: id.generation + 1, prev: noLink,
    next: r.freeHead)
  r.freeHead = id.index
  dec r.count
  some(r)

func get*[T](l: ArenaList[T]; id: NodeId): Option[T] {.raises: [].} =
  if l.isValid(id): some(l.cells[id.index].elem) else: none(T)

func toSeqForward*[T](l: ArenaList[T]): seq[T] {.raises: [].} =
  ## The elements from head to tail, following `next`.
  var i = l.head
  while i != noLink:
    result.add l.cells[i].elem
    i = l.cells[i].next

func toSeqBackward*[T](l: ArenaList[T]): seq[T] {.raises: [].} =
  ## The elements from tail to head, following `prev`.
  var i = l.tail
  while i != noLink:
    result.add l.cells[i].elem
    i = l.cells[i].prev

func invariantsHold*[T](l: ArenaList[T]): bool {.raises: [].} =
  ## Forward and backward links agree, `count` matches the live cells, the head has no `prev`
  ## and the tail no `next`, and every dead cell is on the free list exactly once.
  var seen = 0
  var i = l.head
  var prev = noLink
  while i != noLink:
    if i < 0 or i >= l.cells.len or seen > l.cells.len: return false
    if not l.cells[i].live or l.cells[i].prev != prev: return false
    prev = i
    i = l.cells[i].next
    inc seen
  if prev != l.tail or seen != l.count: return false
  var live = 0
  for c in l.cells:
    if c.live: inc live
  if live != l.count: return false
  var free = 0
  var f = l.freeHead
  while f != noLink:
    if f < 0 or f >= l.cells.len or l.cells[f].live or free > l.cells.len: return false
    inc free
    f = l.cells[f].next
  free + live == l.cells.len

Write the Nim module `merkle_tree.nim` (Content addressing and the Merkle tree).

Content addressing and the Merkle tree: persistent values whose names are their hashes.

`CasStore` is a content-addressed store: the name of a blob is the hash of its bytes, `put` returns
a new store and that name, the same bytes put twice keep one copy, and `get` hashes what it found
again, so a copy that rotted on disk is reported (`ceCorrupt`) instead of returned. `MerkleTree`
is a tree of digests over a sequence of blocks: its root covers every leaf, an audit path
proves one leaf against the root, and an update or an append rebuilds one path of O(log n) nodes
and shares every other node with the old tree.

The hash is a parameter (`Hasher`). The module ships one hash only, `insecureFnv1a64`, whose name
says what it is: it has no resistance to collisions, so anyone can build two blocks with one
digest and substitute one for the other. A store or tree that faces untrusted data needs a
collision-resistant hash such as SHA-256, passed in through `newHasher`.

Leaves and inner nodes are hashed under different prefix bytes (domain separation), so an inner
node's two digests can never pass as a leaf block. The shape of the tree depends only on the
number of leaves (the left subtree is the largest power of two below n), so no leaf is ever
duplicated to fill a level.

Write the Nim module `pairing_heap.nim` (Pairing heap).

Pairing heap: a mergeable persistent min-heap with a very simple shape.

A node holds its element and a list of child heaps. `merge` makes the larger root a child of the
smaller one in O(1); `deleteMin` merges the children pairwise from left to right and then
folds the results from right to left, which is O(log n) amortized (ephemeral use). Use it as a
default priority queue in functional code; see `leftist_heap` for a worst-case bound.

Write the Nim module `pvector.nim` (Persistent vector).

Persistent vector: a 32-way trie giving O(log32 n) indexed `get`, `updated` and `push`.

Elements live in leaves of up to 32 items; interior nodes hold up to 32 children; the index is
read five bits at a time from the top. An update copies the one path from the root to the
leaf (at most 7 nodes for 2^32 elements) and shares everything else, so the old vector stays
valid. Use it for large indexed collections that are updated functionally; use `skew_list`
when you push and pop at the front. The tail optimisation that real implementations add (an
unshared buffer at the end) is left out so the shape stays easy to read.


Write the Nim module `rb_tree.nim` (Red-black tree).

Persistent red-black tree: an ordered map (`RbMap`) and an ordered set (`RbSet`).

A binary search tree whose nodes are coloured so that the root is black, no red node has a red
child, and every path from a node to a leaf holds the same number of black nodes. Those rules
keep the height at most 2 log2(n + 1), so `put`, `get` and `contains` are O(log n) worst case.
`put` copies only the path it walks (O(log n) new nodes) and shares the rest with the old tree,
which stays valid. Use it for ordered iteration, range-like queries and a deterministic order;
use `hamt` for unordered lookup. Deletion is not provided: its case analysis is longer than is worth showing here;
rebuild from `toSeq` without the key, or use `hamt` when you need `remove`.

Write the Nim module `segment_tree.nim` (Segment tree).

Immutable segment tree over a monoid: range queries and point updates in O(log n).

A monoid is an associative `combine` with an `identity`. The tree stores, in every node, the
combination of the elements below it, so a query over a half-open range [l, r) combines at most
about 2 log2(n) stored values. A point update copies one root-to-leaf path and shares the rest,
so the old tree stays valid. Because only associativity is required (not commutativity), the
order of elements is respected: string concatenation works. Use it for repeated range sums,
minima, gcds or any associative summary over an array with updates; use a prefix-sum array when
the data never changes.

```nim
func get[T](t: SegTree[T]; i: int): Option[T]
func total[T](t: SegTree[T]): T
```

Write the Nim module `skew_list.nim` (Skew-binary random-access list).

Skew-binary random-access list: a persistent sequence with O(1) `cons`/`head`/`tail` and
O(log n) indexed `get` and `updated`.

The list is a short spine of complete binary trees whose sizes are of the form 2^k - 1, in
non-decreasing order with at most the first two equal (a skew-binary number). Consing links the
first two trees when they have equal size, otherwise starts a new one-element tree; that is why
no carry ever ripples. Use it when you need a stack that also supports indexing and
functional update; use `pvector` for append-at-the-end with indexing, `cons_list` when you never index.

```nim
func toSeq[T](xs: SkewList[T]): seq[T]
```

Write the Nim module `slot_map.nim` (Generational slot map (handles into one owner)).

Generational slot map: handles into one owner instead of shared references.

When several parts of a program need to refer to the same thing, the shortcut that compiles is a
shared `ref` (and a lock or a counter around it). Here one owner, the `SlotMap`, holds every
value in a flat `seq` of slots and gives out a `Handle` (slot index plus generation) per value.
Other code keeps the handle, not the value, and asks the owner when it needs it. Removing a value
bumps its slot's generation and puts the slot on a free list; `insert` reuses free slots first,
so a handle to a removed value is rejected (`none`, `false`) even after its slot holds
something else. The generation is an `int`; it would need 2^63 removals of one slot to wrap.

Updates take the map as a `sink` parameter and return it with the result, so the caller moves the
map in at its last use and the slots are not copied: `insert`, `put` and `remove` are O(1)
(amortised for the `seq` growth). A caller that keeps using the old map gets a copy of the slots
(O(n)) and an unchanged old value, as for every other structure in this repository. A failed
`remove` or `put` still returns the map, so a moved-in map is never lost. Use it for entities, nodes
and resources that are created, destroyed and referred to over time; the arena list in
`linked_list` uses the same generation idea for list nodes.

Public API:
```nim
type Handle = object
  index*: int
  generation*: int
type SlotMap[T] = object
func emptySlotMap[T](): SlotMap[T]
func len[T](m: SlotMap[T]): int
func isEmpty[T](m: SlotMap[T]): bool
func `==`(a, b: Handle): bool
func contains[T](m: SlotMap[T]; h: Handle): bool
func get[T](m: SlotMap[T]; h: Handle): Option[T]
func insert[T](m: sink SlotMap[T]; x: sink T): tuple[map: SlotMap[T], handle: Handle]
func remove[T](m: sink SlotMap[T]; h: Handle): tuple[map: SlotMap[T], removed: Option[T]]
func put[T](m: sink SlotMap[T]; h: Handle; x: sink T): tuple[map: SlotMap[T], ok: bool]
iterator pairs[T](m: SlotMap[T]): tuple[handle: Handle, value: T]
func `==`[T](a, b: SlotMap[T]): bool
func invariantsHold[T](m: SlotMap[T]): bool
```

## Generational slot map: handles into one owner instead of shared references.
##
## When several parts of a program need to refer to the same thing, the shortcut that compiles is a
## shared `ref` (and a lock or a counter around it). Here one owner, the `SlotMap`, holds every
## value in a flat `seq` of slots and gives out a `Handle` (slot index plus generation) per value.
## Other code keeps the handle, not the value, and asks the owner when it needs it. Removing a value
## bumps its slot's generation and puts the slot on a free list; `insert` reuses free slots first,
## so a handle to a removed value is rejected (`none`, `false`) even after its slot holds
## something else. The generation is an `int`; it would need 2^63 removals of one slot to wrap.
##
## Updates take the map as a `sink` parameter and return it with the result, so the caller moves the
## map in at its last use and the slots are not copied: `insert`, `put` and `remove` are O(1)
## (amortised for the `seq` growth). A caller that keeps using the old map gets a copy of the slots
## (O(n)) and an unchanged old value, as for every other structure in this repository. A failed
## `remove` or `put` still returns the map, so a moved-in map is never lost. Use it for entities, nodes
## and resources that are created, destroyed and referred to over time; the arena list in
## `linked_list` uses the same generation idea for list nodes.

import std/options

const
  noLink = 0   ## the end of the free list; a link holds a slot index plus one, so the zero value is empty

type
  Handle* = object
    ## A reference to one value: the slot and the generation the slot had when it was handed out.
    index*: int
    generation*: int
  Slot[T] = object
    live: bool
    generation: int
    elem: T
    nextFree: int       ## for a dead slot, the next slot of the free list (index + 1), or `noLink`
  SlotMap*[T] = object
    slots: seq[Slot[T]]
    freeHead: int       ## the first slot of the free list (index + 1), or `noLink`
    count: int

func emptySlotMap*[T](): SlotMap[T] {.raises: [].} =
  ## The empty map; `default(SlotMap[T])` is the same value.
  SlotMap[T]()

func len*[T](m: SlotMap[T]): int {.raises: [].} =
  m.count

func isEmpty*[T](m: SlotMap[T]): bool {.raises: [].} =
  m.count == 0

func `==`*(a, b: Handle): bool {.raises: [].} =
  a.index == b.index and a.generation == b.generation

func isLive[T](m: SlotMap[T]; h: Handle): bool =
  h.index >= 0 and h.index < m.slots.len and m.slots[h.index].live and
    m.slots[h.index].generation == h.generation

func contains*[T](m: SlotMap[T]; h: Handle): bool {.raises: [].} =
  m.isLive(h)

func get*[T](m: SlotMap[T]; h: Handle): Option[T] {.raises: [].} =
  if m.isLive(h): some(m.slots[h.index].elem) else: none(T)

func insert*[T](m: sink SlotMap[T]; x: sink T): tuple[map: SlotMap[T], handle: Handle] {.raises: [].} =
  ## Stores `x` in the first free slot, or in a new slot at the end when none is free.
  var r = m
  var at: int
  if r.freeHead != noLink:
    at = r.freeHead - 1
    r.freeHead = r.slots[at].nextFree
    r.slots[at].live = true
    r.slots[at].elem = x
    r.slots[at].nextFree = noLink
  else:
    at = r.slots.len
    r.slots.add Slot[T](live: true, generation: 0, elem: x, nextFree: noLink)
  inc r.count
  let h = Handle(index: at, generation: r.slots[at].generation)
  (r, h)

func remove*[T](m: sink SlotMap[T]; h: Handle): tuple[map: SlotMap[T], removed: Option[T]] {.raises: [].} =
  ## Takes the value out and retires the handle. A stale or unknown handle returns the map as it
  ## was and `none`.
  if not m.isLive(h): return (m, none(T))
  var r = m
  let taken = some(move r.slots[h.index].elem)
  r.slots[h.index].live = false
  inc r.slots[h.index].generation
  r.slots[h.index].nextFree = r.freeHead
  r.freeHead = h.index + 1
  dec r.count
  (r, taken)

func put*[T](m: sink SlotMap[T]; h: Handle; x: sink T): tuple[map: SlotMap[T], ok: bool] {.raises: [].} =
  ## Replaces the value a live handle names; the handle stays valid. A stale or unknown handle
  ## returns the map as it was and `false`.
  if not m.isLive(h): return (m, false)
  var r = m
  r.slots[h.index].elem = x
  (r, true)

iterator pairs*[T](m: SlotMap[T]): tuple[handle: Handle, value: T] {.raises: [].} =
  ## The live handles and values in slot order.
  for i in 0 ..< m.slots.len:
    if m.slots[i].live:
      yield (handle: Handle(index: i, generation: m.slots[i].generation), value: m.slots[i].elem)

func `==`*[T](a, b: SlotMap[T]): bool {.raises: [].} =
  ## Same slots, generations, live values, free list and count. Two maps that hold the same pairs
  ## but reached them by different insert and remove histories can differ here.
  if a.count != b.count or a.freeHead != b.freeHead or a.slots.len != b.slots.len: return false
  for i in 0 ..< a.slots.len:
    let x = a.slots[i]
    let y = b.slots[i]
    if x.live != y.live or x.generation != y.generation or x.nextFree != y.nextFree: return false
    if x.live and x.elem != y.elem: return false
  true

func invariantsHold*[T](m: SlotMap[T]): bool {.raises: [].} =
  ## `count` matches the live slots, every dead slot is on the free list exactly once, the free
  ## list holds nothing live, and every generation is non-negative.
  var live = 0
  for s in m.slots:
    if s.generation < 0: return false
    if s.live: inc live
  if live != m.count: return false
  var free = 0
  var f = m.freeHead
  while f != noLink:
    let i = f - 1
    if i < 0 or i >= m.slots.len or m.slots[i].live or free > m.slots.len: return false
    inc free
    f = m.slots[i].nextFree
  free + live == m.slots.len

Write the Nim module `sparse_table.nim` (Sparse table).

Sparse table: O(1) range queries for an idempotent operation, after an O(n log n) build.

Level `k` stores, for every start `i`, the combination of the `2^k` elements from `i`. A query
over `[l, r)` picks the largest `k` with `2^k <= r - l` and combines two level-`k` entries, one
starting at `l` and one ending at `r`; the two windows overlap in the middle. The overlap
counts the shared elements twice, which is harmless only when `op(x, x) == x` (idempotent):
min, max, gcd, bitwise and/or. Sum, product and xor are not idempotent and give wrong answers
here; use `fenwick_tree` or `segment_tree` for those. The table is built once and never
updated (an update would rewrite O(n) entries per level); use `segment_tree` when the data
changes. Only associativity and idempotence of `op` are used; the two windows are combined in
index order, so non-commutative idempotent operations (such as "keep the left one") also work.

Public API:
```nim
type Op[T] = proc (a, b: T): T {.noSideEffect, raises: [].}
type SparseTable[T] = object
func fromSeq[T](items: openArray[T]; op: Op[T]): SparseTable[T]
func len[T](t: SparseTable[T]): int
func levelCount[T](t: SparseTable[T]): int
func query[T](t: SparseTable[T]; l, r: int): Option[T]
func get[T](t: SparseTable[T]; i: int): Option[T]
func idempotentOn[T](op: Op[T]; samples: openArray[T]): bool
```
output:
## Sparse table: O(1) range queries for an idempotent operation, after an O(n log n) build.
##
## Level `k` stores, for every start `i`, the combination of the `2^k` elements from `i`. A query
## over `[l, r)` picks the largest `k` with `2^k <= r - l` and combines two level-`k` entries, one
## starting at `l` and one ending at `r`; the two windows overlap in the middle. The overlap
## counts the shared elements twice, which is harmless only when `op(x, x) == x` (idempotent):
## min, max, gcd, bitwise and/or. Sum, product and xor are not idempotent and give wrong answers
## here; use `fenwick_tree` or `segment_tree` for those. The table is built once and never
## updated (an update would rewrite O(n) entries per level); use `segment_tree` when the data
## changes. Only associativity and idempotence of `op` are used; the two windows are combined in
## index order, so non-commutative idempotent operations (such as "keep the left one") also work.

import std/[options, bitops]

type
  Op*[T] = proc(a, b: T): T {.noSideEffect, raises: [].}
  SparseTable*[T] = object
    op: Op[T]
    levels: seq[seq[T]]   ## levels[k][i] = op over items[i ..< i + 2^k]
    size: int

func fromSeq*[T](items: openArray[T]; op: Op[T]): SparseTable[T] {.raises: [].} =
  ## Builds all levels; O(n log n) time and space. `op` must be associative and idempotent for
  ## `query` to be correct (see `idempotentOn`).
  var levels = @[@items]
  var width = 1
  while width * 2 <= items.len:
    let prev = levels[^1]
    var next = newSeqOfCap[T](items.len - width * 2 + 1)
    for i in 0 .. items.len - width * 2:
      next.add op(prev[i], prev[i + width])
    levels.add next
    width *= 2
  SparseTable[T](op: op, levels: if items.len == 0: newSeq[seq[T]]() else: levels, size: items.len)

func len*[T](t: SparseTable[T]): int {.raises: [].} =
  t.size

func levelCount*[T](t: SparseTable[T]): int {.raises: [].} =
  ## Number of levels: floor(log2 n) + 1, or 0 for an empty table.
  t.levels.len

func query*[T](t: SparseTable[T]; l, r: int): Option[T] {.raises: [].} =
  ## `op` over elements l ..< r in O(1); none for an empty or out-of-range range (there is no
  ## identity element, so an empty range has no answer).
  if l < 0 or r > t.size or l >= r: return none(T)
  let k = fastLog2(r - l)
  some(t.op(t.levels[k][l], t.levels[k][r - (1 shl k)]))

func get*[T](t: SparseTable[T]; i: int): Option[T] {.raises: [].} =
  ## Element `i`; none when out of range.
  if i < 0 or i >= t.size: none(T) else: some(t.levels[0][i])

func idempotentOn*[T](op: Op[T]; samples: openArray[T]): bool {.raises: [].} =
  ## True when `op(x, x) == x` for every sample. A finite check can refute idempotence, not prove it.
  for x in samples:
    if op(x, x) != x: return false
  true

Write the Nim module `splay_tree.nim` (Splay tree).

Persistent splay tree: a binary search tree that moves the key it just touched to the root.

A classic splay tree rearranges itself on every read, which a persistent value cannot do in
place. Here `lookup` returns the new tree next to the answer, as `tuple[found: bool, tree:
SplayTree[K]]`, and the caller keeps using the returned tree. The splay itself is the usual
zig, zig-zig and zig-zag rotations, written as a recursion that copies the path it walks.
Amortized O(log n) per operation holds only for a sequence of operations where each uses the
tree the previous one returned. A single version used again and again has no such bound: its
deepest key costs O(n) every time. Use it for access patterns with locality (the same few keys
asked for repeatedly) in single-threaded code; use `rb_tree` or `treap` when any version may be
queried at any time. The key type needs `<`.

Write the Nim module `stack_queue.nim` (Stack, queue and the monotonic stack).

Stack (last in, first out) and queue (first in, first out) as values, plus the monotonic stack.

`Stack[T]` wraps a `seq` used from its end; `Queue[T]` wraps a `std/deques` ring buffer. Both are
value types (ADR-NCK-0002): `push`, `pop`, `enqueue` and `dequeue` return a new container and
copy the storage, O(n), so keep a `var` local to one routine when you need the O(1) amortized
in-place operations (the monotonic stack below does exactly that). When old versions must stay
cheap, use `cons_list` as a persistent stack and `bankers_queue` as a persistent queue.
`nextGreaterIndex` is the monotonic-stack technique: scan once while a stack of indices keeps its
values decreasing, and every index leaves the stack exactly when its answer is found.

Write the Nim module `suffix_trie.nim` (Suffix trie (and why not a suffix tree)).

Naive suffix trie for small texts: substring counts, distinct substrings, longest repeat.

This is not a suffix tree. A suffix tree compresses unary paths and is built in O(n) by
Ukkonen's algorithm, which needs suffix links and shared mutable end indices; that does not fit
the persistent, value-only style of this repository without losing the O(n) bound. This module
instead inserts every suffix of the text into a plain trie (one node per character), which is
simple, immutable and obviously correct, but takes O(n^2) nodes: `buildSuffixTrie` refuses texts
longer than `maxTextLen`. Each node stores how many suffixes pass through it, which equals the
number of (possibly overlapping) occurrences of the string spelled by the path. Use it to learn
what a suffix tree answers and to test other implementations on short strings; for real texts
use `suffix_array` in `nimcs/algo`.

Write the Nim module `treap.nim` (Treap).

Persistent treap: an ordered set whose balance comes from priorities derived from a seed.

A treap is a binary search tree on the keys that is also a max-heap on a priority stored in each
node. Here the priority is not drawn from a random generator: it is a fixed mixing function of
the seed and the key, so the same seed and the same key set always give the same tree, whatever
order the keys were inserted in. With priorities that behave like random numbers the expected
height is O(log n). All updates are `split` and `merge`, which copy only the path they walk and
share the rest, so every earlier version stays valid. Use it for an ordered set that also needs
cheap `split` and `merge` (cutting a key range off, joining two disjoint sets); use `rb_tree`
when a worst-case height bound matters more than the simple code. The key type needs `<` and
`hash`.

Write the Nim module `trie.nim` (Persistent trie).

Persistent string trie: a set of words stored as a tree of characters.

Each node has a flag "a word ends here" and children sorted by character. `insert` copies the
nodes along the word (one per character) and shares every other branch. `contains` costs
O(length of the word); `keysWithPrefix` walks to the prefix and lists the words below it in
sorted (byte-wise) order. Recursion depth equals the word length (a release build handles words of
tens of thousands of characters, a debug build about 2,000). Use it for autocompletion and prefix search; use `hamt` or `rb_tree`
when you only need whole-key lookup.

Write the Nim module `union_find.nim` (Persistent union-find).

Persistent union-find (disjoint sets) built on a persistent map.

The classic imperative version keeps parents in an array and compresses paths while it finds,
giving near-constant amortized time but destroying the old state. Here the parent and rank
tables are `RbMap`s, so `union` returns a new structure and every earlier version stays
usable (backtracking, undo, speculative merges). Union by rank alone bounds a root path by
log2(n), so `find` is O(log n * log n) with the map lookups; `findCompress` also returns the
compressed structure, which you must keep to benefit. Use it when you need old versions;
use an array with path compression when only the latest state matters and speed counts.

Write the Nim module `write_ahead_log.nim` (Write-ahead log).

Write-ahead log as a value: an append-only sequence of records, each with a sequence number and a
checksum, that can be replayed to rebuild state and survive a torn tail.

`append` returns a new log holding one more record (the old log is unchanged). `replay` folds a
function over the payloads in order, so the state a program had is the state it rebuilds from the
log; because the fold is pure, replaying twice gives the same state. `encode` turns the log into
one byte string (per record: sequence number, payload length, payload, CRC-32 over those three,
all integers big-endian) and `recover` reads such a string back. A crash can leave the last record
short or half written: `recover` keeps every record up to the first one that is short, fails its
checksum or carries the wrong sequence number, and drops that record and whatever follows,
reporting how many bytes it dropped. A log is trusted only as far as its checksums, so it stops at
the first bad record and never skips over it to a later good one.

Out of scope: files. Writing the bytes, `fsync`, truncating a file to `keptBytes`, rotating and
checkpointing segments are effects, and belong in the imperative shell around this value (use
`encode` to get the bytes to write and `recover` on the bytes read). The checksum is CRC-32: it
finds accidental damage, not tampering.

Public API:
```nim
const maxPayload = 16777216
type WalError = enum
  weTooLarge,               ## a payload longer than `maxPayload`
  weCorrupt                  ## `decodeStrict` found bytes that are not a whole, intact log
type WalEntry = object
  seqNo*: int
  payload*: string
  checksum*: uint32          ## CRC-32 of the sequence number, length and payload as encoded
type Wal = object
type Recovery = object
  log*: Wal                  ## the records that were read intact, a prefix of what was written
  keptBytes*: int            ## length of the prefix of the input that holds exactly those records
  droppedBytes*: int         ## bytes after that prefix: a torn or damaged tail
func emptyLog(): Wal
func len(log: Wal): int
func nextSeq(log: Wal): int
func entries(log: Wal): seq[WalEntry]
func payloads(log: Wal): seq[string]
func at(log: Wal; seqNo: int): Option[WalEntry]
func `==`(a, b: Wal): bool
func crc32(data: string): uint32
func append(log: Wal; payload: string): Result[Wal, WalError]
func appendAll(log: Wal; payloadList: openArray[string]): Result[Wal, WalError]
func replay[S](log: Wal; initial: S; apply: proc (state: S; payload: string): S {. noSideEffect, raises: [].}): S
func encode(log: Wal): string
func recover(bytes: string): Recovery
func decodeStrict(bytes: string): Result[Wal, WalError]
```
output:
## Write-ahead log as a value: an append-only sequence of records, each with a sequence number and a
## checksum, that can be replayed to rebuild state and survive a torn tail.
##
## `append` returns a new log holding one more record (the old log is unchanged). `replay` folds a
## function over the payloads in order, so the state a program had is the state it rebuilds from the
## log; because the fold is pure, replaying twice gives the same state. `encode` turns the log into
## one byte string (per record: sequence number, payload length, payload, CRC-32 over those three,
## all integers big-endian) and `recover` reads such a string back. A crash can leave the last record
## short or half written: `recover` keeps every record up to the first one that is short, fails its
## checksum or carries the wrong sequence number, and drops that record and whatever follows,
## reporting how many bytes it dropped. A log is trusted only as far as its checksums, so it stops at
## the first bad record and never skips over it to a later good one.
##
## Out of scope: files. Writing the bytes, `fsync`, truncating a file to `keptBytes`, rotating and
## checkpointing segments are effects, and belong in the imperative shell around this value (use
## `encode` to get the bytes to write and `recover` on the bytes read). The checksum is CRC-32: it
## finds accidental damage, not tampering.

import std/options
import nimcs/fp/result
export result

const
  maxPayload* = 1 shl 24
    ## The largest payload `append` accepts, in bytes. A length field read from damaged bytes is
    ## compared with this before anything is allocated.
  headerLen = 12            # 8 bytes of sequence number, 4 bytes of payload length
  checksumLen = 4

type
  WalError* = enum
    weTooLarge,             ## a payload longer than `maxPayload`
    weCorrupt               ## `decodeStrict` found bytes that are not a whole, intact log
  WalEntry* = object
    seqNo*: int
    payload*: string
    checksum*: uint32       ## CRC-32 of the sequence number, length and payload as encoded
  Wal* = object
    items: seq[WalEntry]
  Recovery* = object
    log*: Wal               ## the records that were read intact, a prefix of what was written
    keptBytes*: int         ## length of the prefix of the input that holds exactly those records
    droppedBytes*: int      ## bytes after that prefix: a torn or damaged tail

func emptyLog*(): Wal {.raises: [].} =
  Wal(items: @[])

func len*(log: Wal): int {.raises: [].} =
  ## Number of records.
  log.items.len

func nextSeq*(log: Wal): int {.raises: [].} =
  ## The sequence number the next appended record gets: 0 for an empty log, then 1, 2, ...
  log.items.len

func entries*(log: Wal): seq[WalEntry] {.raises: [].} =
  log.items

func payloads*(log: Wal): seq[string] {.raises: [].} =
  for e in log.items:
    result.add e.payload

func at*(log: Wal; seqNo: int): Option[WalEntry] {.raises: [].} =
  ## The record with that sequence number; none when there is none.
  if seqNo < 0 or seqNo >= log.items.len: none(WalEntry)
  else: some(log.items[seqNo])

func `==`*(a, b: Wal): bool {.raises: [].} =
  a.items == b.items

# --- checksum and byte layout ---------------------------------------------------------------------

func crc32*(data: string): uint32 {.raises: [].} =
  ## CRC-32 (the IEEE 802.3 polynomial, reflected, as in zlib and gzip); `crc32("123456789")` is
  ## 0xCBF43926.
  var c = 0xffffffff'u32
  for ch in data:
    c = c xor uint32(ord(ch))
    for _ in 0 ..< 8:
      c = if (c and 1'u32) != 0'u32: (c shr 1) xor 0xedb88320'u32 else: c shr 1
  c xor 0xffffffff'u32

func bigEndian(v: uint64; width: int): string =
  for i in countdown(width - 1, 0):
    result.add char((v shr (i * 8)) and 0xff'u64)

func readBigEndian(s: string; at, width: int): uint64 =
  for i in 0 ..< width:
    result = (result shl 8) or uint64(ord(s[at + i]))

func recordBody(seqNo: int; payload: string): string =
  bigEndian(uint64(seqNo), 8) & bigEndian(uint64(payload.len), 4) & payload

# --- building and reading -------------------------------------------------------------------------

func append*(log: Wal; payload: string): Result[Wal, WalError] {.raises: [].} =
  ## The log with `payload` as a new last record. O(n) in the number of records, because the new
  ## value holds its own sequence (this is a value type, not a file); `appendAll` does a batch in one copy.
  if payload.len > maxPayload: return err(Wal, weTooLarge)
  let n = log.items.len
  let entry = WalEntry(seqNo: n, payload: payload, checksum: crc32(recordBody(n, payload)))
  ok(Wal(items: log.items & @[entry]), WalError)

func appendAll*(log: Wal; payloadList: openArray[string]): Result[Wal, WalError] {.raises: [].} =
  ## Appends the payloads in order, all or none.
  var items = log.items
  for p in payloadList:
    if p.len > maxPayload: return err(Wal, weTooLarge)
    let n = items.len
    items.add WalEntry(seqNo: n, payload: p, checksum: crc32(recordBody(n, p)))
  ok(Wal(items: items), WalError)

func replay*[S](log: Wal; initial: S;
    apply: proc(state: S; payload: string): S {.noSideEffect, raises: [].}): S {.raises: [].} =
  ## The state after applying every payload, oldest first, to `initial`. Pure: replaying the same
  ## log with the same function from the same state always gives the same state.
  result = initial
  for e in log.items:
    result = apply(result, e.payload)

func encode*(log: Wal): string {.raises: [].} =
  ## The log as bytes: record after record, each `seq (8) length (4) payload checksum (4)`.
  for e in log.items:
    result.add recordBody(e.seqNo, e.payload)
    result.add bigEndian(uint64(e.checksum), checksumLen)

func recover*(bytes: string): Recovery {.raises: [].} =
  ## Reads as many whole, intact records as the bytes start with. Never fails and never reads past
  ## the end: a record that is short, whose length field is larger than the bytes left or than
  ## `maxPayload`, whose sequence number is not the next one, or whose checksum does not match,
  ## ends the log there. For every input, `encode(recover(bytes).log)` is the first `keptBytes`
  ## bytes of `bytes`.
  var items: seq[WalEntry]
  var at = 0
  while bytes.len - at >= headerLen + checksumLen:
    let sq = readBigEndian(bytes, at, 8)
    let n = readBigEndian(bytes, at + 8, 4)
    if sq != uint64(items.len): break
    if n > uint64(maxPayload) or n > uint64(bytes.len - at - headerLen - checksumLen): break
    let bodyEnd = at + headerLen + int(n)
    let stored = uint32(readBigEndian(bytes, bodyEnd, checksumLen))
    let body = bytes[at ..< bodyEnd]
    if crc32(body) != stored: break
    items.add WalEntry(seqNo: items.len, payload: bytes[at + headerLen ..< bodyEnd], checksum: stored)
    at = bodyEnd + checksumLen
  Recovery(log: Wal(items: items), keptBytes: at, droppedBytes: bytes.len - at)

func decodeStrict*(bytes: string): Result[Wal, WalError] {.raises: [].} =
  ## The log in `bytes` when every byte belongs to an intact record; `weCorrupt` otherwise. Use it
  ## for a log that was closed cleanly (a snapshot, a shipped segment); use `recover` after a crash.
  let r = recover(bytes)
  if r.droppedBytes == 0: ok(r.log, WalError)
  else: err(Wal, weCorrupt)

Write the Nim module `zipper.nim` (Zipper).

Zippers: a cursor into an immutable list or binary tree.

A zipper is the data structure turned inside out around one focus: the part you have passed
is kept in reverse, ready to be put back. Moving the focus and replacing the focused element
are O(1); rebuilding the whole structure costs one step per level you went down. Nothing is
mutated: every move or edit gives a new zipper that shares the rest. Use it for editors,
parsers that backtrack and tree rewriting where "change this place and keep everything else"
is the operation; use plain recursion when you transform every node.

Public API:
```nim
type ListZipper[T] = object
type Tree[T] = object
type TreeZipper[T] = object
func zipList[T](items: openArray[T]): Option[ListZipper[T]]
func focus[T](z: ListZipper[T]): T
func moveRight[T](z: ListZipper[T]): Option[ListZipper[T]]

func toSeq[T](z: ListZipper[T]): seq[T]

func leaf[T](): Tree[T]

func toSeq[T](t: Tree[T]): seq[T]
```

`compose(f, g)` is "g, then f" as in mathematics; `andThen(f, g)` is the same function written in

a pipeline can be grouped any way without changing its meaning. Use `composeAll` for a list of
steps that all map a type to itself; use plain method-call chains (`x.parse.validate.render`)
when the steps are known at the call site.

##
## `compose(f, g)` is "g, then f" as in mathematics; `andThen(f, g)` is the same function written in
## reading order ("f, then g"). `identity` is the neutral element, and composition is associative, so
## a pipeline can be grouped any way without changing its meaning. Use `composeAll` for a list of

type
  Fn*[A, B] = proc(a: A): B {.noSideEffect, raises: [].}
    ## A pure function value: no side effects, no exceptions.

func identity*[T](x: T): T {.raises: [].} =
  ## The neutral element of composition.
  x

func compose*[A, B, C](f: proc(b: B): C {.noSideEffect, raises: [].};
    g: proc(a: A): B {.noSideEffect, raises: [].}): Fn[A, C] {.raises: [].} =
  ## `compose(f, g)(x) == f(g(x))`.
  result = proc(a: A): C {.noSideEffect, raises: [].} = f(g(a))

func andThen*[A, B, C](f: proc(a: A): B {.noSideEffect, raises: [].};

  let copied = @steps

Equational reasoning: refactoring pure code by replacing a form with an equal one

In pure code a name can be replaced by its definition and a definition by its name without

one pass, an idempotent step removed, a loop replaced by its closed form, a count computed in

Write the Nim module `fold.nim` (Fold).

Folds: one loop that builds any result from a sequence (ADR-NCK-0002 S3, S5).

`foldLeft` consumes from the left, `foldRight` from the right, `scan` keeps every intermediate
accumulator, and `unfold` is the dual: it grows a sequence from a seed. Sum, length, map, filter,
reverse and "rebuild the list" are all folds with a different step function, so a fold is the
loop to write first when a result is built by visiting each element once. The accumulator is a
local `var` inside each routine; callers only see values going in and out. The names differ
from `std/sequtils.foldl` and `foldr` on purpose, so both modules can be imported together.

Public API:
```nim

func unfold[S, T](seed: S; step: proc (s: S): Option[(T, S)] {.noSideEffect, raises: [].}; limit: Natural): seq[T]
```
output:
## Folds: one loop that builds any result from a sequence (ADR-NCK-0002 S3, S5).
##
## `foldLeft` consumes from the left, `foldRight` from the right, `scan` keeps every intermediate
## accumulator, and `unfold` is the dual: it grows a sequence from a seed. Sum, length, map, filter,
## reverse and "rebuild the list" are all folds with a different step function, so a fold is the
## loop to write first when a result is built by visiting each element once. The accumulator is a
## local `var` inside each routine; callers only see values going in and out. The names differ
## from `std/sequtils.foldl` and `foldr` on purpose, so both modules can be imported together.

import std/options

func foldLeft*[T, A](xs: openArray[T]; init: A;
    f: proc(acc: A; x: T): A {.noSideEffect, raises: [].}): A {.raises: [].} =
  ## `f(...f(f(init, xs[0]), xs[1])..., xs[^1])`. An empty input gives `init`.
  var acc = init
  for x in xs:
    acc = f(acc, x)
  acc

func foldRight*[T, A](xs: openArray[T]; init: A;
    f: proc(x: T; acc: A): A {.noSideEffect, raises: [].}): A {.raises: [].} =
  ## `f(xs[0], f(xs[1], ... f(xs[^1], init)))`. The step sees the element first, the accumulator second.
  var acc = init
  for i in countdown(xs.high, 0):
    acc = f(xs[i], acc)
  acc

func scan*[T, A](xs: openArray[T]; init: A;
    f: proc(acc: A; x: T): A {.noSideEffect, raises: [].}): seq[A] {.raises: [].} =
  ## All the accumulators of `foldLeft`, starting with `init`: the result has `xs.len + 1` elements.
  result = newSeqOfCap[A](xs.len + 1)
  var acc = init
  result.add acc
  for x in xs:
    acc = f(acc, x)
    result.add acc

func unfold*[S, T](seed: S;
    step: proc(s: S): Option[(T, S)] {.noSideEffect, raises: [].};
    limit: Natural): seq[T] {.raises: [].} =
  ## Grows a sequence: `step` returns the next element and the next state, or `none` to stop.
  ## At most `limit` elements are produced, so a step that never stops cannot loop forever.
  var state = seed
  while result.len < limit:
    let next = step(state)
    if next.isNone:
      break
    result.add next.get[0]
    state = next.get[1]

Write the Nim module `idempotence.nim` (Idempotence).

Idempotence: doing it twice is the same as doing it once (ADR-NCK-0002 S4, S6).

An operation `f` is idempotent when `f(f(x)) == f(x)` for every `x`. That is what makes a retry
safe: a client that does not know whether its request arrived can send it again. This module
holds four small idempotent operations and the law checker they share:
`normalizeSpaces` (a normal form), `setInsert` (add to a sorted set), `upsertByKey` (insert or
replace by key), and `apply` on a `Ledger` (a state transition guarded by an idempotency key,
"apply this command at most once", where a reused key with a different command is an error).
Every state is a value; nothing is mutated in place.

Write the Nim module `monoid.nim` (Monoid).

Monoids: a way to combine two values, and a value that changes nothing (ADR-NCK-0002 S3, S6).

A `Monoid[T]` bundles `empty` and `combine` and is only a monoid if two laws hold:
`combine(empty, x) == x == combine(x, empty)` (identity) and
`combine(combine(a, b), c) == combine(a, combine(b, c))` (associativity). Associativity is what
lets `mconcat` fold a sequence in any grouping, for example in halves on two threads, and
identity is what gives an empty input a sensible answer. `Monoid` values are built by the
constructors below; the laws are checked by the tests, not by the type.

Integer `sum` and `product` assume no overflow: with overflow they are not even defined, so they
are not a monoid on all of `int`.

output:
## Monoids: a way to combine two values, and a value that changes nothing (ADR-NCK-0002 S3, S6).
##
## A `Monoid[T]` bundles `empty` and `combine` and is only a monoid if two laws hold:
## `combine(empty, x) == x == combine(x, empty)` (identity) and
## `combine(combine(a, b), c) == combine(a, combine(b, c))` (associativity). Associativity is what
## lets `mconcat` fold a sequence in any grouping, for example in halves on two threads, and
## identity is what gives an empty input a sensible answer. `Monoid` values are built by the
## constructors below; the laws are checked by the tests, not by the type.
##
## Integer `sum` and `product` assume no overflow: with overflow they are not even defined, so they
## are not a monoid on all of `int`.

import std/tables

type
  Monoid*[T] = object
    empty*: T
    combine*: proc(a, b: T): T {.noSideEffect, raises: [].}

func sumMonoid*(): Monoid[int] {.raises: [].} =
  Monoid[int](empty: 0, combine: proc(a, b: int): int {.noSideEffect, raises: [].} = a + b)

func productMonoid*(): Monoid[int] {.raises: [].} =
  Monoid[int](empty: 1, combine: proc(a, b: int): int {.noSideEffect, raises: [].} = a * b)

func maxMonoid*(): Monoid[int] {.raises: [].} =
  ## The identity is `low(int)`: the maximum of nothing is the smallest `int`.
  Monoid[int](empty: low(int), combine: proc(a, b: int): int {.noSideEffect, raises: [].} = max(a, b))

func minMonoid*(): Monoid[int] {.raises: [].} =
  ## The identity is `high(int)`.
  Monoid[int](empty: high(int), combine: proc(a, b: int): int {.noSideEffect, raises: [].} = min(a, b))

func stringMonoid*(): Monoid[string] {.raises: [].} =
  ## Concatenation: associative but not commutative.
  Monoid[string](empty: "", combine: proc(a, b: string): string {.noSideEffect, raises: [].} = a & b)

func seqMonoid*[T](): Monoid[seq[T]] {.raises: [].} =
  Monoid[seq[T]](empty: @[], combine: proc(a, b: seq[T]): seq[T] {.noSideEffect, raises: [].} = a & b)

func mapMonoid*[K, V](values: Monoid[V]): Monoid[Table[K, V]] {.raises: [].} =
  ## Merges tables; a key present in both gets `values.combine(left, right)`. The result is a
  ## monoid whenever `values` is, and is commutative exactly when `values.combine` is.
  Monoid[Table[K, V]](
    empty: initTable[K, V](),
    combine: proc(a, b: Table[K, V]): Table[K, V] {.noSideEffect, raises: [].} =
      result = a
      for k, v in b:
        # An absent key counts as `values.empty`, which changes nothing when combined.
        result[k] = values.combine(result.getOrDefault(k, values.empty), v))

func mconcat*[T](m: Monoid[T]; xs: openArray[T]): T {.raises: [].} =
  ## Combines all the elements, left to right; an empty input gives `m.empty`.
  result = m.empty
  for x in xs:
    result = m.combine(result, x)

func foldMap*[A, T](m: Monoid[T]; xs: openArray[A];
    f: proc(x: A): T {.noSideEffect, raises: [].}): T {.raises: [].} =
  ## Maps every element into the monoid and combines the results, without building the mapped list.
  result = m.empty
  for x in xs:
    result = m.combine(result, f(x))

Smart constructors: parse once, then carry a type that cannot be wrong (ADR-NCK-0002 S2, S3).

`Username` and `Quantity` are objects with a private field and `{.requiresInit.}`. Outside this
module there is no way to write `Quantity(...)` or `var q: Quantity` (an unset one would hold
0, out of range): the only routines that build them are `parseUsername`, `parseQuantity` and
`parseQuantityText`, and each returns a `Result`, so a caller cannot get a value without
handling the failure. Every function that takes a `Quantity` can then rely on the range without
checking again ("parse, don't validate"). `parseOrder` shows the railway: the first failing
field decides the error.

A plain `distinct int` is not enough for this: `distinct` stops accidental mixing with other
types, but `Quantity(5000)` still compiles anywhere and a default value is 0. Use `distinct`
for units and identifiers that carry no rule; use a sealed object (as here) when the type must
guarantee a rule. Read a field of a `Result` only after checking `isOk` (or use `valueOr`):
`.value` on an error raises `FieldDefect`.

## Smart constructors: parse once, then carry a type that cannot be wrong (ADR-NCK-0002 S2, S3).
##
## `Username` and `Quantity` are objects with a private field and `{.requiresInit.}`. Outside this
## module there is no way to write `Quantity(...)` or `var q: Quantity` (an unset one would hold
## 0, out of range): the only routines that build them are `parseUsername`, `parseQuantity` and
## `parseQuantityText`, and each returns a `Result`, so a caller cannot get a value without
## handling the failure. Every function that takes a `Quantity` can then rely on the range without
## checking again ("parse, don't validate"). `parseOrder` shows the railway: the first failing
## field decides the error.
##
## A plain `distinct int` is not enough for this: `distinct` stops accidental mixing with other
## types, but `Quantity(5000)` still compiles anywhere and a default value is 0. Use `distinct`
## for units and identifiers that carry no rule; use a sealed object (as here) when the type must
## guarantee a rule. Read a field of a `Result` only after checking `isOk` (or use `valueOr`):
## `.value` on an error raises `FieldDefect`.

import std/strutils
import nimcs/fp/result

type
  ParseError* = enum
    tooShort, tooLong, badCharacter, outOfRange, notANumber

  Username* {.requiresInit.} = object
    ## 3 to 16 characters from `a-z`, `0-9`, `_`; always lower case.
    raw: string
  Quantity* {.requiresInit.} = object
    ## A whole number from 1 to 1000.
    n: int

  Order* {.requiresInit.} = object
    who*: Username
    qty*: Quantity

const
  minNameLen* = 3
  maxNameLen* = 16
  minQuantity* = 1
  maxQuantity* = 1000

func `==`*(a, b: Username): bool {.raises: [].} = a.raw == b.raw
func `==`*(a, b: Quantity): bool {.raises: [].} = a.n == b.n
func `$`*(u: Username): string {.raises: [].} = u.raw
func `$`*(q: Quantity): string {.raises: [].} = $q.n

func value*(u: Username): string {.raises: [].} = u.raw
func value*(q: Quantity): int {.raises: [].} = q.n

func parseUsername*(raw: string): Result[Username, ParseError] {.raises: [].} =
  ## Trims, lower-cases, then checks length and alphabet. Parsing the text of a parsed
  ## username gives the same username back.
  let s = raw.strip.toLowerAscii
  if s.len < minNameLen: return err(Username, tooShort)
  if s.len > maxNameLen: return err(Username, tooLong)
  for c in s:
    if c notin {'a'..'z', '0'..'9', '_'}:
      return err(Username, badCharacter)
  ok(Username(raw: s), ParseError)

func parseQuantity*(n: int): Result[Quantity, ParseError] {.raises: [].} =
  ## Accepts exactly `minQuantity .. maxQuantity`.
  if n < minQuantity or n > maxQuantity: err(Quantity, outOfRange)
  else: ok(Quantity(n: n), ParseError)

func parseQuantityText*(raw: string): Result[Quantity, ParseError] {.raises: [].} =
  ## Like `parseQuantity` for text; text that is not a whole number (or does not fit an `int`)
  ## is `notANumber`.
  var n = 0
  try:
    n = parseInt(raw.strip)
  except ValueError:
    return err(Quantity, notANumber)
  parseQuantity(n)

func plus*(a, b: Quantity): Result[Quantity, ParseError] {.raises: [].} =
  ## Adds two quantities; a total above `maxQuantity` is `outOfRange`, not a wrapped value.
  parseQuantity(a.n + b.n)

func parseOrder*(who: string; qty: int): Result[Order, ParseError] {.raises: [].} =
  ## The username is checked first; the quantity only if the username was fine.
  parseUsername(who).flatMap(proc(u: Username): Result[Order, ParseError] {.noSideEffect, raises: [].} =
    parseQuantity(qty).map(proc(q: Quantity): Order {.noSideEffect, raises: [].} =
      Order(who: u, qty: q)))

Write the Nim module `tail_recursion.nim` (Tail recursion and loops).

Recursion and loops in Nim: the accumulator rewrite and when to stop recursing
(ADR-NCK-0002 S1, S5, S6).

A recursive call is a tail call when it is the last thing a routine does. Nim does not
guarantee that a tail call reuses the stack frame: whether a C compiler turns it into a jump
depends on the backend and its settings, so a recursion whose
depth grows with the input (a list of 100 000 elements, `n = 10^6`) can overflow the stack even
when written in tail form. The portable rule is: write the recursion to find the invariant,
carry the partial result in an accumulator argument, then make the final routine a loop with a
local `var` (invisible outside, ADR S5). Each family here has the naive recursion, the
accumulator form and the loop, and the tests show that all three agree.

```nim

func sumToNaive(n: Natural): int
func sumToAcc(n: Natural; acc: int): int
func sumToLoop(n: Natural): int
func fibNaive(n: FibIndex): int
func fibAcc(n: Natural; a, b: int): int
func fibLoop(n: FibIndex): int
func gcdRec(a, b: Natural): int
func gcdLoop(a, b: Natural): int
```

Write the Nim module `type_class.nim` (Type classes: concepts and generics).

Type classes in Nim: `concept` constraints on generics, and laws checked per instance
(ADR-NCK-0002 S3, S6).

A type class says "any type that supports these operations". In Nim that is a generic routine
whose type parameter is constrained by a `concept`; an instance is simply a type that defines
the operations (`<` and `==` here). The compiler checks that the operations exist, never that
they behave: `Orderable` accepts a type whose `<` is not a total order, and `maxOf` then gives
an arbitrary answer. `isTotalOrderOn` is the missing check; run it on generated values for each
instance, as the tests do. Use a concept when one routine must serve several unrelated types;
use a plain generic (`[T]`) when it only moves values around and never inspects them.

```nim
    (x < y) is bool
    (x == y) is bool
func maxOf[T: Orderable](xs: openArray[T]): Option[T]
func minOf[T: Orderable](xs: openArray[T]): Option[T]
func insertSorted[T: Orderable](sortedXs: openArray[T]; x: T): seq[T]
```

Write the Nim module `typestate.nim` (Typestate).

Typestate: the state of a value is part of its type, so an operation that is wrong in a state
does not compile.

A blob of bytes is first a draft (`Blob[Draft]`: you may write to it) and then published
(`Blob[Published]`: read-only, with a content id). `Draft` and `Published` are empty types that
exist only to be a parameter of `Blob`; they add nothing at run time. `write` takes a
`Blob[Draft]`, so `write(published, ...)` is a compile error, and `contentId` takes a
`Blob[Published]`, so a draft has no id to quote. `publish` takes the draft and returns the
published value; the published value holds its own copy of the bytes, so writing to a stale
draft afterwards cannot change what was published (Nim values are copied, there is no shared
path or handle behind them).

The state of a value is sometimes known only at run time (a record read from disk). That case is
the second half of the module: `Stored` is the unchecked record (an object variant on its
state), `asDraft` and `asPublished` are the only ways from it to a typed blob and each returns a
`Result`, and `writeStored` and `publishStored` act on it directly and answer a wrong state with
a `Result` instead of refusing to compile.

Honest limit: Nim has no affine types. `publish(d)` does not stop the caller from using `d`
again, and a `{.error.}` on `=copy` that would stop it cannot ride through the repository's
`Result` (see `details/typestate.md`), so `Blob` stays copyable. What the types do guarantee is
that no routine accepts a blob in a state it is wrong for.

`contentId` is a 64-bit FNV-1a digest in hexadecimal: deterministic and cheap, not a
cryptographic hash. A system that must resist forged collisions replaces `digest` with a
cryptographic one; the typestate does not change.

Public API:
```nim
type Draft = object
type Published = object
type Blob[S] {.requiresInit.} = object
type ContentId = distinct string
type RecordState = enum
  rsDraft, rsPublished
type Stored = object
  bytes*: string
  case state*: RecordState
  of rsDraft:
    nil
  of rsPublished:
    id*: string              ## the recorded content id
type StateError = enum
  seNotDraft, seNotPublished, seIdMismatch
func `==`(a, b: ContentId): bool
func `$`(c: ContentId): string
func `==`[S](a, b: Blob[S]): bool
func newDraft(): Blob[Draft]
func write(b: Blob[Draft]; data: string): Blob[Draft]
func publish(b: Blob[Draft]): Blob[Published]
func read[S](b: Blob[S]): string
func size[S](b: Blob[S]): int
func contentId(b: Blob[Published]): ContentId
func store(b: Blob[Draft]): Stored
func store(b: Blob[Published]): Stored
func asDraft(r: Stored): Result[Blob[Draft], StateError]
func asPublished(r: Stored): Result[Blob[Published], StateError]
func `==`(a, b: Stored): bool
func writeStored(r: Stored; data: string): Result[Stored, StateError]
func publishStored(r: Stored): Result[Stored, StateError]
```

## Typestate: the state of a value is part of its type, so an operation that is wrong in a state
## does not compile.
##
## A blob of bytes is first a draft (`Blob[Draft]`: you may write to it) and then published
## (`Blob[Published]`: read-only, with a content id). `Draft` and `Published` are empty types that
## exist only to be a parameter of `Blob`; they add nothing at run time. `write` takes a
## `Blob[Draft]`, so `write(published, ...)` is a compile error, and `contentId` takes a
## `Blob[Published]`, so a draft has no id to quote. `publish` takes the draft and returns the
## published value; the published value holds its own copy of the bytes, so writing to a stale
## draft afterwards cannot change what was published (Nim values are copied, there is no shared
## path or handle behind them).
##
## The state of a value is sometimes known only at run time (a record read from disk). That case is
## the second half of the module: `Stored` is the unchecked record (an object variant on its
## state), `asDraft` and `asPublished` are the only ways from it to a typed blob and each returns a
## `Result`, and `writeStored` and `publishStored` act on it directly and answer a wrong state with
## a `Result` instead of refusing to compile.
##
## Honest limit: Nim has no affine types. `publish(d)` does not stop the caller from using `d`
## again, and a `{.error.}` on `=copy` that would stop it cannot ride through the repository's
## `Result` (see `details/typestate.md`), so `Blob` stays copyable. What the types do guarantee is
## that no routine accepts a blob in a state it is wrong for.
##
## `contentId` is a 64-bit FNV-1a digest in hexadecimal: deterministic and cheap, not a
## cryptographic hash. A system that must resist forged collisions replaces `digest` with a
## cryptographic one; the typestate does not change.

import std/strutils
import nimcs/fp/result

export result

type
  Draft* = object
    ## State tag: the blob may be written.
  Published* = object
    ## State tag: the blob is read-only and has a content id.

  Blob*[S] {.requiresInit.} = object
    ## Bytes in state `S` (`Draft` or `Published`). The field is private: the only ways to get a
    ## `Blob[Published]` are `publish` and `asPublished`.
    bytes: string

  ContentId* = distinct string
    ## Hexadecimal digest of the content of a published blob.

  RecordState* = enum
    ## The state tag of a stored record, as read from outside the program.
    rsDraft, rsPublished

  Stored* = object
    ## An unchecked record in a state known only at run time, for example read from disk. Nothing
    ## here is trusted: anyone can build one in any state.
    bytes*: string
    case state*: RecordState
    of rsDraft:
      discard
    of rsPublished:
      id*: string        ## the recorded content id

  StateError* = enum
    seNotDraft, seNotPublished, seIdMismatch

func `==`*(a, b: ContentId): bool {.raises: [].} = string(a) == string(b)
func `$`*(c: ContentId): string {.raises: [].} = string(c)

func `==`*[S](a, b: Blob[S]): bool {.raises: [].} = a.bytes == b.bytes

func digest(bytes: string): ContentId {.raises: [].} =
  const
    offset = 0xcbf29ce484222325'u64
    prime = 0x100000001b3'u64
  var h = offset
  for c in bytes:
    h = (h xor uint64(ord(c))) * prime
  ContentId(toHex(h))

func newDraft*(): Blob[Draft] {.raises: [].} =
  ## An empty draft.
  Blob[Draft](bytes: "")

func write*(b: Blob[Draft]; data: string): Blob[Draft] {.raises: [].} =
  ## The draft with `data` appended. Only a draft can be written.
  Blob[Draft](bytes: b.bytes & data)

func publish*(b: Blob[Draft]): Blob[Published] {.raises: [].} =
  ## The read-only blob with the draft's content. The result owns its bytes.
  Blob[Published](bytes: b.bytes)

func read*[S](b: Blob[S]): string {.raises: [].} =
  ## The content, in either state.
  b.bytes

func size*[S](b: Blob[S]): int {.raises: [].} =
  ## The number of bytes, in either state.
  b.bytes.len

func contentId*(b: Blob[Published]): ContentId {.raises: [].} =
  ## The id of the content. Equal content has an equal id however it was written.
  digest(b.bytes)

func store*(b: Blob[Draft]): Stored {.raises: [].} =
  ## The record of a draft, as written to disk.
  Stored(state: rsDraft, bytes: b.bytes)

func store*(b: Blob[Published]): Stored {.raises: [].} =
  ## The record of a published blob, with its content id.
  Stored(state: rsPublished, bytes: b.bytes, id: $contentId(b))

func asDraft*(r: Stored): Result[Blob[Draft], StateError] {.raises: [].} =
  ## Accepts exactly a record in state `rsDraft`.
  if r.state != rsDraft: return err(Blob[Draft], seNotDraft)
  ok(Blob[Draft](bytes: r.bytes), StateError)

func asPublished*(r: Stored): Result[Blob[Published], StateError] {.raises: [].} =
  ## Accepts exactly a record in state `rsPublished` whose recorded id is the digest of its bytes.
  if r.state != rsPublished: return err(Blob[Published], seNotPublished)
  if r.id != $digest(r.bytes): return err(Blob[Published], seIdMismatch)
  ok(Blob[Published](bytes: r.bytes), StateError)

func `==`*(a, b: Stored): bool {.raises: [].} =
  if a.state != b.state or a.bytes != b.bytes: return false
  case a.state
  of rsDraft: true
  of rsPublished: a.id == b.id

func writeStored*(r: Stored; data: string): Result[Stored, StateError] {.raises: [].} =
  ## `write` for a record of unknown state; a published record is `seNotDraft`.
  case r.state
  of rsDraft: ok(Stored(state: rsDraft, bytes: r.bytes & data), StateError)
  of rsPublished: err(Stored, seNotDraft)

func publishStored*(r: Stored): Result[Stored, StateError] {.raises: [].} =
  ## `publish` for a record of unknown state; a record already published is `seNotDraft`.
  case r.state
  of rsDraft: ok(store(Blob[Published](bytes: r.bytes)), StateError)
  of rsPublished: err(Stored, seNotDraft)

Write the Nim module `abstract_factory.nim` (Abstract Factory).

Abstract Factory as a record of constructor procs: one value makes a consistent family.

The OO pattern groups several `createX()` methods in an interface so that a client gets
products that belong together (all dark, all light). In Nim the family is an object whose
fields are procs; choosing the family is choosing one value. Use it when several products must
stay mutually consistent and the client must not name their concrete shape.

Public API:
```nim
type Theme = enum
  themeLight, themeDark
type WidgetKind = enum
  wkButton, wkCheckbox
type CheckState = enum
  csUnchecked, csChecked
type Widget = object
  family*: string
  kind*: WidgetKind
  text*: string
type MakeButton = proc (label: string): Widget {.noSideEffect, raises: [].}
type MakeCheckbox = proc (label: string; state: CheckState): Widget {.noSideEffect,
    raises: [].}
type WidgetKit = object
  family*: string
  button*: MakeButton
  checkbox*: MakeCheckbox
func kitFor(t: Theme): WidgetKit
func renderWidget(w: Widget): string
func loginForm(kit: WidgetKit; user: string; remember: CheckState): seq[Widget]
```

## Abstract Factory as a record of constructor procs: one value makes a consistent family.
##
## The OO pattern groups several `createX()` methods in an interface so that a client gets
## products that belong together (all dark, all light). In Nim the family is an object whose
## fields are procs; choosing the family is choosing one value. Use it when several products must
## stay mutually consistent and the client must not name their concrete shape.

type
  Theme* = enum
    themeLight, themeDark

  WidgetKind* = enum
    wkButton, wkCheckbox

  CheckState* = enum
    csUnchecked, csChecked

  Widget* = object
    family*: string
    kind*: WidgetKind
    text*: string

  MakeButton* = proc(label: string): Widget {.noSideEffect, raises: [].}
  MakeCheckbox* = proc(label: string; state: CheckState): Widget {.noSideEffect, raises: [].}

  WidgetKit* = object
    family*: string
    button*: MakeButton
    checkbox*: MakeCheckbox

func familyTag(t: Theme): string {.raises: [].} =
  case t
  of themeLight: "light"
  of themeDark: "dark"

func boxMark(s: CheckState): string {.raises: [].} =
  case s
  of csChecked: "[x] "
  of csUnchecked: "[ ] "

func kitFor*(t: Theme): WidgetKit {.raises: [].} =
  ## The only place that knows which concrete products belong to which theme.
  let fam = familyTag(t)
  WidgetKit(
    family: fam,
    button: proc(label: string): Widget {.noSideEffect, raises: [].} =
      Widget(family: fam, kind: wkButton, text: "[" & label & "]"),
    checkbox: proc(label: string; state: CheckState): Widget {.noSideEffect, raises: [].} =
      Widget(family: fam, kind: wkCheckbox, text: boxMark(state) & label))

func renderWidget*(w: Widget): string {.raises: [].} =
  w.family & ":" & w.text

func loginForm*(kit: WidgetKit; user: string; remember: CheckState): seq[Widget] {.raises: [].} =
  ## Client code: sees only the kit, never a concrete theme.
  @[kit.checkbox("remember " & user, remember), kit.button("sign in")]

Write the Nim module `actor.nim` (Actor).

Actor: behaviour is a pure transition and effects are data (ADR-NCK-0002).

An actor is not an object with a mutable handler. Its whole behaviour is one pure function
`step(self, state, msg): Reaction` that returns the next state and a list of effects as data:
send a message to an address, spawn another actor, stop itself. "Become" (changing behaviour)
is therefore a change of the state value, never the replacement of a handler. A mailbox is a
persistent FIFO value. Nothing here delivers anything by itself: the host loop (`deliver`,
`runRounds`) takes one message from a mailbox, calls `step` and applies the effects, so the
actor can be tested without threads, timers or mocks, and a message log replays to the same
states. The `System` value in this module is a small, pure reference host (one thread, one
message at a time, round-robin); a real program replaces it with a host that performs I/O,
time and scheduling, and keeps `step` unchanged.

`self` is passed to `step` because an actor must be able to put its own address in a message
(a reply-to, a greeting); it is a constant of the actor, so the transition stays a function of
its inputs. Spawn gives the child its first message (`greeting`) and the next address; the
parent learns the child's address because the child tells it (see the details page).

Public API:
```nim
type Address = distinct int
type Mailbox[M] = BankersQueue[M]
type EffectKind = enum
  efSend, efSpawn, efStop
type Effect[S; M] = object
  case kind*: EffectKind
  of efSend:
    to*: Address
    msg*: M
  of efSpawn:
    initial*: S
    greeting*: Option[M]
  of efStop:
    nil
type Reaction[S; M] = object
  state*: S
  effects*: seq[Effect[S, M]]
type Step[S; M] = proc (self: Address; state: S; msg: M): Reaction[S, M] {.
    noSideEffect, raises: [].}
type System[S; M] = object
func `==`(a, b: Address): bool
func `$`(a: Address): string
func sendTo[S, M](to: Address; msg: M): Effect[S, M]
func spawnActor[S, M](initial: S; greeting: Option[M]): Effect[S, M]
func stopSelf[S, M](): Effect[S, M]
func `==`[S, M](a, b: Effect[S, M]): bool
func `==`[S, M](a, b: Reaction[S, M]): bool
func emptyMailbox[M](): Mailbox[M]
func post[M](box: Mailbox[M]; msg: M): Mailbox[M]
func take[M](box: Mailbox[M]): Option[(M, Mailbox[M])]
func pending[M](box: Mailbox[M]): int
func initSystem[S, M](behaviour: Step[S, M]): System[S, M]
func addActor[S, M](sys: System[S, M]; initial: S): (System[S, M], Address)
func actorCount[S, M](sys: System[S, M]): int
func delivered[S, M](sys: System[S, M]): int
func isAlive[S, M](sys: System[S, M]; a: Address): bool
func stateOf[S, M](sys: System[S, M]; a: Address): Option[S]
func mailboxLen[S, M](sys: System[S, M]; a: Address): int
func deadLetters[S, M](sys: System[S, M]): seq[(Address, M)]
func isIdle[S, M](sys: System[S, M]): bool
func tell[S, M](sys: System[S, M]; to: Address; msg: M): System[S, M]
func deliver[S, M](sys: System[S, M]; a: Address): System[S, M]
func runRounds[S, M](sys: System[S, M]; budget: int): System[S, M]
```
