## parent learns the child's address because the child tells it (see the details page).

import std/options
import nimcs/ds/bankers_queue

type
  Address* = distinct int
    ## Where a message goes. The host hands them out in order, starting at 0.

  Mailbox*[M] = BankersQueue[M]
    ## A persistent FIFO: posting returns a new mailbox, the old one is unchanged.

  EffectKind* = enum
    efSend, efSpawn, efStop

  Effect*[S, M] = object
    ## A request to the host; performing it is not the actor's business.
    case kind*: EffectKind
    of efSend:
      to*: Address
      msg*: M
    of efSpawn:
      initial*: S
      greeting*: Option[M]
    of efStop:
      discard

  Reaction*[S, M] = object
    state*: S
    effects*: seq[Effect[S, M]]

  Step*[S, M] = proc(self: Address; state: S; msg: M): Reaction[S, M] {.noSideEffect, raises: [].}

  Cell[S, M] = object
    state: S
    mailbox: Mailbox[M]
    alive: bool

  System*[S, M] = object
    ## A pure reference host: the actors (address = position), their mailboxes, the messages
    ## that could not be delivered and the number of deliveries so far.
    behaviour: Step[S, M]
    cells: seq[Cell[S, M]]
    dead: seq[(Address, M)]
    count: int

func `==`*(a, b: Address): bool {.borrow.}
func `$`*(a: Address): string {.borrow.}

func sendTo*[S, M](to: Address; msg: M): Effect[S, M] {.raises: [].} =
  Effect[S, M](kind: efSend, to: to, msg: msg)

func spawnActor*[S, M](initial: S; greeting: Option[M]): Effect[S, M] {.raises: [].} =
  Effect[S, M](kind: efSpawn, initial: initial, greeting: greeting)

func stopSelf*[S, M](): Effect[S, M] {.raises: [].} =
  Effect[S, M](kind: efStop)

func `==`*[S, M](a, b: Effect[S, M]): bool {.raises: [].} =
  if a.kind != b.kind: return false
  case a.kind
  of efSend: a.to == b.to and a.msg == b.msg
  of efSpawn: a.initial == b.initial and a.greeting == b.greeting
  of efStop: true

func `==`*[S, M](a, b: Reaction[S, M]): bool {.raises: [].} =
  a.state == b.state and a.effects == b.effects

func emptyMailbox*[M](): Mailbox[M] {.raises: [].} =
  Mailbox[M](emptyQueue[M]())

func post*[M](box: Mailbox[M]; msg: M): Mailbox[M] {.raises: [].} =
  ## Appends at the back.
  Mailbox[M](BankersQueue[M](box).push(msg))

func take*[M](box: Mailbox[M]): Option[(M, Mailbox[M])] {.raises: [].} =
  ## The oldest message and the mailbox without it; `none` when empty.
  let q = BankersQueue[M](box)
  let head = q.peek
  if head.isNone: none((M, Mailbox[M]))
  else: some((head.get, Mailbox[M](q.pop)))

func pending*[M](box: Mailbox[M]): int {.raises: [].} =
  BankersQueue[M](box).len

func initSystem*[S, M](behaviour: Step[S, M]): System[S, M] {.raises: [].} =
  System[S, M](behaviour: behaviour, cells: @[], dead: @[], count: 0)

func known[S, M](sys: System[S, M]; a: Address): bool =
  int(a) >= 0 and int(a) < sys.cells.len

func addActor*[S, M](sys: System[S, M]; initial: S): (System[S, M], Address) {.raises: [].} =
  ## Adds an actor with an empty mailbox; its address is the number of actors so far.
  var next = sys
  next.cells.add Cell[S, M](state: initial, mailbox: emptyMailbox[M](), alive: true)
  (next, Address(sys.cells.len))

func actorCount*[S, M](sys: System[S, M]): int {.raises: [].} = sys.cells.len

func delivered*[S, M](sys: System[S, M]): int {.raises: [].} =
  ## How many messages the host has handed to an actor.
  sys.count

func isAlive*[S, M](sys: System[S, M]; a: Address): bool {.raises: [].} =
  sys.known(a) and sys.cells[int(a)].alive

func stateOf*[S, M](sys: System[S, M]; a: Address): Option[S] {.raises: [].} =
  if sys.known(a): some(sys.cells[int(a)].state) else: none(S)

func mailboxLen*[S, M](sys: System[S, M]; a: Address): int {.raises: [].} =
  if sys.known(a): sys.cells[int(a)].mailbox.pending else: 0

func deadLetters*[S, M](sys: System[S, M]): seq[(Address, M)] {.raises: [].} =
  ## Messages sent to an unknown or stopped actor, in the order they were refused.
  sys.dead

func isIdle*[S, M](sys: System[S, M]): bool {.raises: [].} =
  ## No live actor has a message waiting.
  for c in sys.cells:
    if c.alive and c.mailbox.pending > 0: return false
  true

func tell*[S, M](sys: System[S, M]; to: Address; msg: M): System[S, M] {.raises: [].} =
  ## Puts `msg` in the mailbox of `to`; a message to an unknown or stopped actor is a dead letter.
  result = sys
  if sys.isAlive(to):
    result.cells[int(to)].mailbox = result.cells[int(to)].mailbox.post(msg)
  else:
    result.dead.add (to, msg)

func apply[S, M](sys: System[S, M]; self: Address; fx: Effect[S, M]): System[S, M] =
  case fx.kind
  of efSend:
    result = sys.tell(fx.to, fx.msg)
  of efSpawn:
    let (grown, child) = sys.addActor(fx.initial)
    result = grown
    if fx.greeting.isSome: result = grown.tell(child, fx.greeting.get)
  of efStop:
    result = sys
    var box = result.cells[int(self)].mailbox
    while true:
      let t = box.take
      if t.isNone: break
      result.dead.add (self, t.get[0])
      box = t.get[1]
    result.cells[int(self)].mailbox = emptyMailbox[M]()
    result.cells[int(self)].alive = false

func deliver*[S, M](sys: System[S, M]; a: Address): System[S, M] {.raises: [].} =
  ## The host's one move: take the oldest message of `a`, call `step`, store the new state and
  ## apply the effects in order. Nothing happens if `a` is unknown, stopped or has no message.
  if not sys.isAlive(a): return sys
  let t = sys.cells[int(a)].mailbox.take
  if t.isNone: return sys
  let (msg, rest) = t.get
  let reaction = sys.behaviour(a, sys.cells[int(a)].state, msg)
  result = sys
  result.cells[int(a)].mailbox = rest
  result.cells[int(a)].state = reaction.state
  inc result.count
  for fx in reaction.effects:
    result = result.apply(a, fx)

func runRounds*[S, M](sys: System[S, M]; budget: int): System[S, M] {.raises: [].} =
  ## Round-robin: each round offers every actor, in address order, one delivery. Stops when the
  ## system is idle or after `budget` deliveries, whichever comes first, so a loop of actors that
  ## message each other forever cannot hang the host.
  result = sys
  let stopAt = sys.count + max(budget, 0)
  while result.count < stopAt and not result.isIdle:
    var a = 0
    while a < result.cells.len and result.count < stopAt:
      result = result.deliver(Address(a))
      inc a

func `==`*[S, M](a, b: System[S, M]): bool {.raises: [].} =
  ## Same actors, states, mailboxes, dead letters and delivery count; the behaviour proc is not
  ## compared.
  if a.cells.len != b.cells.len or a.count != b.count or a.dead != b.dead: return false
  for i in 0 ..< a.cells.len:
    let x = a.cells[i]
    let y = b.cells[i]
    if x.alive != y.alive or x.state != y.state: return false
    if BankersQueue[M](x.mailbox).toSeq != BankersQueue[M](y.mailbox).toSeq: return false
  true

Write the Nim module `adapter.nim` (Adapter).

Adapter as a function between two types.

The OO pattern wraps an object with an incompatible interface so that existing client code can
use it. In Nim the interface is a type, so the adapter is a `func` that converts the old shape to
the new one; adapting a source of values is mapping that func over it. Here a legacy schedule
source returns "HH:MM" strings and the new code wants `Minutes` since midnight. Use it at the
boundary where a foreign shape enters; do not let the foreign shape leak further in.

Public API:
```nim
type Minutes = distinct int
type AdaptError = enum
  aeBadLength, aeBadSeparator, aeBadDigit, aeOutOfRange
type LegacySource = proc (): seq[string] {.noSideEffect, raises: [].}
func `==`(a, b: Minutes): bool
func fromLegacy(s: string): Result[Minutes, AdaptError]
func toLegacy(m: Minutes): string
func adaptAll(src: LegacySource): Result[seq[Minutes], AdaptError]
```

Write the Nim module `anti_corruption_layer.nim` (Anti-corruption layer).

Anti-corruption layer: translate a foreign model at the border so it never leaks inward.

Another system's model (a supplier's order message) has its own words, codes and number formats,
and it changes when they decide. If its types reach into your code, every change of theirs is a
change of yours, and its mistakes (a status code you never meant to support) become your states.
The layer is the only place that knows both. It is a pair of functions per foreign version: one
from the foreign record to your `Order`, built through the same smart constructor as every
order of your own, and one back; your code takes `Order` and cannot be handed a foreign record
(the compiler refuses it). A new foreign version is a new pair, and nothing inward moves.
Refusals are values with a reason and a position, not zeros and defaults. Use it where a model
you do not control meets one you do; do not use it between two parts of your own model.

Public API:
```nim
type OrderStatus = enum
  osActive, osShipped, osCancelled
type Cents = distinct int
type Order = object
  id*: string
  status*: OrderStatus
  total*: Cents
type TranslateError = enum
  teEmptyId, teUnknownStatus, teBadAmount
type ForeignOrderV1 = object
  reference*: string
  statusCode*: string
  amount*: string
type ForeignOrderV2 = object
  orderId*: string
  state*: string
  minorUnits*: int
type Refusal = tuple[index: int, error: TranslateError]
type Translated = tuple[orders: seq[Order], refused: seq[Refusal]]
func `==`(a, b: Cents): bool
func `<`(a, b: Cents): bool
func `$`(c: Cents): string
func initOrder(id: string; status: OrderStatus; total: int): Result[Order, TranslateError]
func canShip(o: Order): bool
func fromV1(f: ForeignOrderV1): Result[Order, TranslateError]
func fromV2(f: ForeignOrderV2): Result[Order, TranslateError]
func toV1(o: Order): ForeignOrderV1
func toV2(o: Order): ForeignOrderV2
func translateAll[F](xs: seq[F]; translate: proc (f: F): Result[Order, TranslateError] {.noSideEffect, raises: [].}): Translated
```

Write the Nim module `atomic_publish.nim` (Atomic publish (temporary name, fsync, rename, fsync the directory)).

Atomic publish: write to a temporary name, flush, rename onto the visible name, flush the directory.

A reader of the visible name must see the old content or the new content, never half of it, even
if the machine stops at any instant. Writing in place cannot promise that; this protocol can,
because `rename` within one directory replaces a name in one step and the file it names was made
durable first. The protocol is five steps: create a temporary file with a unique name in the
target's directory, write it, fsync the file, rename it onto the visible name, fsync the directory.

The core models a directory as a value, `Disk`: a volatile view (what readers see, the page cache)
and a durable view (what survives a crash). `publishPlan` gives the protocol as a list of `Step`s,
`apply` runs one step on a `Disk`, and `crash` gives the state after a stop, where the machine
picks the worst: unflushed bytes may be cut anywhere (`torn`) and a rename that no directory fsync
followed may be lost (`fate`). Everything here is a `func`, so a test can stop the protocol
after any step and ask what a reader finds. `SyncMode` removes the fsyncs, and a test shows that
the law then fails: that is what they are for.

The edge is one `proc`, `publishFile`, which makes the same plan and executes it on disk with
`std/posix`. A visible name that is the hash of the content (`addressedName`) makes publishing
idempotent by construction and lets a reader check what it read.

Public API:
```nim
const TmpPrefix = ".atomic-tmp-"
type SyncMode = enum
  smFull,                   ## fsync the file, rename, fsync the directory: atomic and durable
  smFileOnly,               ## no directory fsync: atomic, but the new content may be lost by a crash
  smNone                     ## no fsync at all: a crash can leave the visible name empty or cut
type StepKind = enum
  skCreate, skWrite, skFsyncFile, skRename, skFsyncDir
type Step = object
  kind*: StepKind
  name*: string
  target*: string
  data*: string
type PublishError = enum
  peBadTarget, peBadToken, peDirMissing, peCreate, peWrite, peFsync, peRename,
  peFsyncDir, peFailedAndLeftover, ## a step failed and the temporary file or descriptor could not be released
  peUnsupported
type DirFate = enum
  dcKept,                   ## the directory as readers saw it survives, a rename not yet flushed included
  dcLost                     ## only the durable directory survives: a rename no directory fsync followed is undone
type Disk = object
func emptyDisk(): Disk
func seeded(d: Disk; name, content: string): Disk
func isTemp(name: string): bool
func tmpName(target, token: string): string
func publishPlan(target, token, content: string; mode: SyncMode): Result[seq[Step], PublishError]
func apply(d: Disk; s: Step): Disk
func runSteps(d: Disk; steps: seq[Step]; upTo: int): Disk
func crash(d: Disk; torn: int; fate: DirFate): Disk
func read(d: Disk; name: string): Option[string]
func names(d: Disk): seq[string]
func snapshot(d: Disk): seq[(string, string)]
func leftovers(d: Disk): seq[string]
func cleanup(d: Disk): Disk
func addressedName(content: string): string
func verifies(name, content: string): bool
func planAddressed(content, token: string; mode: SyncMode): Result[seq[Step], PublishError]
proc publishFile(dir, target, content: string; mode: SyncMode = smFull): Result[string, PublishError]
```

## Atomic publish: write to a temporary name, flush, rename onto the visible name, flush the directory.
##
## A reader of the visible name must see the old content or the new content, never half of it, even
## if the machine stops at any instant. Writing in place cannot promise that; this protocol can,
## because `rename` within one directory replaces a name in one step and the file it names was made
## durable first. The protocol is five steps: create a temporary file with a unique name in the
## target's directory, write it, fsync the file, rename it onto the visible name, fsync the directory.
##
## The core models a directory as a value, `Disk`: a volatile view (what readers see, the page cache)
## and a durable view (what survives a crash). `publishPlan` gives the protocol as a list of `Step`s,
## `apply` runs one step on a `Disk`, and `crash` gives the state after a stop, where the machine
## picks the worst: unflushed bytes may be cut anywhere (`torn`) and a rename that no directory fsync
## followed may be lost (`fate`). Everything here is a `func`, so a test can stop the protocol
## after any step and ask what a reader finds. `SyncMode` removes the fsyncs, and a test shows that
## the law then fails: that is what they are for.
##
## The edge is one `proc`, `publishFile`, which makes the same plan and executes it on disk with
## `std/posix`. A visible name that is the hash of the content (`addressedName`) makes publishing
## idempotent by construction and lets a reader check what it read.

import std/[options, tables, strutils, algorithm, monotimes, os]
when defined(posix):
  import std/posix
import nimcs/fp/result

const
  TmpPrefix* = ".atomic-tmp-"
    ## Every temporary name starts with it, so what a crash leaves behind is recognised by name.

type
  SyncMode* = enum
    smFull      ## fsync the file, rename, fsync the directory: atomic and durable
    smFileOnly  ## no directory fsync: atomic, but the new content may be lost by a crash
    smNone      ## no fsync at all: a crash can leave the visible name empty or cut

  StepKind* = enum
    skCreate, skWrite, skFsyncFile, skRename, skFsyncDir

  Step* = object
    ## One operation of the protocol. `name` is the temporary name; `target` is where a rename
    ## puts it; `data` is what a write writes. Fields that a kind does not use are empty.
    kind*: StepKind
    name*: string
    target*: string
    data*: string

  PublishError* = enum
    peBadTarget, peBadToken, peDirMissing, peCreate, peWrite, peFsync, peRename, peFsyncDir,
    peFailedAndLeftover,  ## a step failed and the temporary file or descriptor could not be released
    peUnsupported

  DirFate* = enum
    dcKept  ## the directory as readers saw it survives, a rename not yet flushed included
    dcLost  ## only the durable directory survives: a rename no directory fsync followed is undone

  Inode = object
    cache: string   ## what readers see
    flushed: int    ## how many leading bytes are on the disk

  Disk* = object
    ## A directory as a value. Opaque: built with `emptyDisk` and `seeded`, changed by `apply`.
    inodes: seq[Inode]
    dir: Table[string, int]         ## names readers see
    durableDir: Table[string, int]  ## names that survive a crash

func emptyDisk*(): Disk {.raises: [].} =
  ## A directory with no file.
  Disk()

func seeded*(d: Disk; name, content: string): Disk {.raises: [].} =
  ## The directory with a file that is already fully on the disk, as one left by an earlier run.
  result = d
  result.inodes.add Inode(cache: content, flushed: content.len)
  result.dir[name] = result.inodes.high
  result.durableDir[name] = result.inodes.high

func isTemp*(name: string): bool {.raises: [].} =
  ## Whether a name is one this protocol made for a temporary file.
  name.startsWith(TmpPrefix)

func tmpName*(target, token: string): string {.raises: [].} =
  ## The temporary name for `target`: in the same directory (it has no separator), unique per token.
  TmpPrefix & token & "-" & target

func plainName(s: string): bool {.raises: [].} =
  s.len > 0 and s.len <= 200 and '/' notin s and '\0' notin s and s != "." and s != ".."

func publishPlan*(target, token, content: string; mode: SyncMode): Result[seq[Step], PublishError] {.raises: [].} =
  ## The steps that publish `content` as `target`. The target must be a plain name that does not
  ## look like a temporary one; the token (a process id and a counter, say) must be a plain name
  ## and differ between two publications to the same target that may overlap.
  if not plainName(target) or isTemp(target): return err(seq[Step], peBadTarget)
  if not plainName(token): return err(seq[Step], peBadToken)
  let tmp = tmpName(target, token)
  var steps = @[Step(kind: skCreate, name: tmp), Step(kind: skWrite, name: tmp, data: content)]
  if mode != smNone: steps.add Step(kind: skFsyncFile, name: tmp)
  steps.add Step(kind: skRename, name: tmp, target: target)
  if mode == smFull: steps.add Step(kind: skFsyncDir)
  ok(steps, PublishError)

func apply*(d: Disk; s: Step): Disk {.raises: [].} =
  ## What one step does to the volatile view, and to the durable one when it is an fsync.
  result = d
  case s.kind
  of skCreate:
    if s.name notin result.dir:
      result.inodes.add Inode(cache: "", flushed: 0)
      result.dir[s.name] = result.inodes.high
  of skWrite:
    let id = result.dir.getOrDefault(s.name, -1)
    if id >= 0: result.inodes[id].cache = s.data
  of skFsyncFile:
    let id = result.dir.getOrDefault(s.name, -1)
    if id >= 0: result.inodes[id].flushed = result.inodes[id].cache.len
  of skRename:
    let id = result.dir.getOrDefault(s.name, -1)
    if id >= 0:
      result.dir.del s.name
      result.dir[s.target] = id
  of skFsyncDir:
    result.durableDir = result.dir

func runSteps*(d: Disk; steps: seq[Step]; upTo: int): Disk {.raises: [].} =
  ## The state after the first `upTo` steps (all of them when it is larger).
  result = d
  for i in 0 ..< min(max(upTo, 0), steps.len): result = result.apply(steps[i])

func crash*(d: Disk; torn: int; fate: DirFate): Disk {.raises: [].} =
  ## The state after the machine stops and starts again. Of the bytes not yet flushed, `torn` leading
  ## ones reached the disk; and `fate` says which directory survived. A test chooses both, so it can pick the worst case.
  let extra = max(torn, 0)
  result.dir = if fate == dcKept: d.dir else: d.durableDir
  result.durableDir = result.dir
  for ino in d.inodes:
    let n = min(ino.cache.len, ino.flushed + extra)
    result.inodes.add Inode(cache: ino.cache[0 ..< n], flushed: n)

func read*(d: Disk; name: string): Option[string] {.raises: [].} =
  ## What a reader of `name` gets: its whole content, or none when there is no such name.
  let id = d.dir.getOrDefault(name, -1)
  if id < 0: none(string) else: some(d.inodes[id].cache)

func names*(d: Disk): seq[string] {.raises: [].} =
  ## The visible names, sorted.
  for name in d.dir.keys: result.add name
  result.sort()

func snapshot*(d: Disk): seq[(string, string)] {.raises: [].} =
  ## Every visible name with its content, sorted by name.
  for name in d.names: result.add (name, d.inodes[d.dir.getOrDefault(name, -1)].cache)

func leftovers*(d: Disk): seq[string] {.raises: [].} =
  ## The temporary files a stop left behind, recognised by their prefix.
  for name in d.names:
    if isTemp(name): result.add name

func cleanup*(d: Disk): Disk {.raises: [].} =
  ## The directory without the temporary files, and without anything else changed. The removal is
  ## durable: a real cleanup unlinks the files and then fsyncs the directory.
  result = d
  for name in d.leftovers:
    result.dir.del name
    result.durableDir.del name

func addressedName*(content: string): string {.raises: [].} =
  ## A name that is a function of the content alone: FNV-1a over 64 bits, as 16 hex digits.
  ## A real store uses a cryptographic hash (SHA-256); this one keeps the module free of packages.
  var h = 14695981039346656037'u64
  for c in content: h = (h xor uint64(ord(c))) * 1099511628211'u64
  result = "sum-"
  for i in 0 ..< 16: result.add "0123456789abcdef"[int((h shr uint64(60 - 4 * i)) and 15'u64)]

func verifies*(name, content: string): bool {.raises: [].} =
  ## Whether `content` is what `name` says it is: a reader's check of what it read.
  addressedName(content) == name

func planAddressed*(content, token: string; mode: SyncMode): Result[seq[Step], PublishError] {.raises: [].} =
  ## The plan that publishes `content` under its own hash.
  publishPlan(addressedName(content), token, content, mode)

when defined(posix):
  proc cRename(oldPath, newPath: cstring): cint {.importc: "rename", header: "<stdio.h>", raises: [].}
    ## rename(2) as the C library has it: atomic when both names are in one directory.

  proc syncFd(fd: cint): bool {.raises: [].} =
    while fsync(fd) != 0:
      if errno != EINTR: return false
    true

  proc writeAll(fd: cint; data: string): bool {.raises: [].} =
    var off = 0
    while off < data.len:
      let rest = data[off ..< data.len]
      let n = write(fd, cstring(rest), rest.len)
      if n < 0:
        if errno == EINTR: continue
        return false
      if n == 0: return false
      off += n
    true

  proc abort(fd: cint; tmpPath: string; tmpExists: bool; why: PublishError): PublishError {.raises: [].} =
    ## The error to report once a step failed: the descriptor is closed and the temporary file removed.
    ## If the descriptor cannot be closed or the file cannot be removed, something stays behind and
    ## the error says so; a file left behind is recognised by its prefix.
    if fd >= 0 and close(fd) != 0: return peFailedAndLeftover
    if tmpExists and unlink(cstring(tmpPath)) != 0 and errno != ENOENT: return peFailedAndLeftover
    why

  proc publishFile*(dir, target, content: string; mode: SyncMode = smFull): Result[string, PublishError] {.raises: [].} =
    ## The edge: publish `content` as `dir/target`, executing `publishPlan` with `std/posix`. The
    ## temporary file is created in `dir` with O_EXCL, so two writers never share one. No exception
    ## escapes; a failed step removes the temporary file and says which step failed. After
    ## `peFsyncDir` the new content is visible but not yet known to be durable.
    let token = $getCurrentProcessId() & "-" & $getMonoTime().ticks
    let plan = publishPlan(target, token, content, mode)
    if plan.isErr: return err(string, plan.error)
    var fd = cint(-1)
    var tmpPath = ""
    for s in plan.value:
      case s.kind
      of skCreate:
        tmpPath = dir / s.name
        fd = open(cstring(tmpPath), O_WRONLY or O_CREAT or O_EXCL, Mode(0o644))
        if fd < 0:
          let why = if errno == ENOENT or errno == ENOTDIR: peDirMissing else: peCreate
          return err(string, why)
      of skWrite:
        if not writeAll(fd, s.data): return err(string, abort(fd, tmpPath, true, peWrite))
      of skFsyncFile:
        if not syncFd(fd): return err(string, abort(fd, tmpPath, true, peFsync))
      of skRename:
        if close(fd) != 0:
          fd = cint(-1)
          return err(string, abort(fd, tmpPath, true, peWrite))
        fd = cint(-1)
        if cRename(cstring(tmpPath), cstring(dir / s.target)) != 0:
          return err(string, abort(fd, tmpPath, true, peRename))
      of skFsyncDir:
        let dfd = open(cstring(dir), O_RDONLY)
        if dfd < 0: return err(string, peFsyncDir)
        if not syncFd(dfd):
          return err(string, abort(dfd, "", false, peFsyncDir))
        if close(dfd) != 0: return err(string, peFsyncDir)
    ok(dir / target, PublishError)
else:
  proc publishFile*(dir, target, content: string; mode: SyncMode = smFull): Result[string, PublishError] {.raises: [].} =
    ## This platform has no `std/posix`; see the page for what Windows needs instead.
    err(string, peUnsupported)

Write the Nim module `branch_by_abstraction.nim` (Branch by abstraction).

Branch by abstraction: replace an implementation inside the trunk, behind an interface, in small steps.

A long-lived branch for a replacement drifts from the trunk until nobody can merge it. Branch by
abstraction keeps one trunk: first the callers are moved behind an abstraction (here a record of
procs, `Pricing`) that the old implementation fills, then the new implementation is written
behind the same abstraction, then a stage value says which one answers: old, shadow (the old
answers while both run and a mismatch is reported) or new. Callers never change when the stage
does. The stage is a plain value moved by `advance` and `retreat`, so going forward, going
back and "the old one is no longer consulted" are functions with laws. Use it for a replacement
that cannot land in one commit and has no seam at the network edge (that is the strangler fig);
remove the abstraction's losing side when the stage reaches `stNew` for good.

Public API:
```nim
type Stage = enum
  stOld, stShadow, stNew
type Pricing = object
  subtotal*: proc (cents: seq[int]): int {.noSideEffect, raises: [].}
type Mismatch = object
  oldTotal*, newTotal*: int
type Answer = tuple[total: int, mismatch: Option[Mismatch]]
func oldPricing(): Pricing
func newPricing(): Pricing
func uncheckedPricing(): Pricing
func invoiceTotal(p: Pricing; cents: seq[int]; taxPercent: int): int
func select(stage: Stage; old, replacement: Pricing): Pricing
func compare(old, replacement: Pricing; cents: seq[int]): Option[Mismatch]
func invoiceAt(stage: Stage; old, replacement: Pricing; cents: seq[int]; taxPercent: int): Answer
func advance(s: Stage): Stage
func retreat(s: Stage): Stage
```
output:
## Branch by abstraction: replace an implementation inside the trunk, behind an interface, in small steps.
##
## A long-lived branch for a replacement drifts from the trunk until nobody can merge it. Branch by
## abstraction keeps one trunk: first the callers are moved behind an abstraction (here a record of
## procs, `Pricing`) that the old implementation fills, then the new implementation is written
## behind the same abstraction, then a stage value says which one answers: old, shadow (the old
## answers while both run and a mismatch is reported) or new. Callers never change when the stage
## does. The stage is a plain value moved by `advance` and `retreat`, so going forward, going
## back and "the old one is no longer consulted" are functions with laws. Use it for a replacement
## that cannot land in one commit and has no seam at the network edge (that is the strangler fig);
## remove the abstraction's losing side when the stage reaches `stNew` for good.

import std/options

type
  Stage* = enum
    stOld, stShadow, stNew

  Pricing* = object
    ## The abstraction. Contract: the sum of the line amounts in cents, a negative line counting as 0.
    subtotal*: proc(cents: seq[int]): int {.noSideEffect, raises: [].}

  Mismatch* = object
    oldTotal*, newTotal*: int

  Answer* = tuple[total: int, mismatch: Option[Mismatch]]

func oldPricing*(): Pricing {.raises: [].} =
  Pricing(subtotal: proc(cents: seq[int]): int {.noSideEffect, raises: [].} =
    var sum = 0
    for c in cents:
      if c > 0: sum += c
    sum)

func newPricing*(): Pricing {.raises: [].} =
  ## The replacement: the same contract, written another way.
  Pricing(subtotal: proc(cents: seq[int]): int {.noSideEffect, raises: [].} =
    var sum = 0
    for c in cents:
      sum += max(c, 0)
    sum)

func uncheckedPricing*(): Pricing {.raises: [].} =
  ## A replacement that forgot the clamp; the shadow stage exists to find this before users do.
  Pricing(subtotal: proc(cents: seq[int]): int {.noSideEffect, raises: [].} =
    var sum = 0
    for c in cents:
      sum += c
    sum)

func invoiceTotal*(p: Pricing; cents: seq[int]; taxPercent: int): int {.raises: [].} =
  ## A caller. It knows the abstraction and nothing about which implementation fills it.
  let sub = p.subtotal(cents)
  sub + sub * taxPercent div 100

func select*(stage: Stage; old, replacement: Pricing): Pricing {.raises: [].} =
  ## Only `stNew` consults the replacement for the answer; the shadow stage answers with the old.
  case stage
  of stOld, stShadow: old
  of stNew: replacement

func compare*(old, replacement: Pricing; cents: seq[int]): Option[Mismatch] {.raises: [].} =
  let (a, b) = (old.subtotal(cents), replacement.subtotal(cents))
  if a == b: none(Mismatch) else: some(Mismatch(oldTotal: a, newTotal: b))

func invoiceAt*(stage: Stage; old, replacement: Pricing; cents: seq[int]; taxPercent: int): Answer {.raises: [].} =
  ## The answer at a stage; the mismatch is looked for only while the stage is `stShadow`.
  let mismatch = if stage == stShadow: compare(old, replacement, cents) else: none(Mismatch)
  (total: invoiceTotal(select(stage, old, replacement), cents, taxPercent), mismatch: mismatch)

func advance*(s: Stage): Stage {.raises: [].} =
  case s
  of stOld: stShadow
  of stShadow, stNew: stNew

func retreat*(s: Stage): Stage {.raises: [].} =
  case s
  of stOld, stShadow: stOld
  of stNew: stShadow

Write the Nim module `bridge.nim` (Bridge).

Bridge: shapes (abstraction) and backends (implementation) vary separately.

The OO pattern splits a hierarchy in two so that N shapes and M backends need N + M definitions,
not N * M. That only works if the implementation side offers a small, *fixed* set of primitives
that every abstraction lowers to. Here the only primitive is `line`: a `Backend` is an object
with one proc field, a `Shape` lowers itself to line `Segment`s (`lower`), and `draw` feeds them
to the backend. A new shape needs only a `lower` case; a new backend needs only a `line` proc;
neither touches the other. (If the backend had one primitive per shape kind, adding a shape
would edit every backend and this would not be a bridge.) Use it when two axes would multiply.
Circles are approximated by an octagon with integer coordinates.

Public API:
```nim
type Point = object
  x*, y*: int
type Segment = object
  a*, b*: Point
type Backend = object
  name*: string
  line*: proc (a, b: Point): string {.noSideEffect, raises: [].}
type ShapeKind = enum
  skRect, skCircle
type Shape = object
  case kind*: ShapeKind
  of skRect:
    x*, y*, w*, h*: int
  of skCircle:
    cx*, cy*, r*: int
func lower(s: Shape): seq[Segment]
func svgBackend(): Backend
func asciiBackend(): Backend
func draw(s: Shape; b: Backend): seq[string]
func drawAll(shapes: seq[Shape]; b: Backend): seq[string]
func moved(s: Shape; dx, dy: int): Shape
```

## Bridge: shapes (abstraction) and backends (implementation) vary separately.
##
## The OO pattern splits a hierarchy in two so that N shapes and M backends need N + M definitions,
## not N * M. That only works if the implementation side offers a small, *fixed* set of primitives
## that every abstraction lowers to. Here the only primitive is `line`: a `Backend` is an object
## with one proc field, a `Shape` lowers itself to line `Segment`s (`lower`), and `draw` feeds them
## to the backend. A new shape needs only a `lower` case; a new backend needs only a `line` proc;
## neither touches the other. (If the backend had one primitive per shape kind, adding a shape
## would edit every backend and this would not be a bridge.) Use it when two axes would multiply.
## Circles are approximated by an octagon with integer coordinates.

type
  Point* = object
    x*, y*: int

  Segment* = object
    a*, b*: Point

  Backend* = object
    name*: string
    line*: proc(a, b: Point): string {.noSideEffect, raises: [].}

  ShapeKind* = enum
    skRect, skCircle

  Shape* = object
    case kind*: ShapeKind
    of skRect:
      x*, y*, w*, h*: int
    of skCircle:
      cx*, cy*, r*: int

func pt(x, y: int): Point {.raises: [].} =
  Point(x: x, y: y)

func lower*(s: Shape): seq[Segment] {.raises: [].} =
  ## The shape's closed outline as line segments, independent of any backend.
  var corners: seq[Point] = @[]
  case s.kind
  of skRect:
    corners = @[pt(s.x, s.y), pt(s.x + s.w, s.y), pt(s.x + s.w, s.y + s.h), pt(s.x, s.y + s.h)]
  of skCircle:
    let d = s.r * 7 div 10 # r * cos 45 degrees, rounded down
    corners = @[pt(s.cx + s.r, s.cy), pt(s.cx + d, s.cy + d), pt(s.cx, s.cy + s.r),
                pt(s.cx - d, s.cy + d), pt(s.cx - s.r, s.cy), pt(s.cx - d, s.cy - d),
                pt(s.cx, s.cy - s.r), pt(s.cx + d, s.cy - d)]
  for i in 0 ..< corners.len:
    result.add(Segment(a: corners[i], b: corners[(i + 1) mod corners.len]))

func svgBackend*(): Backend {.raises: [].} =
  Backend(
    name: "svg",
    line: proc(a, b: Point): string {.noSideEffect, raises: [].} =
      "<line x1=" & $a.x & " y1=" & $a.y & " x2=" & $b.x & " y2=" & $b.y & "/>")

func asciiBackend*(): Backend {.raises: [].} =
  Backend(
    name: "ascii",
    line: proc(a, b: Point): string {.noSideEffect, raises: [].} =
      "LINE " & $a.x & "," & $a.y & " " & $b.x & "," & $b.y)

func draw*(s: Shape; b: Backend): seq[string] {.raises: [].} =
  ## One backend call per lowered segment.
  for seg in lower(s):
    result.add(b.line(seg.a, seg.b))

func drawAll*(shapes: seq[Shape]; b: Backend): seq[string] {.raises: [].} =
  for s in shapes:
    result.add(draw(s, b))

func moved*(s: Shape; dx, dy: int): Shape {.raises: [].} =
  ## A shape operation that is independent of every backend.
  case s.kind
  of skRect: Shape(kind: skRect, x: s.x + dx, y: s.y + dy, w: s.w, h: s.h)
  of skCircle: Shape(kind: skCircle, cx: s.cx + dx, cy: s.cy + dy, r: s.r)

Write the Nim module `builder.nim` (Builder).

Builder as an immutable value with chained `func`s and a validating `build`.

The OO pattern collects many optional settings step by step and creates the object only when it
is complete. In Nim each `withX` returns a changed copy (the old builder stays valid), and
`build` is the single place that checks the whole configuration and returns a `Result`.
Use it when an object has many settings, some optional, with rules that span several fields.

Public API:
```nim
type Port = distinct int
type BuildError = enum
  beEmptyHost, beBadPort, beTlsNeedsCert, beNoWorkers
type ServerConfig = object
  host*: string
  port*: Port
  tls*: bool
  certPath*: Option[string]
  workers*: int
type ConfigBuilder = object
func `==`(a, b: Port): bool
func initConfigBuilder(): ConfigBuilder
func withHost(b: ConfigBuilder; host: string): ConfigBuilder
func withPort(b: ConfigBuilder; port: int): ConfigBuilder
func withTls(b: ConfigBuilder; certPath: string): ConfigBuilder
func withWorkers(b: ConfigBuilder; workers: int): ConfigBuilder
func build(b: ConfigBuilder): Result[ServerConfig, BuildError]
```
output:
## Builder as an immutable value with chained `func`s and a validating `build`.
##
## The OO pattern collects many optional settings step by step and creates the object only when it
## is complete. In Nim each `withX` returns a changed copy (the old builder stays valid), and
## `build` is the single place that checks the whole configuration and returns a `Result`.
## Use it when an object has many settings, some optional, with rules that span several fields.

import std/options
import nimcs/fp/result

type
  Port* = distinct int

  BuildError* = enum
    beEmptyHost, beBadPort, beTlsNeedsCert, beNoWorkers

  ServerConfig* = object
    host*: string
    port*: Port
    tls*: bool
    certPath*: Option[string]
    workers*: int

  ConfigBuilder* = object
    host: string
    port: int
    tls: bool
    certPath: Option[string]
    workers: int

func `==`*(a, b: Port): bool {.borrow.}

func initConfigBuilder*(): ConfigBuilder {.raises: [].} =
  ConfigBuilder(host: "", port: 8080, tls: false, certPath: none(string), workers: 1)

func withHost*(b: ConfigBuilder; host: string): ConfigBuilder {.raises: [].} =
  result = b
  result.host = host

func withPort*(b: ConfigBuilder; port: int): ConfigBuilder {.raises: [].} =
  result = b
  result.port = port

func withTls*(b: ConfigBuilder; certPath: string): ConfigBuilder {.raises: [].} =
  result = b
  result.tls = true
  result.certPath = if certPath.len > 0: some(certPath) else: none(string)

func withWorkers*(b: ConfigBuilder; workers: int): ConfigBuilder {.raises: [].} =
  result = b
  result.workers = workers

func build*(b: ConfigBuilder): Result[ServerConfig, BuildError] {.raises: [].} =
  ## Checks in a fixed order, so the reported error is deterministic.
  if b.host.len == 0:
    err(ServerConfig, beEmptyHost)
  elif b.port < 1 or b.port > 65535:
    err(ServerConfig, beBadPort)
  elif b.tls and b.certPath.isNone:
    err(ServerConfig, beTlsNeedsCert)
  elif b.workers < 1:
    err(ServerConfig, beNoWorkers)
  else:
    ok(ServerConfig(host: b.host, port: Port(b.port), tls: b.tls,
                    certPath: b.certPath, workers: b.workers), BuildError)

Write the Nim module `bulkhead.nim` (Bulkhead).

Bulkhead: a fixed number of permits per compartment, so one partition's load cannot take another's capacity.

A ship's bulkheads keep a flooded compartment from sinking the rest. In a service, one shared pool
of workers lets a slow tenant or a slow dependency hold every worker; giving each partition its
own number of permits keeps the damage inside the partition. The whole state is one value,
`Bulkhead`: the permit limit and the permits in use of every compartment. `tryAcquire` is a pure
admission function that returns the new value and the answer; `release` returns a permit and
refuses to release one that was never taken, so a double release cannot grow the capacity.
Nothing here blocks or waits: a refusal is a value, and what to do with it (queue, shed, fail
fast) belongs to the caller, see `load_shedding` for deciding by queue length and deadline.
Use it around calls that share a scarce resource and can be grouped by tenant, dependency or
priority class.

Public API:
```nim
type Bulkhead = object
type Admission = enum
  aAdmitted, aFull, aUnknownCompartment
type SetupError = enum
  seNoCompartments, seEmptyName, seDuplicateName, seLimitNotPositive
type ReleaseError = enum
  reUnknownCompartment, reNothingToRelease
func `==`(a, b: Bulkhead): bool
func initBulkhead(limits: openArray[(string, int)]): Result[Bulkhead, SetupError]
func limit(b: Bulkhead; compartment: string): int
func inUse(b: Bulkhead; compartment: string): int
func available(b: Bulkhead; compartment: string): int
func usage(b: Bulkhead): seq[(string, int)]
func tryAcquire(b: Bulkhead; compartment: string): tuple[bulkhead: Bulkhead, admission: Admission]
func release(b: Bulkhead; compartment: string): Result[Bulkhead, ReleaseError]
```

Write the Nim module `caretaker.nim` (Caretaker).

Caretaker: revocable forwarding, with the revocation state threaded as data (ADR-NCK-0002).

A caretaker hands out a `Forwarder` (the capability the client holds: it forwards operations to
the target) and a `Revoker` (the capability the grantor keeps: it cuts the forwarder off).
Classic caretakers use a mutable cell that every forwarder reads. Here the cell is a value:
the `Caretaker` holds one slot per forwarder, `forward` takes the caretaker as an argument and
answers `crRevoked` once the slot is empty, and `revoke` returns a new caretaker whose slot has
dropped the target. Nothing is hidden or mutable, so every law is checkable as a function of
values. The price is explicit and deliberate: revocation reaches only the callers that use the
caretaker value that was revoked. Keep the caretaker in the one place that owns the resource
(an actor's state, a store threaded through the program), and let clients call through that
owner (send it a message, or pass the current value). If independent parties must see a
revocation instantly without going through an owner, a shared mutable cell (a `ref` read by
all forwarders) is the right tool; it gives up the value semantics and the replayability of
these laws, so use it only at that edge.

`forward` runs a pure operation (`proc` with `noSideEffect`) on the target; to forward an
effectful call, return a description of the call as the result and perform it in the shell.
Every caretaker has a `brand`; its forwarders and revokers carry it, so capabilities of another
caretaker are refused (`crForeign`) instead of acting on a slot of the same number. Use one
distinct brand per caretaker.

Public API:
```nim
type CaretakerError = enum
  crRevoked, crForeign
type Forwarder {.requiresInit.} = object
type Revoker {.requiresInit.} = object
type Caretaker[T] = object
type Wrapped[T] = object
  caretaker*: Caretaker[T]
  forwarder*: Forwarder
  revoker*: Revoker
func initCaretaker[T](brand: int): Caretaker[T]
func wrap[T](c: Caretaker[T]; target: T): Wrapped[T]
func forward[T, R](c: Caretaker[T]; f: Forwarder; op: proc (t: T): R {.noSideEffect, raises: [].}): Result[R, CaretakerError]
func revoke[T](c: Caretaker[T]; r: Revoker): Result[Caretaker[T], CaretakerError]
func isRevoked[T](c: Caretaker[T]; f: Forwarder): bool
func liveCount[T](c: Caretaker[T]): int
```
output:
## Caretaker: revocable forwarding, with the revocation state threaded as data (ADR-NCK-0002).
##
## A caretaker hands out a `Forwarder` (the capability the client holds: it forwards operations to
## the target) and a `Revoker` (the capability the grantor keeps: it cuts the forwarder off).
## Classic caretakers use a mutable cell that every forwarder reads. Here the cell is a value:
## the `Caretaker` holds one slot per forwarder, `forward` takes the caretaker as an argument and
## answers `crRevoked` once the slot is empty, and `revoke` returns a new caretaker whose slot has
## dropped the target. Nothing is hidden or mutable, so every law is checkable as a function of
## values. The price is explicit and deliberate: revocation reaches only the callers that use the
## caretaker value that was revoked. Keep the caretaker in the one place that owns the resource
## (an actor's state, a store threaded through the program), and let clients call through that
## owner (send it a message, or pass the current value). If independent parties must see a
## revocation instantly without going through an owner, a shared mutable cell (a `ref` read by
## all forwarders) is the right tool; it gives up the value semantics and the replayability of
## these laws, so use it only at that edge.
##
## `forward` runs a pure operation (`proc` with `noSideEffect`) on the target; to forward an
## effectful call, return a description of the call as the result and perform it in the shell.
## Every caretaker has a `brand`; its forwarders and revokers carry it, so capabilities of another
## caretaker are refused (`crForeign`) instead of acting on a slot of the same number. Use one
## distinct brand per caretaker.

import std/options
import nimcs/ds/hamt
import nimcs/fp/result

type
  CaretakerError* = enum
    crRevoked, crForeign

  Forwarder* {.requiresInit.} = object
    brand: int
    slot: int

  Revoker* {.requiresInit.} = object
    brand: int
    slot: int

  Caretaker*[T] = object
    brand: int
    next: int
    slots: Hamt[int, Option[T]]   ## `none` once revoked: the target is no longer referenced

  Wrapped*[T] = object
    caretaker*: Caretaker[T]
    forwarder*: Forwarder
    revoker*: Revoker

func initCaretaker*[T](brand: int): Caretaker[T] {.raises: [].} =
  Caretaker[T](brand: brand, next: 0, slots: emptyHamt[int, Option[T]]())

func wrap*[T](c: Caretaker[T]; target: T): Wrapped[T] {.raises: [].} =
  ## A new forwarder to `target` and the revoker for it. Wrapping the same target twice gives two
  ## independent forwarders.
  Wrapped[T](
    caretaker: Caretaker[T](brand: c.brand, next: c.next + 1,
      slots: c.slots.put(c.next, some(target))),
    forwarder: Forwarder(brand: c.brand, slot: c.next),
    revoker: Revoker(brand: c.brand, slot: c.next))

func forward*[T, R](c: Caretaker[T]; f: Forwarder;
    op: proc(t: T): R {.noSideEffect, raises: [].}): Result[R, CaretakerError] {.raises: [].} =
  ## `ok(op(target))` while the forwarder is live; `err(crRevoked)` after revocation; `err(crForeign)`
  ## for a forwarder that belongs to another caretaker.
  if f.brand != c.brand: return err(R, crForeign)
  let slot = c.slots.get(f.slot)
  if slot.isNone: return err(R, crForeign)
  if slot.get.isNone: err(R, crRevoked)
  else: ok(op(slot.get.get), CaretakerError)

func revoke*[T](c: Caretaker[T]; r: Revoker): Result[Caretaker[T], CaretakerError] {.raises: [].} =
  ## Cuts off the forwarder this revoker belongs to. Revoking again changes nothing (it is `ok` of
  ## an equivalent caretaker). A revoker of another caretaker is `err(crForeign)`: it is refused,
  ## not ignored.
  if r.brand != c.brand or not c.slots.contains(r.slot): err(Caretaker[T], crForeign)
  else:
    ok(Caretaker[T](brand: c.brand, next: c.next, slots: c.slots.put(r.slot, none(T))),
      CaretakerError)

func isRevoked*[T](c: Caretaker[T]; f: Forwarder): bool {.raises: [].} =
  ## True when `f` is one of this caretaker's forwarders and has been revoked.
  if f.brand != c.brand: return false
  let slot = c.slots.get(f.slot)
  slot.isSome and slot.get.isNone

func liveCount*[T](c: Caretaker[T]): int {.raises: [].} =
  ## The forwarders that still reach their target.
  for (_, slot) in c.slots.toSortedSeq:
    if slot.isSome: inc result

Write the Nim module `chain_of_responsibility.nim` (Chain of Responsibility).

Chain of Responsibility: a list of "maybe handle it" functions; the first `some` wins.

The OO pattern links handler objects, each holding a reference to its successor and deciding to
handle or pass on. In Nim a handler is `proc(request): Option[Response]`, a chain is a plain
`seq` of them, and "pass it on" is simply moving to the next element. `orElse` composes two
handlers into one, which makes handlers a monoid (associative, with `never` as identity), so
chains can be nested or built in pieces. Unhandled is a `Result` error, not a nil. Use it for
approvals, middleware, parsers that try alternatives, and fallbacks. The example approves
expense claims by the lowest authority whose limit covers the amount.

Public API:
```nim
type Handler[Req; Resp] = proc (request: Req): Option[Resp] {.noSideEffect,
    raises: [].}
type Unhandled = object
type Claim = object
  amount*: int
  category*: string
type Approval = object
  by*: string
  amount*: int
func `==`(a, b: Approval): bool
func `$`(a: Approval): string
func never[Req, Resp](request: Req): Option[Resp]
func firstSome[Req, Resp](chain: openArray[Handler[Req, Resp]]; request: Req): Option[Resp]
func handle[Req, Resp](chain: openArray[Handler[Req, Resp]]; request: Req): Result[Resp, Unhandled]
func orElse[Req, Resp](first, second: Handler[Req, Resp]): Handler[Req, Resp]
func within(name: string; limit: int): Handler[Claim, Approval]
func onlyCategory(h: Handler[Claim, Approval]; category: string): Handler[Claim, Approval]
func authorityChain(): seq[Handler[Claim, Approval]]
```

Write the Nim module `circuit_breaker.nim` (Circuit breaker).

Circuit breaker: stop calling a dependency that keeps failing, and probe it again after a pause.

Calling a dead dependency costs every caller a timeout and keeps the dependency under load while
it tries to recover. A breaker watches the outcomes and has three states: closed (calls pass,
consecutive failures are counted), open (calls are refused until a pause has passed) and half-open
(one probe call passes; its outcome decides whether to close or to open again). The breaker is an
object variant, so the data that only one state needs (a failure count, the time of opening, the
probe flag) exists only in that state. Every transition is a pure function that returns the new
breaker; the clock is an argument (`now`, in ticks), never read here (see `time_as_input`).
`allow` also returns a `Decision`; a refusal returns the breaker unchanged. Use it around calls to
a remote service, and pair it with `retry_backoff`: backoff spaces out the retries of one caller,
the breaker stops all callers once the failures are persistent. Ticks must be non-negative and
below 2^52, so that adding the pause to the time of opening cannot overflow.

Public API:

## Circuit breaker: stop calling a dependency that keeps failing, and probe it again after a pause.
##
## Calling a dead dependency costs every caller a timeout and keeps the dependency under load while
## it tries to recover. A breaker watches the outcomes and has three states: closed (calls pass,
## consecutive failures are counted), open (calls are refused until a pause has passed) and half-open
## (one probe call passes; its outcome decides whether to close or to open again). The breaker is an
## object variant, so the data that only one state needs (a failure count, the time of opening, the
## probe flag) exists only in that state. Every transition is a pure function that returns the new
## breaker; the clock is an argument (`now`, in ticks), never read here (see `time_as_input`).
## `allow` also returns a `Decision`; a refusal returns the breaker unchanged. Use it around calls to
## a remote service, and pair it with `retry_backoff`: backoff spaces out the retries of one caller,
## the breaker stops all callers once the failures are persistent. Ticks must be non-negative and
## below 2^52, so that adding the pause to the time of opening cannot overflow.

import nimcs/fp/result
export result

const MaxTicks* = 4_503_599_627_370_496  ## 2^52

type
  BreakerState* = enum
    bsClosed, bsOpen, bsHalfOpen

  Decision* = enum
    dAllow, dReject

  BreakerConfig* = object
    failureThreshold: int
    openTicks: int

  ConfigError* = enum
    ceThresholdNotPositive, ceOpenTicksNotPositive, ceOpenTicksTooLarge

  Breaker* = object
    case state: BreakerState
    of bsClosed:
      failures: int      ## consecutive failures so far
    of bsOpen:
      openedAt: int
    of bsHalfOpen:
      probing: bool      ## a probe call has been admitted and has not reported yet

func failureThreshold*(c: BreakerConfig): int {.raises: [].} = c.failureThreshold
func openTicks*(c: BreakerConfig): int {.raises: [].} = c.openTicks

func initConfig*(failureThreshold, openTicks: int): Result[BreakerConfig, ConfigError] {.raises: [].} =
  ## `failureThreshold` consecutive failures open the breaker; it stays open for `openTicks`.
  if failureThreshold < 1: err(BreakerConfig, ceThresholdNotPositive)
  elif openTicks < 1: err(BreakerConfig, ceOpenTicksNotPositive)
  elif openTicks > MaxTicks: err(BreakerConfig, ceOpenTicksTooLarge)
  else: ok(BreakerConfig(failureThreshold: failureThreshold, openTicks: openTicks), ConfigError)

func closedBreaker*(): Breaker {.raises: [].} = Breaker(state: bsClosed, failures: 0)

func state*(b: Breaker): BreakerState {.raises: [].} = b.state

func consecutiveFailures*(b: Breaker): int {.raises: [].} =
  ## The failures counted while closed; 0 in the other states.
  case b.state
  of bsClosed: b.failures
  of bsOpen, bsHalfOpen: 0

func `==`*(a, b: Breaker): bool {.raises: [].} =
  if a.state != b.state: return false
  case a.state
  of bsClosed: a.failures == b.failures
  of bsOpen: a.openedAt == b.openedAt
  of bsHalfOpen: a.probing == b.probing

func openedAtOf*(b: Breaker): int {.raises: [].} =
  ## The tick at which an open breaker opened; -1 when it is not open.
  case b.state
  of bsOpen: b.openedAt
  of bsClosed, bsHalfOpen: -1

func allow*(b: Breaker; c: BreakerConfig; now: int): tuple[breaker: Breaker, decision: Decision] {.raises: [].} =
  ## May a call start at `now`? Closed: yes. Open: no, until `openTicks` have passed since opening;
  ## then the breaker becomes half-open and this call is the probe. Half-open: yes only for the
  ## first call (the probe), no for the others while the probe has not reported. A refusal returns
  ## the breaker unchanged. A `now` earlier than the time of opening counts as "not yet".
  case b.state
  of bsClosed:
    (b, dAllow)
  of bsOpen:
    if now - b.openedAt >= c.openTicks:
      (Breaker(state: bsHalfOpen, probing: true), dAllow)
    else:
      (b, dReject)
  of bsHalfOpen:
    if b.probing: (b, dReject)
    else: (Breaker(state: bsHalfOpen, probing: true), dAllow)

func recordSuccess*(b: Breaker): Breaker {.raises: [].} =
  ## A call reported success. Closed: the failure count restarts. Half-open: the probe succeeded,
  ## close. Open: a late report from a call started before opening; ignored.
  case b.state
  of bsClosed: closedBreaker()
  of bsHalfOpen: closedBreaker()
  of bsOpen: b

func recordFailure*(b: Breaker; c: BreakerConfig; now: int): Breaker {.raises: [].} =
  ## A call reported failure at `now`. Closed: count it, and open when the count reaches the
  ## threshold. Half-open: the probe failed, open again from `now`. Open: ignored, so a late
  ## report does not push the reopening time further away.
  case b.state
  of bsClosed:
    if b.failures + 1 >= c.failureThreshold: Breaker(state: bsOpen, openedAt: now)
    else: Breaker(state: bsClosed, failures: b.failures + 1)
  of bsHalfOpen:
    Breaker(state: bsOpen, openedAt: now)
  of bsOpen:
    b

Write the Nim module `command.nim` (Command).

Command: an edit is a value; undo is another value.

Positions and lengths are byte offsets into a UTF-8 text. A command that would cut a multi-byte
character (a position on a continuation byte) or insert invalid UTF-8 is refused, so a valid
document stays valid and `inverse` always describes the edit that was applied.

The OO pattern wraps a request in an object with `execute` and `undo` so it can be queued,
logged and reversed. In Nim a command is plain data (an object variant), `apply` is a pure
function from document and command to a new document, and undo is the inverse command, computed
from the document as it was before the edit. The editor keeps two stacks of inverse/forward
commands. Use it when operations must be replayed, logged, undone or sent elsewhere; when you
only need "go back to an earlier state", keep the old values instead (see `memento`).

Write the Nim module `command_buffer.nim` (Command buffer (read, then write)).

Command buffer: read, decide, then write, instead of changing a collection while reading it.

A game step has to remove units that die and add units that split, and the natural loop does both
to the collection it is reading. In Nim that fails at run time (the `for` loop over a `seq`
asserts that the length did not change), and the ways around it that compile are a copy of the
collection per frame or a `ref` per unit that several places mutate. This module splits the work
in two. `plan` only reads the world and returns the changes as data: a `seq[WorldCmd]`. `applyAll`
applies them in order to a world the caller moves in. Units live in a `SlotMap`, so a command
names its target by `Handle`; a command whose handle is stale (the unit was despawned earlier in
the batch, or before it) does nothing, which makes a double despawn harmless and a damage after a
despawn ignored. The shell of the pattern is the same as a command log: the plan can be inspected,
logged, replayed or sent elsewhere before it is applied (see `command` for undo, and
`functional_core` for effects as data).

Rules of the example world. `plan` with a damage of zero or less returns no commands (healing
is not modelled). A live unit whose `hp` is at most the damage is despawned; it does not split.
Any other unit takes the damage, and a unit with `splits` set whose `hp` falls from above
`SplitThreshold` to `SplitThreshold` or below spawns one child with the parent's new `hp` and
`splits` unset, so a unit splits at most once and children do not split. Units spawned during a
step are not visited by that step's `plan`: it was computed from the world before the step.

Public API:
```nim
const SplitThreshold = 3
type Unit = object
  hp*: int
  splits*: bool
type World = object
  units*: SlotMap[Unit]
type WorldCmdKind = enum
  wcSpawn, wcDespawn, wcDamage
type WorldCmd = object
  case kind*: WorldCmdKind
  of wcSpawn:
    unit*: Unit
  of wcDespawn:
    target*: Handle
  of wcDamage:
    victim*: Handle
    amount*: int
func emptyWorld(): World
func `==`(a, b: Unit): bool
func `==`(a, b: World): bool
func `==`(a, b: WorldCmd): bool
func spawnCmd(unit: Unit): WorldCmd
func despawnCmd(target: Handle): WorldCmd
func damageCmd(victim: Handle; amount: int): WorldCmd
func spawn(w: sink World; unit: Unit): tuple[world: World, handle: Handle]
func plan(w: World; damage: int): seq[WorldCmd]
func applyCmd(w: sink World; c: WorldCmd): World
func applyAll(w: sink World; cmds: openArray[WorldCmd]): World
func step(w: sink World; damage: int): World
```

## Command buffer: read, decide, then write, instead of changing a collection while reading it.
##
## A game step has to remove units that die and add units that split, and the natural loop does both
## to the collection it is reading. In Nim that fails at run time (the `for` loop over a `seq`
## asserts that the length did not change), and the ways around it that compile are a copy of the
## collection per frame or a `ref` per unit that several places mutate. This module splits the work
## in two. `plan` only reads the world and returns the changes as data: a `seq[WorldCmd]`. `applyAll`
## applies them in order to a world the caller moves in. Units live in a `SlotMap`, so a command
## names its target by `Handle`; a command whose handle is stale (the unit was despawned earlier in
## the batch, or before it) does nothing, which makes a double despawn harmless and a damage after a
## despawn ignored. The shell of the pattern is the same as a command log: the plan can be inspected,
## logged, replayed or sent elsewhere before it is applied (see `command` for undo, and
## `functional_core` for effects as data).
##
## Rules of the example world. `plan` with a damage of zero or less returns no commands (healing
## is not modelled). A live unit whose `hp` is at most the damage is despawned; it does not split.
## Any other unit takes the damage, and a unit with `splits` set whose `hp` falls from above
## `SplitThreshold` to `SplitThreshold` or below spawns one child with the parent's new `hp` and
## `splits` unset, so a unit splits at most once and children do not split. Units spawned during a
## step are not visited by that step's `plan`: it was computed from the world before the step.

import std/options
import nimcs/ds/slot_map

const
  SplitThreshold* = 3   ## a splitting unit spawns a child when damage takes its hp from above this to this or below

type
  Unit* = object
    hp*: int
    splits*: bool
  World* = object
    units*: SlotMap[Unit]
  WorldCmdKind* = enum
    wcSpawn, wcDespawn, wcDamage
  WorldCmd* = object
    ## A change to the world, as data (not `command.Cmd`, so both modules import together). `wcDamage` lowers `hp` and never removes the unit;
    ## removal is a separate `wcDespawn`, which `plan` emits.
    case kind*: WorldCmdKind
    of wcSpawn:
      unit*: Unit
    of wcDespawn:
      target*: Handle
    of wcDamage:
      victim*: Handle
      amount*: int

func emptyWorld*(): World {.raises: [].} =
  World(units: emptySlotMap[Unit]())

func `==`*(a, b: Unit): bool {.raises: [].} =
  a.hp == b.hp and a.splits == b.splits

func `==`*(a, b: World): bool {.raises: [].} =
  a.units == b.units

func `==`*(a, b: WorldCmd): bool {.raises: [].} =
  if a.kind != b.kind: return false
  case a.kind
  of wcSpawn: a.unit == b.unit
  of wcDespawn: a.target == b.target
  of wcDamage: a.victim == b.victim and a.amount == b.amount

func spawnCmd*(unit: Unit): WorldCmd {.raises: [].} =
  WorldCmd(kind: wcSpawn, unit: unit)

func despawnCmd*(target: Handle): WorldCmd {.raises: [].} =
  WorldCmd(kind: wcDespawn, target: target)

func damageCmd*(victim: Handle; amount: int): WorldCmd {.raises: [].} =
  WorldCmd(kind: wcDamage, victim: victim, amount: amount)

func spawn*(w: sink World; unit: Unit): tuple[world: World, handle: Handle] {.raises: [].} =
  ## Adds a unit directly and returns its handle (a `wcSpawn` command does not report one).
  var cur = w
  let r = move(cur.units).insert(unit)
  (World(units: r.map), r.handle)

func satSub(hp, amount: int): int =
  ## `hp - amount`, held at the ends of `int` instead of wrapping.
  if amount > 0 and hp < low(int) + amount: low(int)
  elif amount < 0 and hp > high(int) + amount: high(int)
  else: hp - amount

func plan*(w: World; damage: int): seq[WorldCmd] {.raises: [].} =
  ## Reads only: the commands one step with `damage` would apply, in slot order.
  if damage <= 0: return @[]
  for h, u in w.units.pairs:
    if u.hp <= damage:
      result.add despawnCmd(h)
    else:
      result.add damageCmd(h, damage)
      let left = u.hp - damage
      if u.splits and u.hp > SplitThreshold and left <= SplitThreshold:
        result.add spawnCmd(Unit(hp: left, splits: false))

func applyCmd*(w: sink World; c: WorldCmd): World {.raises: [].} =
  ## One command. A handle that is stale or unknown changes nothing.
  var cur = w
  case c.kind
  of wcSpawn:
    let r = move(cur.units).insert(c.unit)
    World(units: r.map)
  of wcDespawn:
    let r = move(cur.units).remove(c.target)
    World(units: r.map)
  of wcDamage:
    let u = cur.units.get(c.victim)
    if u.isNone: return cur
    let r = move(cur.units).put(c.victim, Unit(hp: satSub(u.get.hp, c.amount), splits: u.get.splits))
    World(units: r.map)

func applyAll*(w: sink World; cmds: openArray[WorldCmd]): World {.raises: [].} =
  ## The commands in order; the same as folding `applyCmd` over them.
  var cur = w
  for c in cmds:
    cur = applyCmd(cur, c)
  cur

func step*(w: sink World; damage: int): World {.raises: [].} =
  ## Plan from the world as it is, then apply.
  let cmds = plan(w, damage)
  applyAll(w, cmds)

Write the Nim module `composite.nim` (Composite).

Composite as a recursive object variant plus a fold.

The OO pattern lets clients treat a single object and a group of objects through one interface.
In Nim the tree is one object variant (`File` or `Dir` holding a `seq` of children, no `ref`
needed) and every operation on the whole tree is an instance of one `fold`. Use it for
part-whole structures (file trees, UI trees, expressions); write new operations as folds
instead of adding a method to every node kind.

Public API:
```nim
type EntryKind = enum
  ekFile, ekDir
type Entry = object
  name*: string
  case kind*: EntryKind
  of ekFile:
    size*: int
  of ekDir:
    children*: seq[Entry]
func file(name: string; size: int): Entry
func dir(name: string; children: seq[Entry]): Entry
func fold[A](e: Entry; onFile: proc (name: string; size: int): A {.noSideEffect, raises: [].}; onDir: proc (name: string; parts: seq[A]): A {.noSideEffect, raises: [].}): A
func totalSize(e: Entry): int
func fileCount(e: Entry): int
func depth(e: Entry): int
func leafSizes(e: Entry): seq[int]
```

## Composite as a recursive object variant plus a fold.
##
## The OO pattern lets clients treat a single object and a group of objects through one interface.
## In Nim the tree is one object variant (`File` or `Dir` holding a `seq` of children, no `ref`
## needed) and every operation on the whole tree is an instance of one `fold`. Use it for
## part-whole structures (file trees, UI trees, expressions); write new operations as folds
## instead of adding a method to every node kind.

type
  EntryKind* = enum
    ekFile, ekDir

  Entry* = object
    name*: string
    case kind*: EntryKind
    of ekFile:
      size*: int
    of ekDir:
      children*: seq[Entry]

func file*(name: string; size: int): Entry {.raises: [].} =
  Entry(name: name, kind: ekFile, size: size)

func dir*(name: string; children: seq[Entry]): Entry {.raises: [].} =
  Entry(name: name, kind: ekDir, children: children)

func fold*[A](e: Entry;
              onFile: proc(name: string; size: int): A {.noSideEffect, raises: [].};
              onDir: proc(name: string; parts: seq[A]): A {.noSideEffect, raises: [].}): A {.raises: [].} =
  ## The one recursion; every other operation below is a choice of `onFile` and `onDir`.
  case e.kind
  of ekFile:
    onFile(e.name, e.size)
  of ekDir:
    var parts: seq[A] = @[]
    for c in e.children:
      parts.add(fold(c, onFile, onDir))
    onDir(e.name, parts)

func totalSize*(e: Entry): int {.raises: [].} =
  e.fold(
    proc(name: string; size: int): int {.noSideEffect, raises: [].} = size,
    proc(name: string; parts: seq[int]): int {.noSideEffect, raises: [].} =
      var sum = 0
      for p in parts: sum += p
      sum)

func fileCount*(e: Entry): int {.raises: [].} =
  e.fold(
    proc(name: string; size: int): int {.noSideEffect, raises: [].} = 1,
    proc(name: string; parts: seq[int]): int {.noSideEffect, raises: [].} =
      var sum = 0
      for p in parts: sum += p
      sum)

func depth*(e: Entry): int {.raises: [].} =
  e.fold(
    proc(name: string; size: int): int {.noSideEffect, raises: [].} = 0,
    proc(name: string; parts: seq[int]): int {.noSideEffect, raises: [].} =
      var deepest = 0
      for p in parts:
        if p > deepest: deepest = p
      deepest + 1)

func leafSizes*(e: Entry): seq[int] {.raises: [].} =
  ## Sizes of all files, left to right.
  e.fold(
    proc(name: string; size: int): seq[int] {.noSideEffect, raises: [].} = @[size],
    proc(name: string; parts: seq[seq[int]]): seq[int] {.noSideEffect, raises: [].} =
      var all: seq[int] = @[]
      for p in parts: all.add(p)
      all)

Write the Nim module `cqrs.nim` (CQRS (command query responsibility segregation)).

CQRS: commands are decided into events on one side, read models are folds of the same events on the other.

Command and query responsibility segregation splits a system in two. The write side takes a
command, checks it against the current state and answers with events or a reason for refusing;
it keeps only the state needed to decide. The read side never decides anything: each read model
is a projection, a fold over the events, shaped for the question it answers. Here both sides
consume the same event log (CQRS does not require event sourcing; the log is what makes the
projections easy to state), so read models can be added or rebuilt at will. The example is a
small warehouse: receive and ship units, with a stock table (write side) and a dashboard
(read side).

Public API:
```nim
type StockLine = object
  sku*: string
  qty*: int
type Stock = object
  lines*: seq[StockLine]
type CommandKind = enum
  ckReceive, ckShip
type Command = object
  kind*: CommandKind
  sku*: string
  qty*: int
type EventKind = enum
  evReceived, evShipped
type Event = object
  kind*: EventKind
  sku*: string
  qty*: int
type CommandError = enum
  ceNonPositiveQty, ceEmptySku, ceInsufficientStock
type Session = object
  stock*: Stock
  events*: seq[Event]
  rejected*: seq[CommandError]
type Dashboard = object
  received*: int
  shipped*: int
  shipments*: int
func initStock(): Stock
func qtyOf(stock: Stock; sku: string): int
func evolve(stock: Stock; e: Event): Stock
func decide(stock: Stock; cmd: Command): Result[seq[Event], CommandError]
func initSession(): Session
func submit(s: Session; cmd: Command): Session
func runAll(cmds: openArray[Command]): Session
func stockOf(events: openArray[Event]): Stock
func continueDashboard(d: Dashboard; events: openArray[Event]): Dashboard
func dashboard(events: openArray[Event]): Dashboard
```

## CQRS: commands are decided into events on one side, read models are folds of the same events on the other.
##
## Command and query responsibility segregation splits a system in two. The write side takes a
## command, checks it against the current state and answers with events or a reason for refusing;
## it keeps only the state needed to decide. The read side never decides anything: each read model
## is a projection, a fold over the events, shaped for the question it answers. Here both sides
## consume the same event log (CQRS does not require event sourcing; the log is what makes the
## projections easy to state), so read models can be added or rebuilt at will. The example is a
## small warehouse: receive and ship units, with a stock table (write side) and a dashboard
## (read side).

import std/algorithm
import nimcs/fp/result

type
  StockLine* = object
    sku*: string
    qty*: int

  Stock* = object
    ## Write-side state: one line per sku that is on hand, sorted by sku, never a zero line.
    lines*: seq[StockLine]

  CommandKind* = enum
    ckReceive, ckShip

  Command* = object
    kind*: CommandKind
    sku*: string
    qty*: int

  EventKind* = enum
    evReceived, evShipped

  Event* = object
    kind*: EventKind
    sku*: string
    qty*: int

  CommandError* = enum
    ceNonPositiveQty, ceEmptySku, ceInsufficientStock

  Session* = object
    ## The application service state: current stock, the event log, and the refusals.
    stock*: Stock
    events*: seq[Event]
    rejected*: seq[CommandError]

  Dashboard* = object
    ## A read model: totals only, no per-sku detail.
    received*: int
    shipped*: int
    shipments*: int

# ── write side ─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────

func initStock*(): Stock {.raises: [].} = Stock(lines: @[])

func qtyOf*(stock: Stock; sku: string): int {.raises: [].} =
  for l in stock.lines:
    if l.sku == sku: return l.qty
  0

func evolve*(stock: Stock; e: Event): Stock {.raises: [].} =
  ## Applies a fact to the stock. Lines whose quantity becomes zero disappear, so equal stocks
  ## are equal values. An event that `decide` never produced (shipping more than is on hand)
  ## would leave a negative line; the guard against that lives in `decide`, not here.
  let delta = if e.kind == evReceived: e.qty else: -e.qty
  var lines: seq[StockLine]
  var seen = false
  for l in stock.lines:
    if l.sku == e.sku:
      seen = true
      if l.qty + delta != 0: lines.add StockLine(sku: l.sku, qty: l.qty + delta)
    else:
      lines.add l
  if not seen and delta != 0: lines.add StockLine(sku: e.sku, qty: delta)
  lines.sort(proc(a, b: StockLine): int = cmp(a.sku, b.sku))
  Stock(lines: lines)

func decide*(stock: Stock; cmd: Command): Result[seq[Event], CommandError] {.raises: [].} =
  ## Validates a command against the stock. It returns the events that record what happens, or
  ## the first reason it must be refused; it changes nothing.
  if cmd.sku.len == 0:
    return err(seq[Event], ceEmptySku)
  if cmd.qty <= 0:
    return err(seq[Event], ceNonPositiveQty)
  case cmd.kind
  of ckReceive:
    ok(@[Event(kind: evReceived, sku: cmd.sku, qty: cmd.qty)], CommandError)
  of ckShip:
    if stock.qtyOf(cmd.sku) < cmd.qty:
      err(seq[Event], ceInsufficientStock)
    else:
      ok(@[Event(kind: evShipped, sku: cmd.sku, qty: cmd.qty)], CommandError)

func initSession*(): Session {.raises: [].} =
  Session(stock: initStock(), events: @[], rejected: @[])

func submit*(s: Session; cmd: Command): Session {.raises: [].} =
  ## Decides the command; an accepted one appends its events and evolves the stock, a refused
  ## one is recorded in `rejected` and changes nothing else.
  let decided = s.stock.decide(cmd)
  if decided.isOk:
    result = s
    for e in decided.value:
      result.events.add e
      result.stock = result.stock.evolve(e)
  else:
    result = s
    result.rejected.add decided.error

func runAll*(cmds: openArray[Command]): Session {.raises: [].} =
  result = initSession()
  for c in cmds:
    result = result.submit(c)

# ── read side ──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────

func stockOf*(events: openArray[Event]): Stock {.raises: [].} =
  ## Rebuilds the write-side stock from the events alone.
  result = initStock()
  for e in events:
    result = result.evolve(e)

func continueDashboard*(d: Dashboard; events: openArray[Event]): Dashboard {.raises: [].} =
  ## Folds more events into an existing dashboard.
  result = d
  for e in events:
    case e.kind
    of evReceived:
      result.received += e.qty
    of evShipped:
      result.shipped += e.qty
      result.shipments += 1

func dashboard*(events: openArray[Event]): Dashboard {.raises: [].} =
  ## The dashboard read model, projected from the whole log.
  continueDashboard(Dashboard(), events)

Write the Nim module `decompose_conditional.nim` (Decompose conditional).

Decompose conditional: give each part of a long condition a name, and each branch a result type.

A condition that mixes ages, weekdays and hours in one expression is read by running it in your
head. Decomposing it means a small `func` per idea in the condition (`isChild`, `isWeekdaySenior`,
`isDaytimeStudent`, `isEvening`), and a decision that is a short `case` or `if` over those names.
Here the price of a museum ticket in yen. `priceBefore` is the single tangled expression;
`tierOf` names the rule that applied and `priceOf` turns a tier into money, so the answer to
"why did this visitor pay that?" is a value (`Tier`) and not a trace. Use it when a condition
has more than two clauses or when you cannot say the rule aloud. It changes no result: the test
compares both shapes on generated visitors.

Public API:
```nim
type Visitor = object
  age*: int                  ## whole years
  isStudent*: bool
  weekday*: int              ## 0 = Monday .. 6 = Sunday
  hour*: int                 ## 0 .. 23
type Tier = enum
  tFree, tReduced, tFull
const FullPrice = 1500
const ReducedPrice = 800
func priceBefore(v: Visitor): int
func isChild(v: Visitor): bool
func isSenior(v: Visitor): bool
func isWeekday(v: Visitor): bool
func isDaytimeStudent(v: Visitor): bool
func isEvening(v: Visitor): bool
func tierOf(v: Visitor): Tier
func priceOf(t: Tier): int
func price(v: Visitor): int
```

## Decompose conditional: give each part of a long condition a name, and each branch a result type.
##
## A condition that mixes ages, weekdays and hours in one expression is read by running it in your
## head. Decomposing it means a small `func` per idea in the condition (`isChild`, `isWeekdaySenior`,
## `isDaytimeStudent`, `isEvening`), and a decision that is a short `case` or `if` over those names.
## Here the price of a museum ticket in yen. `priceBefore` is the single tangled expression;
## `tierOf` names the rule that applied and `priceOf` turns a tier into money, so the answer to
## "why did this visitor pay that?" is a value (`Tier`) and not a trace. Use it when a condition
## has more than two clauses or when you cannot say the rule aloud. It changes no result: the test
## compares both shapes on generated visitors.

type
  Visitor* = object
    age*: int          ## whole years
    isStudent*: bool
    weekday*: int      ## 0 = Monday .. 6 = Sunday
    hour*: int         ## 0 .. 23

  Tier* = enum
    tFree, tReduced, tFull

const
  FullPrice* = 1500
  ReducedPrice* = 800

func priceBefore*(v: Visitor): int {.raises: [].} =
  ## Before: every rule inline, precedence hidden in the parentheses.
  if v.age < 6 or (v.age >= 65 and v.weekday < 5):
    0
  elif (v.isStudent and v.age < 26 and v.hour < 17) or v.hour >= 20 or (v.age >= 65):
    ReducedPrice
  else:
    FullPrice

func isChild*(v: Visitor): bool {.raises: [].} = v.age < 6

func isSenior*(v: Visitor): bool {.raises: [].} = v.age >= 65

func isWeekday*(v: Visitor): bool {.raises: [].} = v.weekday < 5

func isDaytimeStudent*(v: Visitor): bool {.raises: [].} =
  v.isStudent and v.age < 26 and v.hour < 17

func isEvening*(v: Visitor): bool {.raises: [].} = v.hour >= 20

func tierOf*(v: Visitor): Tier {.raises: [].} =
  ## After: the rules read in priority order, first match wins.
  if v.isChild or (v.isSenior and v.isWeekday): tFree
  elif v.isDaytimeStudent or v.isEvening or v.isSenior: tReduced
  else: tFull

func priceOf*(t: Tier): int {.raises: [].} =
  case t
  of tFree: 0
  of tReduced: ReducedPrice
  of tFull: FullPrice

func price*(v: Visitor): int {.raises: [].} = v.tierOf.priceOf
