Write the Nim module `decorator.nim` (Decorator).

Decorator as a function from handler to handler.

The OO pattern adds behaviour to an object by wrapping it in another object with the same
interface. In Nim a handler is a proc value `Request -> Response` and a decorator is
`proc(h: Handler): Handler`; stacking decorators is function composition. Use it for
cross-cutting behaviour (headers, authorisation, tracing) around a core handler without
changing the core. The pipeline is pure: there is no I/O, the "log" is a trace in the response.

Public API:
```nim
type Request = object
  path*: string
  token*: string
type Response = object
  status*: int
  body*: string
  trace*: seq[string]
type Handler = proc (r: Request): Response {.noSideEffect, raises: [].}
type Decorator = proc (h: Handler): Handler {.noSideEffect, raises: [].}
func identityDecorator(): Decorator
func withTrace(label: string): Decorator
func withAuth(expected: string): Decorator
func withBodySuffix(suffix: string): Decorator
func compose(outer, inner: Decorator): Decorator
func stack(ds: seq[Decorator]): Decorator
```
output:
## Decorator as a function from handler to handler.
##
## The OO pattern adds behaviour to an object by wrapping it in another object with the same
## interface. In Nim a handler is a proc value `Request -> Response` and a decorator is
## `proc(h: Handler): Handler`; stacking decorators is function composition. Use it for
## cross-cutting behaviour (headers, authorisation, tracing) around a core handler without
## changing the core. The pipeline is pure: there is no I/O, the "log" is a trace in the response.

type
  Request* = object
    path*: string
    token*: string

  Response* = object
    status*: int
    body*: string
    trace*: seq[string]

  Handler* = proc(r: Request): Response {.noSideEffect, raises: [].}
  Decorator* = proc(h: Handler): Handler {.noSideEffect, raises: [].}

func identityDecorator*(): Decorator {.raises: [].} =
  proc(h: Handler): Handler {.noSideEffect, raises: [].} = h

func withTrace*(label: string): Decorator {.raises: [].} =
  ## Records `label` before the inner handler runs and again, as `label/done`, after it returns.
  proc(h: Handler): Handler {.noSideEffect, raises: [].} =
    proc(r: Request): Response {.noSideEffect, raises: [].} =
      var res = h(r)
      res.trace = @[label] & res.trace & @[label & "/done"]
      res

func withAuth*(expected: string): Decorator {.raises: [].} =
  ## Short-circuits with 401 when the token differs; the inner handler is not called.
  proc(h: Handler): Handler {.noSideEffect, raises: [].} =
    proc(r: Request): Response {.noSideEffect, raises: [].} =
      if r.token == expected:
        h(r)
      else:
        Response(status: 401, body: "unauthorized", trace: @[])

func withBodySuffix*(suffix: string): Decorator {.raises: [].} =
  proc(h: Handler): Handler {.noSideEffect, raises: [].} =
    proc(r: Request): Response {.noSideEffect, raises: [].} =
      var res = h(r)
      res.body.add(suffix)
      res

func compose*(outer, inner: Decorator): Decorator {.raises: [].} =
  ## `compose(a, b)(h)` is `a(b(h))`: `a` is the outermost wrapper and sees the request first.
  proc(h: Handler): Handler {.noSideEffect, raises: [].} =
    outer(inner(h))

func stack*(ds: seq[Decorator]): Decorator {.raises: [].} =
  ## The first element is the outermost decorator.
  var acc = identityDecorator()
  for i in countdown(ds.high, 0):
    acc = compose(ds[i], acc)
  acc

Write the Nim module `dependency_record.nim` (Dependency record (dependency injection by passing a record of procs)).

Dependency record: dependencies are an object of procs, and a test double is another object.

Business logic that needs the clock and a mail sender takes a `Deps` value instead of calling
them. The production record holds the real procs; a test builds a record from a fixed clock
and a sender that writes into a list. No interface type, no framework, no global to reset.
`withClock` and `withSender` replace one field and keep the rest, so a test changes only the
dependency it cares about. Use it for the few effects a unit needs. When the sequence of
effects itself must be inspected or optimised, make the program data instead
(`free_interpreter`).

Public API:
```nim
type Clock = proc (): int {.raises: [].}
type Sender = proc (to, body: string): Result[int, string] {.raises: [].}
type Deps = object
  now*: Clock
  send*: Sender
type RemindError = object
  reason*: string
  sentIds*: seq[int]
type Invoice = object
  id*: int
  customer*: string
  dueDay*: int
  paid*: bool
func withClock(deps: Deps; now: Clock): Deps
func withSender(deps: Deps; send: Sender): Deps
proc remindOverdue(deps: Deps; invoices: openArray[Invoice]): Result[seq[int], RemindError]
```
output:
## Dependency record: dependencies are an object of procs, and a test double is another object.
##
## Business logic that needs the clock and a mail sender takes a `Deps` value instead of calling
## them. The production record holds the real procs; a test builds a record from a fixed clock
## and a sender that writes into a list. No interface type, no framework, no global to reset.
## `withClock` and `withSender` replace one field and keep the rest, so a test changes only the
## dependency it cares about. Use it for the few effects a unit needs. When the sequence of
## effects itself must be inspected or optimised, make the program data instead
## (`free_interpreter`).

import nimcs/fp/result

type
  Clock* = proc(): int {.raises: [].}
    ## Today as a day number.

  Sender* = proc(to, body: string): Result[int, string] {.raises: [].}
    ## Sends one message; the `int` is the message id, the error says why it failed.

  Deps* = object
    now*: Clock
    send*: Sender

  RemindError* = object
    ## Why a run stopped, and what had already gone out before it did.
    reason*: string
    sentIds*: seq[int]

  Invoice* = object
    id*: int
    customer*: string
    dueDay*: int
    paid*: bool

func withClock*(deps: Deps; now: Clock): Deps {.raises: [].} =
  ## The same dependencies with another clock.
  Deps(now: now, send: deps.send)

func withSender*(deps: Deps; send: Sender): Deps {.raises: [].} =
  ## The same dependencies with another sender.
  Deps(now: deps.now, send: send)

proc remindOverdue*(deps: Deps; invoices: openArray[Invoice]): Result[seq[int], RemindError] {.raises: [].} =
  ## Sends one reminder per unpaid invoice that is due before today, in list order, and returns
  ## the message ids. It is a `proc`, not a `func`, because the record it is given may perform
  ## effects. The first send that fails stops the run; the error carries the sender's reason and the ids
  ## of the messages already sent, which cannot be taken back.
  let today = deps.now()
  var ids: seq[int]
  for inv in invoices:
    if not inv.paid and inv.dueDay < today:
      let sent = deps.send(inv.customer, "Invoice " & $inv.id & " was due on day " & $inv.dueDay)
      if sent.isErr:
        return err(seq[int], RemindError(reason: sent.error, sentIds: ids))
      ids.add sent.value
  ok(ids, RemindError)

Write the Nim module `event_sourcing.nim` (Event sourcing).

Event sourcing: the state of an entity is a fold over the facts that happened to it.

Instead of storing the current balance, store the list of events (deposited, withdrawn) and
compute the balance by folding `apply` over them. The log is the source of truth and is only
ever appended to; any past state can be rebuilt, and a snapshot is nothing but a saved
intermediate value of the same fold. Use it when the history matters (audit, undo, temporal
queries) or when several read models must be derived from the same facts (see `cqrs`).

Public API:
```nim
type EventKind = enum
  evDeposited, evWithdrawn
type Event = object
  kind*: EventKind
  amount*: int
type Account = object
  balance*: int
  version*: int
func deposited(amount: Positive): Event
func withdrawn(amount: Positive): Event
func initAccount(): Account
func apply(a: Account; e: Event): Account
func replayFrom(snapshot: Account; tail: openArray[Event]): Account
func replay(events: openArray[Event]): Account
func snapshotAt(events: openArray[Event]; upTo: int): Account
func appended(log: seq[Event]; e: Event): seq[Event]
```
output:
## Event sourcing: the state of an entity is a fold over the facts that happened to it.
##
## Instead of storing the current balance, store the list of events (deposited, withdrawn) and
## compute the balance by folding `apply` over them. The log is the source of truth and is only
## ever appended to; any past state can be rebuilt, and a snapshot is nothing but a saved
## intermediate value of the same fold. Use it when the history matters (audit, undo, temporal
## queries) or when several read models must be derived from the same facts (see `cqrs`).

type
  EventKind* = enum
    evDeposited, evWithdrawn

  Event* = object
    ## A fact in the past tense. `amount` is positive; the direction is in `kind`.
    kind*: EventKind
    amount*: int

  Account* = object
    ## The folded state. `version` counts the events folded in.
    balance*: int
    version*: int

func deposited*(amount: Positive): Event {.raises: [].} =
  Event(kind: evDeposited, amount: amount)

func withdrawn*(amount: Positive): Event {.raises: [].} =
  Event(kind: evWithdrawn, amount: amount)

func initAccount*(): Account {.raises: [].} =
  ## The state before any event: the fold's starting value.
  Account(balance: 0, version: 0)

func apply*(a: Account; e: Event): Account {.raises: [].} =
  ## One step of the fold. Total: events are facts, so it never refuses one (a command that
  ## would overdraw is refused before an event exists, see `cqrs`).
  let delta =
    case e.kind
    of evDeposited: e.amount
    of evWithdrawn: -e.amount
  Account(balance: a.balance + delta, version: a.version + 1)

func replayFrom*(snapshot: Account; tail: openArray[Event]): Account {.raises: [].} =
  ## Continues the fold from a saved state.
  result = snapshot
  for e in tail:
    result = result.apply(e)

func replay*(events: openArray[Event]): Account {.raises: [].} =
  ## The whole fold from the empty account.
  initAccount().replayFrom(events)

func snapshotAt*(events: openArray[Event]; upTo: int): Account {.raises: [].} =
  ## The state after the first `upTo` events; a count below 0 or beyond the log is clamped.
  let n = max(0, min(upTo, events.len))
  replay(events.toOpenArray(0, n - 1))

func appended*(log: seq[Event]; e: Event): seq[Event] {.raises: [].} =
  ## A new log with `e` at the end; `log` itself is untouched.
  result = log
  result.add e

Write the Nim module `extract_function.nim` (Extract function).

Extract function: cut a long routine at the seams where it computes a named thing.

`summaryBefore` totals an order, applies a bulk discount, adds tax and formats a line, all in
one body with four local variables that each step reads. `summary` is the same behaviour as a
sequence of small functions (`subtotal`, `discountOf`, `taxOf`, `render`), each of which takes
what it needs as arguments and returns one value, so each has a name, a signature and a law
of its own. Extract when a comment would otherwise say "now compute the discount", when a block
has one input and one output, or when you want to test one step without the others. A block
that reads and writes many locals is not ready: introduce a parameter object first
(`introduce_parameter_object`). Money is whole yen; tax is rounded down.

Public API:
```nim
type Line = object
  unitPrice*: int
  quantity*: int
type Summary = object
  subtotal*: int
  discount*: int
  tax*: int
  total*: int
const BulkThreshold = 10000
const BulkPercent = 5
const TaxPercent = 10
func summaryBefore(lines: openArray[Line]): string
func subtotal(lines: openArray[Line]): int
func discountOf(subtotal: int): int
func taxOf(amount: int): int
func summarize(lines: openArray[Line]): Summary
func render(s: Summary): string
func summary(lines: openArray[Line]): string
```
output:
## Extract function: cut a long routine at the seams where it computes a named thing.
##
## `summaryBefore` totals an order, applies a bulk discount, adds tax and formats a line, all in
## one body with four local variables that each step reads. `summary` is the same behaviour as a
## sequence of small functions (`subtotal`, `discountOf`, `taxOf`, `render`), each of which takes
## what it needs as arguments and returns one value, so each has a name, a signature and a law
## of its own. Extract when a comment would otherwise say "now compute the discount", when a block
## has one input and one output, or when you want to test one step without the others. A block
## that reads and writes many locals is not ready: introduce a parameter object first
## (`introduce_parameter_object`). Money is whole yen; tax is rounded down.

type
  Line* = object
    unitPrice*: int
    quantity*: int

  Summary* = object
    ## The parts, so a caller can use them without parsing text.
    subtotal*: int
    discount*: int
    tax*: int
    total*: int

const
  BulkThreshold* = 10000   ## subtotal from which the discount applies
  BulkPercent* = 5
  TaxPercent* = 10

func summaryBefore*(lines: openArray[Line]): string {.raises: [].} =
  ## Before: one body, four phases separated by comments.
  # subtotal
  var sub = 0
  for l in lines:
    sub += l.unitPrice * l.quantity
  # discount
  var disc = 0
  if sub >= BulkThreshold:
    disc = sub * BulkPercent div 100
  # tax
  let taxed = (sub - disc) * TaxPercent div 100
  # format
  "subtotal " & $sub & ", discount " & $disc & ", tax " & $taxed & ", total " & $(sub - disc + taxed)

func subtotal*(lines: openArray[Line]): int {.raises: [].} =
  ## Sum of `unitPrice * quantity`; additive over concatenation of lists.
  for l in lines: result += l.unitPrice * l.quantity

func discountOf*(subtotal: int): int {.raises: [].} =
  ## Bulk discount: a percentage once the subtotal reaches the threshold, else nothing.
  if subtotal >= BulkThreshold: subtotal * BulkPercent div 100 else: 0

func taxOf*(amount: int): int {.raises: [].} =
  ## Tax on an amount already discounted, rounded down.
  amount * TaxPercent div 100

func summarize*(lines: openArray[Line]): Summary {.raises: [].} =
  let sub = lines.subtotal
  let disc = sub.discountOf
  let tax = (sub - disc).taxOf
  Summary(subtotal: sub, discount: disc, tax: tax, total: sub - disc + tax)

func render*(s: Summary): string {.raises: [].} =
  "subtotal " & $s.subtotal & ", discount " & $s.discount & ", tax " & $s.tax & ", total " & $s.total

func summary*(lines: openArray[Line]): string {.raises: [].} =
  ## After: the same text as `summaryBefore`, as a pipeline of named steps.
  lines.summarize.render

Write the Nim module `extract_type.nim` (Extract type).

Extract type: fields that always travel together become a value type that guards its own rules.

`amount: int` and `currency: string` appear side by side in every signature of the loose code
(`addLoose`), so every caller must remember that two amounts may be added only in the same
currency, that the code is one of a few known ones, and that cents are integers. Extracting
`Money` moves those rules into one smart constructor (`initMoney`) and one operation (`plus`)
that returns a `Result`. The values for which the loose code was right behave the same
(tested); the value for which it was silently wrong, adding yen to dollars, becomes an error
the caller has to look at. Use it when two or more fields are passed together in three or more
places, or when a rule mentions them together.

Public API:
```nim
type Currency = enum
  cJpy = "JPY", cUsd = "USD", cEur = "EUR"
type MoneyError = enum
  meUnknownCurrency, meCurrencyMismatch, meNegative
type Money = object
func parseCurrency(code: string): Result[Currency, MoneyError]
func initMoney(minor: int; code: string): Result[Money, MoneyError]
func minor(m: Money): int
func currency(m: Money): Currency
func plus(a, b: Money): Result[Money, MoneyError]
func `==`(a, b: Money): bool
func addLoose(aMinor: int; aCode: string; bMinor: int; bCode: string): (int, string)
```
output:
## Extract type: fields that always travel together become a value type that guards its own rules.
##
## `amount: int` and `currency: string` appear side by side in every signature of the loose code
## (`addLoose`), so every caller must remember that two amounts may be added only in the same
## currency, that the code is one of a few known ones, and that cents are integers. Extracting
## `Money` moves those rules into one smart constructor (`initMoney`) and one operation (`plus`)
## that returns a `Result`. The values for which the loose code was right behave the same
## (tested); the value for which it was silently wrong, adding yen to dollars, becomes an error
## the caller has to look at. Use it when two or more fields are passed together in three or more
## places, or when a rule mentions them together.

import nimcs/fp/result
export result

type
  Currency* = enum
    cJpy = "JPY", cUsd = "USD", cEur = "EUR"

  MoneyError* = enum
    meUnknownCurrency, meCurrencyMismatch, meNegative

  Money* = object
    ## `minor` is in the smallest unit of `currency` and is never negative (see `initMoney`).
    minor: int
    currency: Currency

func parseCurrency*(code: string): Result[Currency, MoneyError] {.raises: [].} =
  for c in Currency:
    if $c == code:
      return ok(c, MoneyError)
  err(Currency, meUnknownCurrency)

func initMoney*(minor: int; code: string): Result[Money, MoneyError] {.raises: [].} =
  ## The one door: a known code and a non-negative amount, or the reason it is refused.
  let c = parseCurrency(code)
  if c.isErr:
    err(Money, c.error)
  elif minor < 0:
    err(Money, meNegative)
  else:
    ok(Money(minor: minor, currency: c.value), MoneyError)

func minor*(m: Money): int {.raises: [].} = m.minor

func currency*(m: Money): Currency {.raises: [].} = m.currency

func plus*(a, b: Money): Result[Money, MoneyError] {.raises: [].} =
  ## Amounts add only in one currency; a mismatch is an error, not a wrong number.
  if a.currency != b.currency:
    err(Money, meCurrencyMismatch)
  else:
    ok(Money(minor: a.minor + b.minor, currency: a.currency), MoneyError)

func `==`*(a, b: Money): bool {.raises: [].} =
  a.minor == b.minor and a.currency == b.currency

func addLoose*(aMinor: int; aCode: string; bMinor: int; bCode: string): (int, string) {.raises: [].} =
  ## Before: the two fields of each amount travel apart; nothing stops yen being added to dollars,
  ## and the result takes the first code whatever the second was.
  (aMinor + bMinor, aCode)

Write the Nim module `facade.nim` (Facade).

Facade as a module that exports a small API over several private steps.

The OO pattern puts one simple class in front of a set of subsystem classes. In Nim the module
boundary is the facade: the steps (`tokenize`, `countWords`, ...) are not exported, and the
exported surface is `normalizeText` and `summarize`. Use it when callers need one or two
answers and should not know the order or number of internal steps. No class is needed.

Public API:
```nim
type Summary = object
  words*: int
  unique*: int
  longest*: Option[string]
  top*: seq[(string, int)]
func normalizeText(text: string): string
func summarize(text: string; topN: int = 3): Summary
```

Write the Nim module `factory_method.nim` (Factory Method).

Factory Method as a proc value: the step that creates the product is a parameter.

The OO pattern lets a subclass override `createX()` so that a shared algorithm can work with a
product it does not know. In Nim the shared algorithm (`publish`) takes the creating step as
an `ExporterFactory` value; no base class is needed. Use it when one routine must be reusable
with several ways to make its collaborator and the choice is made by the caller.

Public API:
```nim
type Format = enum
  fmtText, fmtMarkdown, fmtHtml
type Doc = object
  title*: string
  paras*: seq[string]
type Render = proc (d: Doc): string {.noSideEffect, raises: [].}
type Exporter = object
  ext*: string
  render*: Render
type ExporterFactory = proc (f: Format): Result[Exporter, string] {.noSideEffect,
    raises: [].}
type PublishedFile = object
  name*: string
  body*: string
func standardFactory(f: Format): Result[Exporter, string]
func textOnlyFactory(f: Format): Result[Exporter, string]
func publish(d: Doc; make: ExporterFactory; f: Format): Result[PublishedFile, string]
```

Write the Nim module `flyweight.nim` (Flyweight).

Flyweight as interning against an explicit immutable pool value.

The OO pattern shares one object among many users when the objects are identical, to save memory
and to make equality a cheap comparison. In Nim the shared thing is a `Sym` (an index) and the
pool is a value you pass in and get back: `intern` returns the new pool and the symbol. No
global table, so interning is deterministic and testable. `intern` copies the pool when it adds a
string (O(pool)); to intern many strings use `internAll`, which copies once. Use it for many repeated strings
(identifiers, font names, tags); skip it when the data is small or unique.

Public API:
```nim

type Pool = object
func `==`(a, b: Sym): bool
func `==`(a, b: Pool): bool
func initPool(): Pool
func size(p: Pool): int
func intern(p: Pool; s: string): tuple[pool: Pool, sym: Sym]
func resolve(p: Pool; sym: Sym): Option[string]
func internAll(p: Pool; items: seq[string]): tuple[pool: Pool, syms: seq[Sym]]
```

Write the Nim module `free_interpreter.nim` (Free interpreter (program as data)).

Free interpreter: a program is a value, and what it means is decided by whoever runs it.

Instead of calling a key-value store directly, build a `Program`, a list of instruction
values (`put`, `get`, `delete`, `whenMissing`). Nothing happens while building. Then hand the
program to an interpreter: `runPure` folds it over an in-memory store, `pretty` prints it,
a real interpreter could talk to a database. This is dependency injection by interpreter, and
because the program is data it can also be rewritten (`simplify`) before it runs, which a
closure cannot be. Use it when you want to test, inspect or optimise the sequence of effects
without performing them. When programs are fixed and only the backend varies, a record of
procs (`dependency_record`) is lighter; for new interpreters without a data type see
`tagless_final`.

Public API:
```nim
type InstrKind = enum
  ikPut, ikGet, ikDelete, ikWhenMissing
type Instr = object
  case kind*: InstrKind
  of ikPut:
    putKey*, putValue*: string
  of ikGet, ikDelete:
    key*: string
  of ikWhenMissing:
    missingKey*: string
    body*: seq[Instr]        ## runs only when `missingKey` has no value
type Program = seq[Instr]
type Entry = object
  key*, value*: string
type Outcome = object
  store*: seq[Entry]
  output*: seq[string]
func `==`(a, b: Instr): bool
func put(key, value: string): Instr
func get(key: string): Instr
func del(key: string): Instr
func whenMissing(key: string; body: Program): Instr
func ensureDefault(key, value: string): Program
func runPure(p: Program; start: seq[Entry] = @[]): Outcome
func pretty(p: Program): string
func `$`(i: Instr): string
func size(p: Program): int
func simplify(p: Program): Program
```
output:
## Free interpreter: a program is a value, and what it means is decided by whoever runs it.
##
## Instead of calling a key-value store directly, build a `Program`, a list of instruction
## values (`put`, `get`, `delete`, `whenMissing`). Nothing happens while building. Then hand the
## program to an interpreter: `runPure` folds it over an in-memory store, `pretty` prints it,
## a real interpreter could talk to a database. This is dependency injection by interpreter, and
## because the program is data it can also be rewritten (`simplify`) before it runs, which a
## closure cannot be. Use it when you want to test, inspect or optimise the sequence of effects
## without performing them. When programs are fixed and only the backend varies, a record of
## procs (`dependency_record`) is lighter; for new interpreters without a data type see
## `tagless_final`.

import std/[algorithm, options]

type
  InstrKind* = enum
    ikPut, ikGet, ikDelete, ikWhenMissing

  Instr* = object
    case kind*: InstrKind
    of ikPut:
      putKey*, putValue*: string
    of ikGet, ikDelete:
      key*: string
    of ikWhenMissing:
      missingKey*: string
      body*: seq[Instr]   ## runs only when `missingKey` has no value

  Program* = seq[Instr]

  Entry* = object
    key*, value*: string

  Outcome* = object
    ## What the pure interpreter produces: the final store (sorted by key) and the lines `get`
    ## printed, `key=value` or `key=<missing>`.
    store*: seq[Entry]
    output*: seq[string]

func `==`*(a, b: Instr): bool {.raises: [].} =
  if a.kind != b.kind: return false
  case a.kind
  of ikPut: a.putKey == b.putKey and a.putValue == b.putValue
  of ikGet, ikDelete: a.key == b.key
  of ikWhenMissing: a.missingKey == b.missingKey and a.body == b.body

func put*(key, value: string): Instr {.raises: [].} =
  Instr(kind: ikPut, putKey: key, putValue: value)

func get*(key: string): Instr {.raises: [].} = Instr(kind: ikGet, key: key)

func del*(key: string): Instr {.raises: [].} = Instr(kind: ikDelete, key: key)

func whenMissing*(key: string; body: Program): Instr {.raises: [].} =
  Instr(kind: ikWhenMissing, missingKey: key, body: body)

func ensureDefault*(key, value: string): Program {.raises: [].} =
  ## Sets `key` only if it has no value. Running it twice equals running it once.
  @[whenMissing(key, @[put(key, value)])]

# ── interpreter 1: pure ────────────────────────────────────────────────────

func lookup(store: seq[Entry]; key: string): Option[string] {.raises: [].} =
  for e in store:
    if e.key == key: return some(e.value)
  none(string)

func upsert(store: seq[Entry]; key, value: string): seq[Entry] {.raises: [].} =
  var found = false
  for e in store:
    if e.key == key:
      found = true
      result.add Entry(key: key, value: value)
    else:
      result.add e
  if not found:
    result.add Entry(key: key, value: value)
    result.sort(proc(a, b: Entry): int = cmp(a.key, b.key))

func remove(store: seq[Entry]; key: string): seq[Entry] {.raises: [].} =
  for e in store:
    if e.key != key: result.add e

func exec(state: Outcome; p: openArray[Instr]): Outcome {.raises: [].} =
  result = state
  for i in p:
    case i.kind
    of ikPut:
      result.store = result.store.upsert(i.putKey, i.putValue)
    of ikGet:
      let found = result.store.lookup(i.key)
      result.output.add i.key & "=" & (if found.isSome: found.get else: "<missing>")
    of ikDelete:
      result.store = result.store.remove(i.key)
    of ikWhenMissing:
      if result.store.lookup(i.missingKey).isNone:
        result = exec(result, i.body)

func runPure*(p: Program; start: seq[Entry] = @[]): Outcome {.raises: [].} =
  ## Interprets `p` over `start` (a store as `runPure` itself returns it, sorted by key).
  exec(Outcome(store: start, output: @[]), p)

# ── interpreter 2: printer ─────────────────────────────────────────────────

func prettyLines(p: openArray[Instr]; indent: string): seq[string] {.raises: [].} =
  for i in p:
    case i.kind
    of ikPut: result.add indent & "put " & i.putKey & " = " & i.putValue
    of ikGet: result.add indent & "get " & i.key
    of ikDelete: result.add indent & "delete " & i.key
    of ikWhenMissing:
      result.add indent & "when-missing " & i.missingKey
      result.add prettyLines(i.body, indent & "  ")

func pretty*(p: Program): string {.raises: [].} =
  ## One line per instruction, bodies indented by two spaces; an empty program prints as "".
  let lines = prettyLines(p, "")
  for n, line in lines:
    if n > 0: result.add "\n"
    result.add line

func `$`*(i: Instr): string {.raises: [].} =
  ## The instruction as `pretty` prints it.
  pretty(@[i])

func size*(p: Program): int {.raises: [].} =
  ## Number of instructions, bodies included.
  for i in p:
    result += 1
    if i.kind == ikWhenMissing: result += size(i.body)

# ── a program-to-program rewrite ───────────────────────────────────────────

func isWrite(i: Instr): bool {.raises: [].} = i.kind in {ikPut, ikDelete}

func writtenKey(i: Instr): string {.raises: [].} =
  if i.kind == ikPut: i.putKey else: i.key

func simplify*(p: Program): Program {.raises: [].} =
  ## Drops a `put` or `delete` that the next instruction overwrites with another `put` or
  ## `delete` of the same key (nothing could read it in between), inside bodies too. The result
  ## runs to the same store and output (PAT-FREEINTERPRETER-04) and simplifying again changes
  ## nothing.
  for instr in p:
    var cur = instr
    if cur.kind == ikWhenMissing:
      cur = whenMissing(cur.missingKey, simplify(cur.body))
    if isWrite(cur):
      while result.len > 0 and isWrite(result[^1]) and writtenKey(result[^1]) == writtenKey(cur):
        result.delete(result.high)
    result.add cur

Write the Nim module `functional_core.nim` (Functional core, imperative shell).

Functional core, imperative shell: decide with a pure function, act with a thin loop.

The core is a `func` from (configuration, current state, new input) to a decision: the next
state plus a list of effect descriptions, which are plain data. It never touches the world, so
every rule about when the system acts is a property of a function. The shell is the small loop
that reads an input, calls the core and performs the effects it returned; it holds no rules.
Use it whenever logic and I/O are tangled. The example is a thermostat with a dead band: it
switches only when the reading leaves the band, so the same reading twice never acts twice.

Public API:
```nim
type HeaterState = enum
  hsOff, hsOn
type Config = object
  target*: int
  band*: int                 ## half-width of the dead band, never negative (see `initConfig`)
type EffectKind = enum
  ekSetHeater, ekLog
type Effect = object
  case kind*: EffectKind
  of ekSetHeater:
    heater*: HeaterState
  of ekLog:
    line*: string
type Decision = object
  state*: HeaterState
  effects*: seq[Effect]
func `==`(a, b: Effect): bool
func initConfig(target, band: int): Result[Config, string]
func decide(cfg: Config; current: HeaterState; reading: int): Decision
```

## Functional core, imperative shell: decide with a pure function, act with a thin loop.
##
## The core is a `func` from (configuration, current state, new input) to a decision: the next
## state plus a list of effect descriptions, which are plain data. It never touches the world, so
## every rule about when the system acts is a property of a function. The shell is the small loop
## that reads an input, calls the core and performs the effects it returned; it holds no rules.
## Use it whenever logic and I/O are tangled. The example is a thermostat with a dead band: it
## switches only when the reading leaves the band, so the same reading twice never acts twice.

import nimcs/fp/result

type
  HeaterState* = enum
    hsOff, hsOn

  Config* = object
    ## Temperatures are in tenths of a degree.
    target*: int
    band*: int   ## half-width of the dead band, never negative (see `initConfig`)

  EffectKind* = enum
    ekSetHeater, ekLog

  Effect* = object
    ## An effect described, not performed. The shell decides how to perform it.
    case kind*: EffectKind
    of ekSetHeater:
      heater*: HeaterState
    of ekLog:
      line*: string

  Decision* = object
    state*: HeaterState
    effects*: seq[Effect]

func `==`*(a, b: Effect): bool {.raises: [].} =
  if a.kind != b.kind: return false
  case a.kind
  of ekSetHeater: a.heater == b.heater
  of ekLog: a.line == b.line

func initConfig*(target, band: int): Result[Config, string] {.raises: [].} =
  ## Smart constructor: a negative band has no meaning.
  if band < 0: err(Config, "band must not be negative")
  else: ok(Config(target: target, band: band), string)

func decide*(cfg: Config; current: HeaterState; reading: int): Decision {.raises: [].} =
  ## Pure decision. Inside the dead band (`|reading - target| <= band`) the state is kept and no
  ## effect is emitted; outside it the heater is driven toward the target, and a change is
  ## reported as one `ekSetHeater` followed by one `ekLog`.
  let wanted =
    if reading < cfg.target - cfg.band: hsOn
    elif reading > cfg.target + cfg.band: hsOff
    else: current
  if wanted == current:
    Decision(state: current, effects: @[])
  else:
    let word = if wanted == hsOn: "on" else: "off"
    Decision(state: wanted, effects: @[
      Effect(kind: ekSetHeater, heater: wanted),
      Effect(kind: ekLog, line: "heater " & word & " at " & $reading)])

Write the Nim module `idempotent_command.nim` (Idempotent command).

Idempotent command: the same command with the same key is applied once, however often it arrives.

Networks deliver at least once, so a client that did not hear back sends the command again.
Each command carries a key chosen by the client. The ledger stores, for every key it has
seen, the command and the response it produced; a repeat of the same command returns the
stored response and changes nothing, and a different command under a used key is a conflict.
`handle` is a pure function from (ledger, command) to (ledger, response), so "applying twice
equals applying once" is a property of a function, not a hope about a server. Use it for any
operation a client may retry (payments, orders, sign-ups). In production the entry list
would be a keyed table with an expiry; the list keeps the example short and ordered.

Public API:
```nim
type CommandKind = enum
  ckDeposit, ckWithdraw
type Command = object
  key*: string
  kind*: CommandKind
  amount*: int
type ResponseKind = enum
  rkAccepted, rkInsufficientFunds, rkInvalidAmount, rkKeyConflict
type Response = object
  kind*: ResponseKind
  balance*: int
type Entry = object
  cmd*: Command
  response*: Response
type Ledger = object
  balance*: int
  entries*: seq[Entry]       ## in order of first arrival; one per key
type Handled = tuple[ledger: Ledger, response: Response]
func initLedger(): Ledger
func handle(l: Ledger; cmd: Command): Handled
```

## Idempotent command: the same command with the same key is applied once, however often it arrives.
##
## Networks deliver at least once, so a client that did not hear back sends the command again.
## Each command carries a key chosen by the client. The ledger stores, for every key it has
## seen, the command and the response it produced; a repeat of the same command returns the
## stored response and changes nothing, and a different command under a used key is a conflict.
## `handle` is a pure function from (ledger, command) to (ledger, response), so "applying twice
## equals applying once" is a property of a function, not a hope about a server. Use it for any
## operation a client may retry (payments, orders, sign-ups). In production the entry list
## would be a keyed table with an expiry; the list keeps the example short and ordered.

type
  CommandKind* = enum
    ckDeposit, ckWithdraw

  Command* = object
    key*: string
    kind*: CommandKind
    amount*: int

  ResponseKind* = enum
    rkAccepted, rkInsufficientFunds, rkInvalidAmount, rkKeyConflict

  Response* = object
    ## `balance` is the balance the command left (accepted) or found (every refusal that was
    ## stored); for a conflict it is the current balance.
    kind*: ResponseKind
    balance*: int

  Entry* = object
    cmd*: Command
    response*: Response

  Ledger* = object
    balance*: int
    entries*: seq[Entry]   ## in order of first arrival; one per key

  Handled* = tuple[ledger: Ledger, response: Response]

func initLedger*(): Ledger {.raises: [].} = Ledger(balance: 0, entries: @[])

func decideNew(l: Ledger; cmd: Command): Handled {.raises: [].} =
  ## First arrival of a key: decide, then record the outcome under the key.
  var balance = l.balance
  var kind = rkAccepted
  if cmd.amount <= 0:
    kind = rkInvalidAmount
  else:
    case cmd.kind
    of ckDeposit:
      balance += cmd.amount
    of ckWithdraw:
      if balance < cmd.amount: kind = rkInsufficientFunds
      else: balance -= cmd.amount
  let response = Response(kind: kind, balance: balance)
  var entries = l.entries
  entries.add Entry(cmd: cmd, response: response)
  (ledger: Ledger(balance: balance, entries: entries), response: response)

func handle*(l: Ledger; cmd: Command): Handled {.raises: [].} =
  ## A key seen before returns its stored response and the same ledger when the command is
  ## identical, and `rkKeyConflict` (ledger unchanged, nothing stored) when it is not. A new key
  ## is decided once; refusals are stored too, so a retry sees the same refusal even if the
  ## balance would now allow the command.
  for e in l.entries:
    if e.cmd.key == cmd.key:
      if e.cmd == cmd:
        return (ledger: l, response: e.response)
      return (ledger: l, response: Response(kind: rkKeyConflict, balance: l.balance))
  decideNew(l, cmd)

Write the Nim module `interpreter.nim` (Interpreter).

Interpreter: a grammar is a data type and the interpreter is a fold over it.

The OO pattern gives each grammar rule a class with an `interpret(context)` method. In Nim the
rules are the cases of one object variant (`Expr`), and each interpretation (evaluate, print,
simplify) is one `func` with an exhaustive `case`. Adding an interpretation never touches the
type; variable names are validated by `variable`, so `show` is injective. Adding a rule makes every `case` fail to compile until it is handled. Use it for small
languages (formulas, filters, rules). For a full language reach for a parser generator and keep
this shape for the tree after parsing.

Arithmetic here is checked: every value must stay within `+-Limit`, so no operation can
overflow `int`. Division by zero, an unbound variable and a limit breach are `EvalError`s.

Public API:
```nim
const Limit = 1000000000
type ExprKind = enum
  ekNum, ekVar, ekNeg, ekAdd, ekMul, ekDiv
type Expr = ref object
  case
  of ekNum:
  of ekVar:
  of ekNeg:
  of ekAdd, ekMul, ekDiv:
type Binding = (string, int)
type EvalError = enum
  evUnbound, evDivByZero, evLimit
type VarError = enum
  veBadName                  ## a variable name must be an identifier
func kind(e: Expr): ExprKind
func num(e: Expr): int
func name(e: Expr): string
func operand(e: Expr): Expr
func left(e: Expr): Expr
func right(e: Expr): Expr
func num(n: int): Expr
func variable(name: string): Result[Expr, VarError]
func neg(e: Expr): Expr
func add(a, b: Expr): Expr
func mul(a, b: Expr): Expr
func divide(a, b: Expr): Expr
func same(a, b: Expr): bool
func show(e: Expr): string
func size(e: Expr): int
func eval(e: Expr; env: openArray[Binding]): Result[int, EvalError]
func fold(e: Expr): Expr
```

## Interpreter: a grammar is a data type and the interpreter is a fold over it.
##
## The OO pattern gives each grammar rule a class with an `interpret(context)` method. In Nim the
## rules are the cases of one object variant (`Expr`), and each interpretation (evaluate, print,
## simplify) is one `func` with an exhaustive `case`. Adding an interpretation never touches the
## type; variable names are validated by `variable`, so `show` is injective. Adding a rule makes every `case` fail to compile until it is handled. Use it for small
## languages (formulas, filters, rules). For a full language reach for a parser generator and keep
## this shape for the tree after parsing.
##
## Arithmetic here is checked: every value must stay within `+-Limit`, so no operation can
## overflow `int`. Division by zero, an unbound variable and a limit breach are `EvalError`s.

import std/options
import nimcs/fp/result

const Limit* = 1_000_000_000

type
  ExprKind* = enum
    ekNum, ekVar, ekNeg, ekAdd, ekMul, ekDiv

  Expr* = ref object
    ## Immutable: the fields are private, so a node can only be made by the constructors below
    ## (`num`, `variable`, `neg`, `add`, `mul`, `divide`) and read through the accessors. That is
    ## what keeps variable names valid. Reading an accessor of the wrong kind (`num` of an `ekAdd`)
    ## is a precondition violation: test `kind` first, as the `case` in `eval` does.
    case kind: ExprKind
    of ekNum:
      num: int
    of ekVar:
      name: string
    of ekNeg:
      operand: Expr
    of ekAdd, ekMul, ekDiv:
      left, right: Expr

  Binding* = (string, int)

  EvalError* = enum
    evUnbound, evDivByZero, evLimit

  VarError* = enum
    veBadName   ## a variable name must be an identifier

func kind*(e: Expr): ExprKind {.raises: [].} = e.kind
func num*(e: Expr): int {.raises: [].} = e.num
func name*(e: Expr): string {.raises: [].} = e.name
func operand*(e: Expr): Expr {.raises: [].} = e.operand
func left*(e: Expr): Expr {.raises: [].} = e.left
func right*(e: Expr): Expr {.raises: [].} = e.right

func num*(n: int): Expr {.raises: [].} = Expr(kind: ekNum, num: n)
func isIdentifier(s: string): bool {.raises: [].} =
  if s.len == 0: return false
  for i, c in s:
    let letter = c in {'a' .. 'z', 'A' .. 'Z', '_'}
    if not (letter or (i > 0 and c in {'0' .. '9'})): return false
  true

func variable*(name: string): Result[Expr, VarError] {.raises: [].} =
  ## Smart constructor. A name is a letter or underscore followed by letters, digits and
  ## underscores; anything else (spaces, parentheses, operators, empty) would make `show` ambiguous
  ## and is refused. Build `Expr` nodes through the constructors, not by naming `ekVar` directly.
  if isIdentifier(name): ok(Expr(kind: ekVar, name: name), VarError)
  else: err(Expr, veBadName)
func neg*(e: Expr): Expr {.raises: [].} = Expr(kind: ekNeg, operand: e)
func add*(a, b: Expr): Expr {.raises: [].} = Expr(kind: ekAdd, left: a, right: b)
func mul*(a, b: Expr): Expr {.raises: [].} = Expr(kind: ekMul, left: a, right: b)
func divide*(a, b: Expr): Expr {.raises: [].} = Expr(kind: ekDiv, left: a, right: b)

func same*(a, b: Expr): bool {.raises: [].} =
  ## Structural equality.
  if a.kind != b.kind: return false
  case a.kind
  of ekNum: a.num == b.num
  of ekVar: a.name == b.name
  of ekNeg: same(a.operand, b.operand)
  of ekAdd, ekMul, ekDiv: same(a.left, b.left) and same(a.right, b.right)

func show*(e: Expr): string {.raises: [].} =
  ## One interpretation: a fully parenthesised rendering.
  case e.kind
  of ekNum: $e.num
  of ekVar: e.name
  of ekNeg: "(-" & show(e.operand) & ")"
  of ekAdd: "(" & show(e.left) & " + " & show(e.right) & ")"
  of ekMul: "(" & show(e.left) & " * " & show(e.right) & ")"
  of ekDiv: "(" & show(e.left) & " / " & show(e.right) & ")"

func size*(e: Expr): int {.raises: [].} =
  ## Number of nodes.
  case e.kind
  of ekNum, ekVar: 1
  of ekNeg: 1 + size(e.operand)
  of ekAdd, ekMul, ekDiv: 1 + size(e.left) + size(e.right)

func checked(n: int): Result[int, EvalError] {.raises: [].} =
  if n > Limit or n < -Limit: err(int, evLimit) else: ok(n, EvalError)

func lookup(env: openArray[Binding]; name: string): Option[int] {.raises: [].} =
  for b in env:
    if b[0] == name: return some(b[1])
  none(int)

func combine(kind: ExprKind; a, b: int): Result[int, EvalError] {.raises: [].} =
  ## The meaning of one binary node. Both operands are range-checked here, so `eval` and `fold`
  ## (which may hand over raw literals) agree on every input, including out-of-range literals.
  let ca = checked(a)
  if ca.isErr: return ca
  let cb = checked(b)
  if cb.isErr: return cb
  case kind
  of ekAdd: checked(a + b)
  of ekMul: checked(a * b)
  of ekDiv:
    if b == 0: err(int, evDivByZero) else: checked(a div b)
  of ekNum, ekVar, ekNeg: err(int, evLimit)   # not binary; unreachable through `eval`/`fold`

func eval*(e: Expr; env: openArray[Binding]): Result[int, EvalError] {.raises: [].} =
  ## Left operand first, so the first error in reading order is the one reported.
  case e.kind
  of ekNum: checked(e.num)
  of ekVar:
    let v = lookup(env, e.name)
    if v.isNone: err(int, evUnbound) else: checked(v.get)
  of ekNeg:
    let r = eval(e.operand, env)
    if r.isErr: r else: checked(-r.value)
  of ekAdd, ekMul, ekDiv:
    let l = eval(e.left, env)
    if l.isErr: return l
    let r = eval(e.right, env)
    if r.isErr: return r
    combine(e.kind, l.value, r.value)

func foldBinary(kind: ExprKind; l, r: Expr;
                rebuild: proc(a, b: Expr): Expr {.noSideEffect, raises: [].}): Expr {.raises: [].} =
  if l.kind == ekNum and r.kind == ekNum:
    let v = combine(kind, l.num, r.num)
    if v.isOk: return num(v.value)
  rebuild(l, r)

func fold*(e: Expr): Expr {.raises: [].} =
  ## Constant folding: replaces every subtree made only of numbers that evaluates successfully.
  ## A subtree that would fail (division by zero, limit) is kept, so `eval` still reports it.
  case e.kind
  of ekNum, ekVar: e
  of ekNeg:
    let o = fold(e.operand)
    if o.kind == ekNum:
      let inRange = checked(o.num)   # -low(int) would overflow, so check before negating
      if inRange.isOk:
        let r = checked(-o.num)
        if r.isOk: return num(r.value)
    neg(o)
  of ekAdd: foldBinary(ekAdd, fold(e.left), fold(e.right), add)
  of ekMul: foldBinary(ekMul, fold(e.left), fold(e.right), mul)
  of ekDiv: foldBinary(ekDiv, fold(e.left), fold(e.right), divide)

Write the Nim module `introduce_parameter_object.nim` (Introduce parameter object).

Introduce parameter object: a group of arguments that travel together becomes one value.

`selectLoose` takes six arguments, four of them integers in a row, so swapping `maxPrice` and
`minRating` compiles and returns nonsense. The parameter object `Filter` names each field,
carries defaults that mean "no limit", and gets its own small operations: `withPrice`,
`withMinRating`, `inStockOnly`, `limited`. `select` takes the products and the filter. Because
the filter is data, it can be stored, compared, combined (`narrowedBy`) and tested on its own,
which six loose arguments cannot. Use it when the same group of three or more parameters is
passed through more than one routine, or when callers must remember an argument order. For
variants of behaviour, not of data, pass a record of procs instead (`dependency_record`).

Public API:
```nim
type Product = object
  id*: int
  price*: int                ## yen
  rating*: int               ## 0 .. 5
  inStock*: bool
type Filter = object
  minPrice*: int
  maxPrice*: int
  minRating*: int
  onlyInStock*: bool
  limit*: int                ## 0 means no limit
type StockRule = enum
  srAny, srInStockOnly
const NoLimit = 0
func noFilter(): Filter
func selectLoose(items: openArray[Product]; minPrice, maxPrice, minRating: int; stock: StockRule; limit: int): seq[Product]
func withPrice(f: Filter; minPrice, maxPrice: int): Filter
func withMinRating(f: Filter; minRating: int): Filter
func inStockOnly(f: Filter): Filter
func limited(f: Filter; limit: int): Filter
func matches(f: Filter; p: Product): bool
func select(items: openArray[Product]; f: Filter): seq[Product]
func narrowedBy(a, b: Filter): Filter
```

## Introduce parameter object: a group of arguments that travel together becomes one value.
##
## `selectLoose` takes six arguments, four of them integers in a row, so swapping `maxPrice` and
## `minRating` compiles and returns nonsense. The parameter object `Filter` names each field,
## carries defaults that mean "no limit", and gets its own small operations: `withPrice`,
## `withMinRating`, `inStockOnly`, `limited`. `select` takes the products and the filter. Because
## the filter is data, it can be stored, compared, combined (`narrowedBy`) and tested on its own,
## which six loose arguments cannot. Use it when the same group of three or more parameters is
## passed through more than one routine, or when callers must remember an argument order. For
## variants of behaviour, not of data, pass a record of procs instead (`dependency_record`).

type
  Product* = object
    id*: int
    price*: int        ## yen
    rating*: int       ## 0 .. 5
    inStock*: bool

  Filter* = object
    ## The default value of every field means "no restriction".
    minPrice*: int
    maxPrice*: int
    minRating*: int
    onlyInStock*: bool
    limit*: int        ## 0 means no limit

type
  StockRule* = enum
    srAny, srInStockOnly

const NoLimit* = 0

func noFilter*(): Filter {.raises: [].} =
  Filter(minPrice: 0, maxPrice: high(int), minRating: 0, onlyInStock: false, limit: NoLimit)

func selectLoose*(items: openArray[Product]; minPrice, maxPrice, minRating: int;
    stock: StockRule; limit: int): seq[Product] {.raises: [].} =
  ## Before: the order of the three integers is the whole contract.
  for p in items:
    if limit != NoLimit and result.len >= limit: break
    if p.price >= minPrice and p.price <= maxPrice and p.rating >= minRating and
        (stock == srAny or p.inStock):
      result.add p

func withPrice*(f: Filter; minPrice, maxPrice: int): Filter {.raises: [].} =
  Filter(minPrice: minPrice, maxPrice: maxPrice, minRating: f.minRating,
    onlyInStock: f.onlyInStock, limit: f.limit)

func withMinRating*(f: Filter; minRating: int): Filter {.raises: [].} =
  Filter(minPrice: f.minPrice, maxPrice: f.maxPrice, minRating: minRating,
    onlyInStock: f.onlyInStock, limit: f.limit)

func inStockOnly*(f: Filter): Filter {.raises: [].} =
  Filter(minPrice: f.minPrice, maxPrice: f.maxPrice, minRating: f.minRating,
    onlyInStock: true, limit: f.limit)

func limited*(f: Filter; limit: int): Filter {.raises: [].} =
  Filter(minPrice: f.minPrice, maxPrice: f.maxPrice, minRating: f.minRating,
    onlyInStock: f.onlyInStock, limit: limit)

func matches*(f: Filter; p: Product): bool {.raises: [].} =
  p.price >= f.minPrice and p.price <= f.maxPrice and p.rating >= f.minRating and
    (not f.onlyInStock or p.inStock)

func select*(items: openArray[Product]; f: Filter): seq[Product] {.raises: [].} =
  ## After: the same selection, in list order, up to `limit` matches.
  for p in items:
    if f.limit != NoLimit and result.len >= f.limit: break
    if f.matches(p):
      result.add p

func narrowedBy*(a, b: Filter): Filter {.raises: [].} =
  ## Both filters at once: the tighter bound of each field and the smaller non-zero limit.
  let lim =
    if a.limit == NoLimit: b.limit
    elif b.limit == NoLimit: a.limit
    else: min(a.limit, b.limit)
  Filter(minPrice: max(a.minPrice, b.minPrice), maxPrice: min(a.maxPrice, b.maxPrice),
    minRating: max(a.minRating, b.minRating), onlyInStock: a.onlyInStock or b.onlyInStock, limit: lim)

Write the Nim module `iterator_pattern.nim` (Iterator).

Iterator: traversal is a Nim `iterator`, or a cursor that is itself a value.

The OO pattern hides a collection's structure behind an object with `hasNext`/`next`. Nim has the
pattern built in: an `iterator` is the traversal and a `for` loop is the client. Two shapes are
shown over an immutable binary search tree. `items` is an inline iterator (internal iteration:
the loop body runs inside the traversal). `Cursor` is external iteration done functionally: a
value holding the traversal's pending work, where `next` returns the element and the *next
cursor*, so a cursor can be kept, copied and resumed any number of times. External iteration is
what you need to walk two collections in lockstep (`mergeUnion`). Use `iterator` first; reach
for `Cursor` only when two traversals must advance independently.

Public API:
```nim
type Tree = ref Node
type Cursor = object
func insert(t: Tree; v: int): Tree
func fromSeq(xs: openArray[int]): Tree
func cursor(t: Tree): Cursor
func next(c: Cursor): Option[(int, Cursor)]
iterator items(t: Tree): int
func toSeq(t: Tree): seq[int]
func mergeUnion(a, b: Tree): seq[int]
```
output:
## Iterator: traversal is a Nim `iterator`, or a cursor that is itself a value.
##
## The OO pattern hides a collection's structure behind an object with `hasNext`/`next`. Nim has the
## pattern built in: an `iterator` is the traversal and a `for` loop is the client. Two shapes are
## shown over an immutable binary search tree. `items` is an inline iterator (internal iteration:
## the loop body runs inside the traversal). `Cursor` is external iteration done functionally: a
## value holding the traversal's pending work, where `next` returns the element and the *next
## cursor*, so a cursor can be kept, copied and resumed any number of times. External iteration is
## what you need to walk two collections in lockstep (`mergeUnion`). Use `iterator` first; reach
## for `Cursor` only when two traversals must advance independently.

import std/options

type
  Tree* = ref Node
    ## Empty tree is `nil`. Nodes are immutable by convention.
  Node = object
    left, right: Tree
    value: int

  Cursor* = object
    ## The left spine still to visit; the top of `pending` is the next element.
    pending: seq[Tree]

func insert*(t: Tree; v: int): Tree {.raises: [].} =
  ## Returns a new tree containing `v`; `t` is unchanged and shares its untouched subtrees.
  ## A value already present is not added again (set semantics).
  if t.isNil: return Tree(value: v)
  if v < t.value: Tree(value: t.value, left: insert(t.left, v), right: t.right)
  elif v > t.value: Tree(value: t.value, left: t.left, right: insert(t.right, v))
  else: t

func fromSeq*(xs: openArray[int]): Tree {.raises: [].} =
  for x in xs: result = result.insert(x)

func pushSpine(stack: seq[Tree]; t: Tree): seq[Tree] {.raises: [].} =
  result = stack
  var cur = t
  while not cur.isNil:
    result.add cur
    cur = cur.left

func cursor*(t: Tree): Cursor {.raises: [].} =
  Cursor(pending: pushSpine(@[], t))

func next*(c: Cursor): Option[(int, Cursor)] {.raises: [].} =
  ## The next element in ascending order and the cursor after it; `none` at the end.
  if c.pending.len == 0: return none((int, Cursor))
  let node = c.pending[^1]
  let rest = c.pending[0 ..< c.pending.len - 1]
  some((node.value, Cursor(pending: pushSpine(rest, node.right))))

iterator items*(t: Tree): int =
  ## In-order (ascending) traversal. Internal iteration: use it in a `for` loop.
  var c = cursor(t)
  while true:
    let n = c.next
    if n.isNone: break
    yield n.get[0]
    c = n.get[1]

func toSeq*(t: Tree): seq[int] {.raises: [].} =
  for x in t.items: result.add x

func mergeUnion*(a, b: Tree): seq[int] {.raises: [].} =
  ## Ascending union of two trees, each element once, walking both with cursors in lockstep.
  var ca = cursor(a)
  var cb = cursor(b)
  while true:
    let na = ca.next
    let nb = cb.next
    if na.isNone and nb.isNone: break
    if nb.isNone or (na.isSome and na.get[0] < nb.get[0]):
      result.add na.get[0]
      ca = na.get[1]
    elif na.isNone or nb.get[0] < na.get[0]:
      result.add nb.get[0]
      cb = nb.get[1]
    else:
      result.add na.get[0]
      ca = na.get[1]
      cb = nb.get[1]

Write the Nim module `layered_architecture.nim` (Layered architecture).

Layered architecture: modules in layers, imports in one direction, rules in the lowest layer.

The program is a task board driven by text commands, split into three layers that live in
`layered_architecture/`: `domain` (rules, imports nothing of the program), `service` (parsing
and replies, imports `domain`) and `shell` (the effects, imports `service` and `domain`). A
module may import a layer below it and never one above or beside it; with this rule the domain
can be tested with no parser and the service with no terminal, and a cycle cannot form. This
file is the composition root: it re-exports the layers and keeps `tangledBefore`, the same
behaviour written as one routine that parses, decides and formats together. Use layers when a
program has rules, a protocol and effects that change at different rates; skip them for a
script. The functional-core pattern (`functional_core`) is the same split seen from the effects.

Public API:
```nim
func tangledBefore(lines: openArray[string]): seq[string]
```

Write the Nim module `lens.nim` (Lens).

Lens: a getter and a setter bundled so that a deep field of an immutable value can be read and replaced.

Updating `company.ceo.address.city` in immutable data means rebuilding three levels by hand.
A `Lens[S, A]` focuses on an `A` inside an `S`: `view` reads it, `put` returns a new `S` with
it replaced, and `compose` chains a lens into a lens so deep access is the composition of
shallow ones. A lens is only trustworthy if it obeys three laws (get-set, set-get, set-set),
which are properties to test for every lens you write. Use lenses for nested records that are
updated often; for one field one level down, plain object copy (`fp/immutable_update`) is
simpler.

Public API:
```nim
type Address = object
  street*, city*: string
  zip*: int
type Person = object
  name*: string
  age*: int
  address*: Address
type Company = object
  name*: string
  ceo*: Person
type Lens[S; A] = object
func lens[S, A](getter: proc (s: S): A {.noSideEffect, raises: [].}; setter: proc (s: S; a: A): S {.noSideEffect, raises: [].}): Lens[S, A]
func view[S, A](l: Lens[S, A]; s: S): A
func put[S, A](l: Lens[S, A]; s: S; a: A): S
func over[S, A](l: Lens[S, A]; s: S; f: proc (a: A): A {.noSideEffect, raises: [].}): S
func compose[S, M, A](outer: Lens[S, M]; inner: Lens[M, A]): Lens[S, A]
func companyCeo(): Lens[Company, Person]
func addressLens(): Lens[Person, Address]
func ageLens(): Lens[Person, int]
func cityLens(): Lens[Address, string]
func ceoAge(): Lens[Company, int]
func ceoCity(): Lens[Company, string]
```
output:
## Lens: a getter and a setter bundled so that a deep field of an immutable value can be read and replaced.
##
## Updating `company.ceo.address.city` in immutable data means rebuilding three levels by hand.
## A `Lens[S, A]` focuses on an `A` inside an `S`: `view` reads it, `put` returns a new `S` with
## it replaced, and `compose` chains a lens into a lens so deep access is the composition of
## shallow ones. A lens is only trustworthy if it obeys three laws (get-set, set-get, set-set),
## which are properties to test for every lens you write. Use lenses for nested records that are
## updated often; for one field one level down, plain object copy (`fp/immutable_update`) is
## simpler.

type
  Address* = object
    street*, city*: string
    zip*: int

  Person* = object
    name*: string
    age*: int
    address*: Address

  Company* = object
    name*: string
    ceo*: Person

  Lens*[S, A] = object
    getter: proc(s: S): A {.noSideEffect, raises: [].}
    setter: proc(s: S; a: A): S {.noSideEffect, raises: [].}

func lens*[S, A](getter: proc(s: S): A {.noSideEffect, raises: [].};
                 setter: proc(s: S; a: A): S {.noSideEffect, raises: [].}): Lens[S, A] {.raises: [].} =
  ## Bundles a getter and a setter. Nothing checks the laws; test them.
  Lens[S, A](getter: getter, setter: setter)

func view*[S, A](l: Lens[S, A]; s: S): A {.raises: [].} = l.getter(s)

func put*[S, A](l: Lens[S, A]; s: S; a: A): S {.raises: [].} =
  ## A copy of `s` with the focus replaced; `s` is untouched.
  l.setter(s, a)

func over*[S, A](l: Lens[S, A]; s: S; f: proc(a: A): A {.noSideEffect, raises: [].}): S {.raises: [].} =
  ## Replaces the focus by `f` of the focus.
  l.put(s, f(l.view(s)))

func compose*[S, M, A](outer: Lens[S, M]; inner: Lens[M, A]): Lens[S, A] {.raises: [].} =
  ## Focuses first through `outer`, then through `inner`.
  lens(
    proc(s: S): A {.noSideEffect, raises: [].} = inner.view(outer.view(s)),
    proc(s: S; a: A): S {.noSideEffect, raises: [].} = outer.put(s, inner.put(outer.view(s), a)))

# ── lenses for the example records ─────────────────────────────────────────

func companyCeo*(): Lens[Company, Person] {.raises: [].} =
  lens(
    proc(c: Company): Person {.noSideEffect, raises: [].} = c.ceo,
    proc(c: Company; p: Person): Company {.noSideEffect, raises: [].} = Company(name: c.name, ceo: p))

func addressLens*(): Lens[Person, Address] {.raises: [].} =
  lens(
    proc(p: Person): Address {.noSideEffect, raises: [].} = p.address,
    proc(p: Person; a: Address): Person {.noSideEffect, raises: [].} =
      Person(name: p.name, age: p.age, address: a))

func ageLens*(): Lens[Person, int] {.raises: [].} =
  lens(
    proc(p: Person): int {.noSideEffect, raises: [].} = p.age,
    proc(p: Person; a: int): Person {.noSideEffect, raises: [].} =
      Person(name: p.name, age: a, address: p.address))

func cityLens*(): Lens[Address, string] {.raises: [].} =
  lens(
    proc(a: Address): string {.noSideEffect, raises: [].} = a.city,
    proc(a: Address; c: string): Address {.noSideEffect, raises: [].} =
      Address(street: a.street, city: c, zip: a.zip))

func ceoAge*(): Lens[Company, int] {.raises: [].} =
  companyCeo().compose(ageLens())

func ceoCity*(): Lens[Company, string] {.raises: [].} =
  companyCeo().compose(addressLens()).compose(cityLens())

Write the Nim module `load_shedding.nim` (Load shedding).

Load shedding: under overload, refuse some work early and say why, instead of slowing everyone.

A service with a queue that grows without bound answers late to every caller. Shedding is the
decision, taken before the work is queued, to reject a request that cannot succeed: the queue is
full, only important work is wanted now, or the request's deadline passes before it would be
served. `decide` is that decision as a pure function of the limits, the time, the current
queue length and the request, so every rule is a law of a function. The ledger makes it
idempotent per request id: a client that retries the same id gets the answer it got the first
time, even if the queue has changed meanwhile, so a retry cannot turn a refusal into a
double admission or an admission into a surprise. Time and queue length are arguments; the
caller reads them. Use it at the entry of any queue with callers who can retry or give up;
pair it with `retry_backoff` on the client side.

Public API:
```nim
type Priority = enum
  pLow, pHigh
type Request = object
  id*: string
  priority*: Priority
  deadline*: int             ## absolute tick by which the answer is useless to the caller
type Reason = enum
  rNoId, rExpired, rQueueFull, rLowPriorityShed, rDeadlineUnreachable
type Decision = object
  case admitted*: bool
  of true:
    nil
  of false:
    reason*: Reason
type Limits = object
type Ledger = object
func `==`(a, b: Decision): bool
func `==`(a, b: Ledger): bool
func initLimits(maxQueue, softQueue, ticksPerItem: int): Result[Limits, string]
func emptyLedger(): Ledger
func judge(l: Limits; now, queueLen: int; req: Request): Decision
func decide(ledger: Ledger; l: Limits; now, queueLen: int; req: Request): tuple[ledger: Ledger, decision: Decision]
func decidedCount(ledger: Ledger): int
func knows(ledger: Ledger; id: string): bool
```

Write the Nim module `mediator.nim` (Mediator).

Mediator: participants never address each other; a pure routing function does.

The OO pattern puts the knowledge of "who talks to whom" into one mediator object so the
colleagues stay decoupled. In Nim the colleagues are just names in a room value, a message is
data, and the mediator is `route(room, message)`, which returns the new room and the list of
deliveries (who receives what). Nothing is sent from inside; the caller performs the deliveries,
so the whole chat logic is testable without sockets. Use it when many parties interact by rules
(chat, form-field dependencies, air-traffic hand-offs). Members are kept sorted, so delivery
order is deterministic.

Public API:
```nim
type MsgKind = enum
  mkJoin, mkLeave, mkSay, mkWhisper
type Msg = object
  sender*: string
  case kind*: MsgKind
  of mkJoin, mkLeave:
    nil
  of mkSay:
    text*: string
  of mkWhisper:
    to*: string
    secret*: string
type Delivery = object
  to*: string
  body*: string
type Room = object
type RoomError = enum
  reAlreadyMember, reNotMember, reNoSuchRecipient, reSelfWhisper
type Routed = object
  room*: Room
  deliveries*: seq[Delivery]
type RunReport = object
  room*: Room
  deliveries*: seq[Delivery]
  rejected*: seq[(int, RoomError)] ## (index in the log, reason)
func `==`(a, b: Delivery): bool
func `==`(a, b: Room): bool
func `==`(a, b: Routed): bool
func `==`(a, b: RunReport): bool
func `$`(d: Delivery): string
func `$`(r: Room): string
func join(name: string): Msg
func leave(name: string): Msg
func say(name, text: string): Msg
func whisper(name, to, text: string): Msg
func emptyRoom(): Room
func members(r: Room): seq[string]
func has(r: Room; name: string): bool
func route(room: Room; m: Msg): Result[Routed, RoomError]
func runLog(room: Room; log: openArray[Msg]): RunReport
```

## Mediator: participants never address each other; a pure routing function does.
##
## The OO pattern puts the knowledge of "who talks to whom" into one mediator object so the
## colleagues stay decoupled. In Nim the colleagues are just names in a room value, a message is
## data, and the mediator is `route(room, message)`, which returns the new room and the list of
## deliveries (who receives what). Nothing is sent from inside; the caller performs the deliveries,
## so the whole chat logic is testable without sockets. Use it when many parties interact by rules
## (chat, form-field dependencies, air-traffic hand-offs). Members are kept sorted, so delivery
## order is deterministic.

import std/[algorithm, strutils]
import nimcs/fp/result

type
  MsgKind* = enum
    mkJoin, mkLeave, mkSay, mkWhisper

  Msg* = object
    sender*: string
    case kind*: MsgKind
    of mkJoin, mkLeave: discard
    of mkSay:
      text*: string
    of mkWhisper:
      to*: string
      secret*: string

  Delivery* = object
    to*: string
    body*: string

  Room* = object
    members: seq[string]   ## sorted, no duplicates

  RoomError* = enum
    reAlreadyMember, reNotMember, reNoSuchRecipient, reSelfWhisper

  Routed* = object
    room*: Room
    deliveries*: seq[Delivery]

  RunReport* = object
    room*: Room
    deliveries*: seq[Delivery]
    rejected*: seq[(int, RoomError)]   ## (index in the log, reason)

func `==`*(a, b: Delivery): bool {.raises: [].} = a.to == b.to and a.body == b.body
func `==`*(a, b: Room): bool {.raises: [].} = a.members == b.members
func `==`*(a, b: Routed): bool {.raises: [].} = a.room == b.room and a.deliveries == b.deliveries
func `==`*(a, b: RunReport): bool {.raises: [].} =
  a.room == b.room and a.deliveries == b.deliveries and a.rejected == b.rejected
func `$`*(d: Delivery): string {.raises: [].} = d.to & ": " & d.body
func `$`*(r: Room): string {.raises: [].} = "Room(" & r.members.join(",") & ")"

func join*(name: string): Msg {.raises: [].} = Msg(kind: mkJoin, sender: name)
func leave*(name: string): Msg {.raises: [].} = Msg(kind: mkLeave, sender: name)
func say*(name, text: string): Msg {.raises: [].} = Msg(kind: mkSay, sender: name, text: text)
func whisper*(name, to, text: string): Msg {.raises: [].} =
  Msg(kind: mkWhisper, sender: name, to: to, secret: text)

func emptyRoom*(): Room {.raises: [].} = Room(members: @[])
func members*(r: Room): seq[string] {.raises: [].} = r.members
func has*(r: Room; name: string): bool {.raises: [].} = name in r.members

func route*(room: Room; m: Msg): Result[Routed, RoomError] {.raises: [].} =
  ## The mediator. Joins and leaves are announced to everyone else; a say reaches every member but
  ## the sender; a whisper reaches exactly its recipient.
  case m.kind
  of mkJoin:
    if room.has(m.sender): return err(Routed, reAlreadyMember)
    let next = Room(members: (room.members & m.sender).sorted)
    var ds: seq[Delivery]
    for who in room.members: ds.add Delivery(to: who, body: m.sender & " joined")
    ok(Routed(room: next, deliveries: ds), RoomError)
  of mkLeave:
    if not room.has(m.sender): return err(Routed, reNotMember)
    var rest: seq[string]
    for who in room.members:
      if who != m.sender: rest.add who
    var ds: seq[Delivery]
    for who in rest: ds.add Delivery(to: who, body: m.sender & " left")
    ok(Routed(room: Room(members: rest), deliveries: ds), RoomError)
  of mkSay:
    if not room.has(m.sender): return err(Routed, reNotMember)
    var ds: seq[Delivery]
    for who in room.members:
      if who != m.sender: ds.add Delivery(to: who, body: m.sender & ": " & m.text)
    ok(Routed(room: room, deliveries: ds), RoomError)
  of mkWhisper:
    if not room.has(m.sender): return err(Routed, reNotMember)
    if m.to == m.sender: return err(Routed, reSelfWhisper)
    if not room.has(m.to): return err(Routed, reNoSuchRecipient)
    ok(Routed(room: room, deliveries: @[Delivery(to: m.to,
        body: m.sender & " (private): " & m.secret)]), RoomError)

func runLog*(room: Room; log: openArray[Msg]): RunReport {.raises: [].} =
  ## Routes a whole log. A message the room rejects delivers nothing and leaves the room as it
  ## was; its index and reason are listed in `rejected`, in log order, so nothing is lost.
  result = RunReport(room: room, deliveries: @[], rejected: @[])
  for i, m in log:
    let r = route(result.room, m)
    if r.isOk:
      result.room = r.value.room
      result.deliveries.add r.value.deliveries
    else:
      result.rejected.add (i, r.error)

Write the Nim module `memento.nim` (Memento).

Memento: a snapshot is just an old value.

The OO pattern exists because objects are mutable and hide their fields: to roll one back, you
need a sealed copy of its private state that only the object can open. With value semantics the
problem disappears: `let saved = settings` is the memento, later changes build *new* values and
cannot reach it. The guarantee holds for values made of value fields; a `ref` field is copied as a
pointer, so the data behind it is shared and a later change through the original shows in the
snapshot (GOF-MEMENTO-08). Keep snapshotted state free of mutable `ref`s, or rebuild the referent
when snapshotting. What is left to design is the history policy, shown here as `Timeline[T]`: the
values before the present, the present, the values that were undone, and a capacity so the past
cannot grow without bound. Use it for undo-by-snapshot of small or structurally shared values;
for large state or replication, store commands instead (see `command`).

Public API:
```nim
type Timeline[T] = object
func initTimeline[T](start: T; capacity: int): Timeline[T]
func current[T](t: Timeline[T]): T
func pastLen[T](t: Timeline[T]): int
func futureLen[T](t: Timeline[T]): int
func history[T](t: Timeline[T]): seq[T]
func record[T](t: Timeline[T]; v: T): Timeline[T]
func undo[T](t: Timeline[T]): Option[Timeline[T]]
func redo[T](t: Timeline[T]): Option[Timeline[T]]
```
output:
## Memento: a snapshot is just an old value.
##
## The OO pattern exists because objects are mutable and hide their fields: to roll one back, you
## need a sealed copy of its private state that only the object can open. With value semantics the
## problem disappears: `let saved = settings` is the memento, later changes build *new* values and
## cannot reach it. The guarantee holds for values made of value fields; a `ref` field is copied as a
## pointer, so the data behind it is shared and a later change through the original shows in the
## snapshot (GOF-MEMENTO-08). Keep snapshotted state free of mutable `ref`s, or rebuild the referent
## when snapshotting. What is left to design is the history policy, shown here as `Timeline[T]`: the
## values before the present, the present, the values that were undone, and a capacity so the past
## cannot grow without bound. Use it for undo-by-snapshot of small or structurally shared values;
## for large state or replication, store commands instead (see `command`).

import std/options

type
  Timeline*[T] = object
    past: seq[T]      ## oldest first
    present: T
    future: seq[T]    ## the value to redo next is last
    capacity: int     ## at most this many past values are kept (>= 1)

func initTimeline*[T](start: T; capacity: int): Timeline[T] {.raises: [].} =
  ## `capacity` below 1 is raised to 1 so that one undo is always possible.
  Timeline[T](past: @[], present: start, future: @[], capacity: max(1, capacity))

func current*[T](t: Timeline[T]): T {.raises: [].} = t.present
func pastLen*[T](t: Timeline[T]): int {.raises: [].} = t.past.len
func futureLen*[T](t: Timeline[T]): int {.raises: [].} = t.future.len
func history*[T](t: Timeline[T]): seq[T] {.raises: [].} =
  ## Oldest first, ending with the present.
  t.past & t.present

func record*[T](t: Timeline[T]; v: T): Timeline[T] {.raises: [].} =
  ## Makes `v` the present. The old present becomes the newest past value, the oldest past value
  ## is dropped when the capacity is exceeded, and redo is cleared.
  var past = t.past & t.present
  if past.len > t.capacity: past = past[past.len - t.capacity .. ^1]
  Timeline[T](past: past, present: v, future: @[], capacity: t.capacity)

func undo*[T](t: Timeline[T]): Option[Timeline[T]] {.raises: [].} =
  if t.past.len == 0: return none(Timeline[T])
  some(Timeline[T](past: t.past[0 ..< t.past.len - 1], present: t.past[^1],
                   future: t.future & t.present, capacity: t.capacity))

func redo*[T](t: Timeline[T]): Option[Timeline[T]] {.raises: [].} =
  if t.future.len == 0: return none(Timeline[T])
  some(Timeline[T](past: t.past & t.present, present: t.future[^1],
                   future: t.future[0 ..< t.future.len - 1], capacity: t.capacity))

Write the Nim module `model_view_update.nim` (Model, view, update).

Model, view, update (the Elm architecture): state, a pure transition and a pure rendering.

All state is one `Model` value. Everything that can happen is a `Msg` (a closed variant). The
program is two functions: `update(model, msg): model` says what each message does, and
`view(model): string` says what the model looks like. Neither performs an effect, so a session
is a list of messages and nothing else: `replay` folds the list, the same log always gives the
same model and the same screen, and `trace` gives every intermediate model for time-travel
debugging and for bug reports that are just a log. The effects (reading keys, drawing the
string) stay in a thin loop outside. Use it for interactive state with many events (a form, a
game, an editor buffer); for one value that changes once, a function is enough. The example is
a counter with a step size and an undo stack.

Public API:
```nim
type Model = object
  count*: int
  step*: int                 ## always in `MinStep .. MaxStep`, see `update`
  history*: seq[int]         ## earlier counts, newest last, for `mUndo`
type MsgKind = enum
  mIncrement, mDecrement, mSetStep, mUndo, mReset
type Msg = object
  case kind*: MsgKind
  of mSetStep:
    step*: int
  of mIncrement, mDecrement, mUndo, mReset:
    nil
const MinStep = 1
const MaxStep = 10
func init(): Model
func increment(): Msg
func decrement(): Msg
func setStep(n: int): Msg
func undo(): Msg
func reset(): Msg
func update(m: Model; msg: Msg): Model
func view(m: Model): string
func replay(log: openArray[Msg]; start = init()): Model
func trace(log: openArray[Msg]; start = init()): seq[Model]
```
output:
## Model, view, update (the Elm architecture): state, a pure transition and a pure rendering.
##
## All state is one `Model` value. Everything that can happen is a `Msg` (a closed variant). The
## program is two functions: `update(model, msg): model` says what each message does, and
## `view(model): string` says what the model looks like. Neither performs an effect, so a session
## is a list of messages and nothing else: `replay` folds the list, the same log always gives the
## same model and the same screen, and `trace` gives every intermediate model for time-travel
## debugging and for bug reports that are just a log. The effects (reading keys, drawing the
## string) stay in a thin loop outside. Use it for interactive state with many events (a form, a
## game, an editor buffer); for one value that changes once, a function is enough. The example is
## a counter with a step size and an undo stack.

type
  Model* = object
    count*: int
    step*: int          ## always in `MinStep .. MaxStep`, see `update`
    history*: seq[int]  ## earlier counts, newest last, for `mUndo`

  MsgKind* = enum
    mIncrement, mDecrement, mSetStep, mUndo, mReset

  Msg* = object
    case kind*: MsgKind
    of mSetStep:
      step*: int
    of mIncrement, mDecrement, mUndo, mReset:
      discard

const
  MinStep* = 1
  MaxStep* = 10

func init*(): Model {.raises: [].} = Model(count: 0, step: 1, history: @[])

func increment*(): Msg {.raises: [].} = Msg(kind: mIncrement)
func decrement*(): Msg {.raises: [].} = Msg(kind: mDecrement)
func setStep*(n: int): Msg {.raises: [].} = Msg(kind: mSetStep, step: n)
func undo*(): Msg {.raises: [].} = Msg(kind: mUndo)
func reset*(): Msg {.raises: [].} = Msg(kind: mReset)

func update*(m: Model; msg: Msg): Model {.raises: [].} =
  ## One transition. Total: every model and message gives a model; a step outside the range is
  ## clamped, an undo with nothing to undo changes nothing, and a reset forgets the history.
  case msg.kind
  of mIncrement:
    Model(count: m.count + m.step, step: m.step, history: m.history & m.count)
  of mDecrement:
    Model(count: m.count - m.step, step: m.step, history: m.history & m.count)
  of mSetStep:
    Model(count: m.count, step: min(max(msg.step, MinStep), MaxStep), history: m.history)
  of mUndo:
    if m.history.len == 0: m
    else: Model(count: m.history[^1], step: m.step, history: m.history[0 ..< m.history.high])
  of mReset:
    Model(count: 0, step: m.step, history: @[])

func view*(m: Model): string {.raises: [].} =
  ## The whole screen as text, a function of the model alone.
  "count=" & $m.count & " step=" & $m.step & " undo=" & $m.history.len

func replay*(log: openArray[Msg]; start = init()): Model {.raises: [].} =
  ## The model after the messages, in order, from `start`.
  result = start
  for msg in log:
    result = result.update(msg)

func trace*(log: openArray[Msg]; start = init()): seq[Model] {.raises: [].} =
  ## `log.len + 1` models: the start, then the model after each message.
  var cur = start
  result.add cur
  for msg in log:
    cur = cur.update(msg)
    result.add cur
